Brolin, Senior Staff Attorney, Division of Regulations and Legislation, Office of General Counsel, at 1775 Duke Street, Alexandria, VA 22314 or by telephone at (703) 518-6540.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
In response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the Board issued an IFR on April 29, 2020 (April 29th IFR), which provided credit unions with greater access to liquidity to help ensure they remain operational throughout the crisis.
[
1
]
The IFR made it easier and more attractive for credit unions to join the NCUA's CLF. In addition, the rule made several amendments to conform to the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security Act (CARES Act).
[
2
]
The CLF, a mixed-ownership government corporation managed by the Board, established in 1979, serves as a liquidity source for its member credit unions.
[
3
]
Its purpose is to improve general financial stability by meeting the liquidity needs of credit unions and thereby encouraging savings, supporting consumer and mortgage lending, and providing basic financial resources to all segments of the economy.
Section 307 of the FCU Act,
12 U.S.C. 1795f
, among other things, gives the Board the authority to prescribe the manner in which the general business of the CLF shall be conducted and to prescribe rules and regulations to carry out the CLF-related provisions of the FCU Act.
[
4
]
Under this authority, the Board issued the April 29th IFR to enhance liquidity for credit unions during the COVID-19 pandemic and to make regulatory changes that cohere to the CARES Act.
The Board emphasized in the April 29th IFR that, while some of the amendments in the rule were temporary, they would afford significant liquidity support to the entire credit union system. The Board also noted that several of the changes in the IFR were conforming changes based on the recently enacted CARES Act, which temporarily amended the FCU Act. As such, the changes in the IFR that corresponded to the CARES Act were initially set to sunset in accordance with the CARES Act on December 31, 2020. To provide clarity and transparency, the Board included the temporary changes in the IFR and explained what would occur upon the sunset of the amendments.
(
printed page 65482)
In December 2020, the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2021 (CAA) was passed by Congress.
[
5
]
The CAA, among other things, extended the sunset date of the CLF enhancements made by the CARES Act until December 31, 2021.
[
6
]
In response, the Board issued a second IFR on March 24, 2021 (March 24th IFR), to amend its regulations to reflect the extensions.
[
7
]
The March 24th IFR responded to comments on the April 29th IFR and also extended the withdrawal from CLF membership provisions that the Board included in the April 29th IFR.
The Board received 15 comments in response to the April 29th IFR and the March 24th IFR. All the comments supported the IFRs. The comments also requested legislative changes, other changes outside the scope of the IFRs, or both.
In addition to the changes made by the April 29th IFR and the March 24th IFR, the proposal would also remove or modify certain filing requirements and criteria the Board uses to approve CLF members. Finally, the proposal would amend the timing requirements related to pay adjustments to the capital stock subscription, clarify various regulatory provisions, and make necessary conforming edits. The changes to the NCUA's CLF regulations are discussed in more detail in the section-by-section analysis below.
B. Legal Authority
The Board has the legal authority to issue this proposed rule pursuant to its plenary rulemaking authority under the Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act) and its specific rulemaking authority under the various provisions the Board administers.
[
8
]
In particular, section 307 of the FCU Act,
12 U.S.C. 1795f
, gives the Board the authority to prescribe the manner in which the general business of the CLF shall be conducted and to prescribe rules and regulations to carry out the CLF-related provisions of the FCU Act.
[
9
]
II. Proposed Rule
A. Nomenclature Changes Throughout Part 725
Current part 725 uses the term “NCUA Board” and “Facility” interchangeably in numerous places throughout part 725. The Board acts through the CLF, a mixed-ownership government corporation within the NCUA, and the Office of the Board. They are separate offices, however, with separate duties and functions. The interchangeable use of terminology in part 725 causes confusion for members and applicants because it is sometimes unclear, in places where the term “NCUA Board” is used, whether the Board is acting through the CLF or the Office of the Board. The proposed rule would replace the term “NCUA Board” with the term “Facility” throughout part 725, unless the context indicates that the Board would be acting through the Office of the Board. Regardless of whether the term “NCUA Board” or “Facility” is used, actions carried out by the CLF pursuant to part 725 originate with the NCUA Board. Accordingly, the proposal would replace the term “NCUA Board” with the term “Facility” in current §§ 725.4(c)(1), (d), and (e); 725.5(c), (d), and (e); 725.6(a), (b), and the second and third sentences in paragraph (c); 725.17(b)(2)(iii); 725.22(a) and (b); 725.23(a) and (b).
B. Definition of “Facility Lending Officer” Under § 725.2(g)
Current § 725.2(g) defines the term “facility lending officer” as any employee of the CLF or the NCUA who has been designated by the NCUA Board as a Facility lending officer. The title Facility lending officer is antiquated and no longer used by the CLF. Accordingly, the proposal would remove this definition from § 725.2(g).
C. Definition of “Liquidity Needs” Under 725.2(i)
In accordance with the CARES Act, the April 29th IFR amended the definition of “liquidity needs” to remove the words “primarily serving natural persons.” This change was intended to mirror the statutory change in the CARES Act and clarified that liquidity needs are not limited to only natural person credit unions but may also include those of corporate credit unions or a corporate credit union group. The change allowed corporate credit unions to obtain loans for their own liquidity needs. The amendment was initially set to sunset in accordance with the CARES Act on December 31, 2020.
The CAA extended this provision in the CARES Act until December 31, 2021. To address this extension, the NCUA's March 24th IFR amended the regulatory definition of “liquidity needs” to make it clear when the definition under the CARES Act applied and when such definition would revert to the pre-CARES Act version after December 31, 2021.
Current § 725.2(i)(1) defines “liquidity needs” from April 29, 2020, to December 31, 2021, as the needs of credit unions for short-term adjustment credit available to assist in meeting temporary requirements for funds or to cushion more persistent outflows of funds pending an orderly adjustment of credit union assets and liabilities; seasonal credit available for longer periods to assist in meeting seasonal needs for funds arising from a combination of expected patterns of movement in share and deposit accounts and loans; and protracted adjustment credit available in the event of unusual or emergency circumstances of a longer-term nature resulting from national, regional, or local difficulties. Current § 725.2(i)(2) defines “liquidity needs” after December 31, 2021, as the needs of credit unions primarily serving natural persons for short-term adjustment credit available to assist in meeting temporary requirements for funds or to cushion more persistent outflows of funds pending an orderly adjustment of credit union assets and liabilities; seasonal credit available for longer periods to assist in meeting seasonal needs for funds arising from a combination of expected patterns of movement in share and deposit accounts and loans; and protracted adjustment credit available in the event of unusual or emergency circumstances of a longer-term nature resulting from national, regional, or local difficulties.
Given that the definition of liquidity needs under current § 725.2(i)(1) sunset on January 1, 2022, the Board is proposing to remove paragraph (i)(1) and replace it with the definition of liquidity needs under current § 725.2(i)(2). Accordingly, this proposal would amend § 725.2(i) to provide that “liquidity needs” means the needs of credit unions primarily serving natural persons for short-term adjustment credit available to assist in meeting temporary requirements for funds or to cushion more persistent outflows of funds pending an orderly adjustment of credit union assets and liabilities; seasonal credit available for longer periods to assist in meeting seasonal needs for funds arising from a combination of expected patterns of movement in share and deposit accounts and loans; and protracted adjustment credit available in the event of unusual or emergency circumstances of a longer-term nature resulting from national, regional, or local difficulties.
(
printed page 65483)
D. Requirement for Natural-Person Credit Unions To Furnish Certain Reports and Documents Under § 725.3(a)(3)
Current § 725.3(a)(3) requires that a natural-person credit union applying to become a regular member of the CLF furnish certain reports and documents with its completed membership application. In particular, the natural-person credit union must provide a copy of the credit union's financial and statistical report for the most recent calendar month; and copies of the credit union's charter and bylaws, unless the credit union is federally chartered. These requirements were adopted in nearly identical form in 1979.
[
10
]
NCUA has determined that it no longer needs to require that copies of such reports and documents be provided to the CLF for federally insured natural-person credit unions because copies of the reports and documents can already be obtained by the CLF through other means, in particular, through the NCUA's examination process. This is not the case, however, for non-federally insured natural-person credit unions. Accordingly, to streamline the NCUA's CLF regulations and eliminate outdated and unnecessary regulatory requirements, the NCUA is proposing to amend current § 725.3(a)(3) to provide that in the case of a non-federally insured natural-person credit union not otherwise subject to examination by the NCUA, the CLF may require that the credit union provide financial reports and other information to determine the financial condition of the credit union.
E. Regular Membership Requirements Under § 725.3(b)
Section 725.3(b) had previously provided that, with limited exception, any credit union that becomes a regular member of the CLF may not receive CLF advances, without approval of the Board, for six months after becoming a member. The April 29th IFR eliminated the six-month waiting period on obtaining CLF advances for a credit union that becomes a regular member. The Board continues to believe it was important to remove this restriction in response to the overarching need to make liquidity assistance timely and the advantages of accelerating liquidity-need loans to new members outweighed the practical reasons that having the waiting period afforded to the CLF's operations. Accordingly, the Board is proposing to adopt this change to § 725.3(b) as final.
F. Agent Membership in the CLF Under 725.4(a)(2)(ii)
The April 29th IFR, in accordance with the CARES Act, amended the nature of the requirement for a corporate credit union or group of corporate credit unions to subscribe to the capital stock of the CLF in an amount equal to one-half of one percent of the paid-in and unimpaired capital and surplus of all of the corporate credit union's or corporate credit union group's natural person credit union members. This change to prior § 725.4(a)(2) mirrored the statutory change in the CARES Act and allowed the Board, in its sole discretion, to determine which grouping of natural person member credit unions of the applying corporate credit union or corporate credit union group were considered covered by the agent's membership in the CLF. In turn, the approved group was the basis for calculating the amount of CLF capital stock the corporate credit union or corporate credit union group was required to purchase. This change provided a corporate credit union with the flexibility to subscribe to the capital stock of the CLF up to the maximum extent it could afford to do so.
This amendment was initially set to sunset in accordance with the CARES Act on December 31, 2020. Upon the sunset of the amendment, any corporate credit union or corporate credit union group that became an agent member under this provision was required to, within one year from the sunset date, either (1) purchase CLF stock in accordance with the terms of the regulation as written post-sunset of the CARES Act amendments; or (2) terminate its membership in the CLF. The Board believed that the two options accounted for the temporary nature of the CARES Act amendments while not causing undue disruption to the operations of a corporate credit union or corporate credit union group that joined the CLF under the CARES Act amendments.
The CAA extended this provision in the CARES Act until December 31, 2021.
[
11
]
To address this extension, the NCUA's March 24th IFR amended § 725.4(a)(2) to make conforming date changes to the section.
Current § 725.4(a)(2)(ii) sunset on January 1, 2022. Upon the sunset of the amendment, any corporate credit union or corporate credit union group that became an agent member under this provision was required, before January 1, 2023, to either (1) purchase CLF stock in accordance with the terms of the regulation as written post-sunset of the CARES Act amendments; or (2) terminate its membership in the CLF. It has been over two years since the January 1, 2023, deadline passed, giving credit unions ample time to comply with the requirements of current § 725.4(a)(2)(ii). Accordingly, this proposal would remove the language in current § 725.4(a)(2)(ii) and renumber the section to conform with this change.
G. Agent Member Borrowing Under §§ 725.4(a)(2), 725.18(a) and (d), 725.19(a) and (b)
To effectuate the intent of the CARES Act in a safe and sound manner, the April 29th IFR included a clarifying amendment to § 725.4(a)(2). Section 725.4(a)(2)(iii) clarified that, from April 29, 2020, until December 31, 2020, an agent member may borrow from the CLF for its own liquidity needs but, to do so, the agent must first subscribe to the capital stock of the CLF in an amount equal to one-half of one percent of the Agent's own paid-in and unimpaired capital and surplus.
[
12
]
Paragraph (a)(2)(iii) provided further that upon approval of the application, the Agent shall forward funds equal to one-half of this stock subscription to the CLF. Paragraph (a)(2)(iii) also provided that this amount shall be in addition to the amounts required by paragraph (a)(2)(i) or (ii) of § 725.4, if a corporate credit union or corporate credit union group joined the CLF as an Agent and intended to borrow for its own liquidity needs. Finally, paragraph (a)(2)(iii) provided that any corporate credit union or corporate credit union group that received a CLF advance for its own liquidity need under the temporary requirements set forth in this paragraph must, as of January 1, 2021, and thereafter, not request any additional CLF advances for its own liquidity needs and continue to follow the terms of the CLF advance agreement entered into between the Agent and the CLF. The Board believed the inclusion of this provision appropriately accounted for the temporary nature of this provision while assuring agents that loan agreements made during this period will not also be subject to a sunset provision or be terminated before maturity. The Board believed the provision struck the appropriate balance between congressional intent and the tenets of contract law.
(
printed page 65484)
Pursuant to the extension provided in the CAA, the Board's March 24th IFR extended the periods in § 725.4(a)(2)(iii) to end on January 1, 2022. The expanded authority provided for in current paragraph (a)(2)(iii) has expired by its own terms and no loans remain outstanding. Accordingly, this proposal would remove the language in current § 725.4(a)(2)(iii) and renumber the section to conform with this change.
H. Application Requirements for Corporate Credit Unions Under § 725.4(a)(3) Through (a)(6)
Current § 725.4(a)(3) through (a)(6) set forth certain requirements that a corporate credit union or a group of corporate credit unions applying to become an Agent member of the CLF must follow. In particular, current paragraph (a)(3) requires the applicant to furnish a copy of the corporate credit union's or unions' financial and statistical report for the most recent calendar month; copies of the credit union's or unions' charter and bylaws, unless such credit union is federally chartered; and a list of all the credit union's or unions' member natural person credit unions. Current paragraph (a)(4) requires the applicant to agree to submit to the supervision of the Board and to comply with all regulations and reporting requirements which the Board shall prescribe for Agent members. Current paragraph (a)(5) requires the applicant to agree to submit to periodic unrestricted examinations by the Board or its designee. Current paragraph (a)(6) requires the applicant to obtain the written approval of the Board. These requirements were adopted in nearly identical form in 1979.
[
13
]
Copies of the aforementioned reports, documents, agreements, and written approvals remains necessary for the CLF to approve a corporate credit union or group of corporate credit unions' application to become an agent member of the CLF. For a federally insured corporate credit union or a federally insured group of corporate credit unions, however, copies of the credit union's or unions' financial and statistical report for the most recent calendar month, copies of the credit union's or unions' charter and bylaws, and a list of all the credit union's or unions' member natural person credit unions are already available to the CLF through the examination process. In addition, the examination and reporting provisions under current paragraphs (a)(4) and (a)(5) are already codified in the FCU Act.
[
14
]
Finally, while approval of the Board is required under the FCU Act,
[
15
]
the NCUA believes including an express requirement that the Board approval must be in writing as currently required under paragraph (b)(6) is unnecessary. Accordingly, to streamline the NCUA's CLF regulations and eliminate outdated and unnecessary regulatory requirements, the NCUA is proposing to remove current § 725.4(a)(3) through (a)(6) in their entirety.
For non-federally insured corporate credit unions,
[
16
]
however, the NCUA would not already have a copy of the credit union's or unions' financial and statistical report for the most recent calendar month, copies of the credit union's or unions' charter and bylaws, or a list of all the credit union's or unions' member natural person credit unions, which are currently required under 725.4(a)(3). To ensure that the CLF can obtain copies of this information as part of the Agent application process, the Board is proposing to generally retain the requirements in current paragraph (a)(3), but for only non-federally insured corporate credit unions credit unions not otherwise subject to NCUA examination. Proposed new paragraph (a)(3) would provide that in the case of a non-federally insured corporate credit union not otherwise subject to examination by the NCUA, the CLF may require that the credit union provide financial reports and other information to determine the financial condition of the credit union.
I. Criteria Corporate Credit Unions Must Meet To Be Agent Members Under § 725.4(b)
Current § 725.4(b) requires that the Board may approve a corporate credit union or group of corporate credit unions as an Agent member if certain criteria are met. In particular, a corporate credit union or each corporate credit union in a group must meet the following criteria:
1. The management policies are in writing, approved by the corporate credit union's board of directors, and reviewed annually by such board;
2. Adequate internal controls are in place to assure accurate and timely reporting of transactions and the safeguarding of assets;
3. The financial condition of the corporate credit union is sound with adequate reserves for losses;
4. Surety bond coverage provides protection for the corporate credit union while the corporate credit union is performing the duties of an Agent member of the CLF;
5. Management has demonstrated its ability to use such techniques as cash flow analysis, budgeting, and projections of sources and uses of funds to manage the affairs of the corporate credit union efficiently and in conformity with sound business practices; and
6. There are no practices, procedures, policies, or other factors that would result in discrimination by the corporate credit union among natural person credit unions or inhibit its ability to act independently in its role as an Agent member of the CLF.
The criteria listed in paragraph (b) were originally adopted in a 1979 final rule regarding CLF membership and lending.
[
17
]
A comprehensive explanation of how or why the criteria were chosen was not provided.
[
18
]
The criteria, however, appear to have been adopted to implement
12 U.S.C. 1795c(b)(1)
, which requires that an agent member of the CLF “obtain[ ] the approval of the Board.” While Board approval is required under the Federal Credit Union Act, the particular criteria listed in § 725.4(b) are not expressly listed in the Act. After careful review of the criteria, the Board has determined that the list of criteria is obsolete and does not provide a full, accurate list of all the criteria that should be considered, particularly since extensions of credit sometimes requires additional analysis to protect the CLF. Accordingly, the Board is proposing to remove current paragraph (b) to streamline the NCUA's CLF regulations and eliminate outdated regulatory requirements. Consistent with the
(
printed page 65485)
removal of paragraph (b), the proposed rule would renumber the remaining paragraphs in § 725.4.
J. Independent Audits of Books and Records Under § 725.4(d)
Current § 725.4(d) requires that each Agent, or in the case of an Agent group, each corporate credit union in the group, must have on an annual basis a third-party independent audit of its books and records and provide the CLF with copies of the report of such audit. Paragraph (d) provides further that the auditor selected must be recognized by a State or territorial licensing authority as possessing the requisite knowledge and experience to perform audits. Section 704.15 already requires that federally insured corporate credit unions provide independently audited financial statements to the NCUA. The Board believes duplicating that requirement in current § 725.4(d) is redundant and unnecessary. No such requirement exists, however, for non-federally insured corporate credit unions. Accordingly, to eliminate outdated, duplicative, and unnecessary regulatory requirements, the Board is proposing to revise the language in current § 725.4(d) to limit its application to only non-federally insured corporate credit unions. Accordingly, the Board is proposing to revise the language in current paragraph (d) to provide that each non-federally insured Agent, or in the case of an Agent group, each non-federally insured corporate credit union in the group, must have on an annual basis a third-party independent audit of its books and records and provide the CLF with copies of the report of such audit. The proposed language would provide further that the auditor selected must be recognized by a State or territorial licensing authority as possessing the requisite knowledge and experience to perform audits. Consistent with other edits discussed above to § 725.4, current paragraph (d) would be renumbered as paragraph (c).
K. Limit on CLF Advances for Six Months After Membership Under § 725.4(f)
Current § 725.4(f) provides that a corporate credit union or group of corporate credit unions which becomes an Agent member of the CLF after February 23, 1980, may not receive a CLF advance without approval of the CLF for a period of six months after becoming a member. The date, February 23, 1980, has long since past and is no longer necessary in paragraph (f). Accordingly, to streamline the NCUA's CLF regulations and eliminate outdated and unnecessary provisions, the Board is proposing to remove the reference to February 23, 1980, in its entirety. No substantiative changes to the requirements of paragraph (f) are intended by this amendment. Consistent with the other edits discussed above to § 725.4, current paragraph (f) would be renumbered as paragraph (e).
L. Payments to the Capital Stock Subscription Under § 725.5(b)(2)
Current § 725.5(b)(2) requires, among other things, that payments for adjustments to the capital stock subscription must be received by the CLF no later than March 31 of the following year. This timing requirement is overly restrictive and has led to unnecessarily difficult turn-round times for both CLF members and CLF staff. The NCUA Board believes that providing additional time for calculating, processing, and making such payments would benefit CLF members and CLF staff. Accordingly, the NCUA is proposing to amend the last sentence in current § 725.5(b)(2) to provide that payments for adjustments must be received within 90 calendar days of receipt of a capital stock subscription invoice from the CLF.
M. Termination of Membership Under 725.6
The April 29th IFR amended the waiting periods for a credit union to terminate its membership in the CLF between April 29, 2020, and January 1, 2022. Under the FCU Act and prior § 725.6 of the NCUA's regulations, a credit union member could terminate its membership after a specified time based on that credit union's stock subscription in the CLF. Previously, a member of the CLF could terminate its membership as follows:
1. Six months after notifying the Board in writing of its intention to do so, if the member's stock subscription constituted less than five percent of total subscribed CLF stock; or
2. Twenty-four months after notifying the Board in writing of its intention to do so if the member's stock subscription constituted five percent or more of total subscribed CLF stock.
[
19
]
The April 29th IFR amended § 725.6 to temporarily permit a credit union, regardless of its percentage amount of stock subscription, to withdraw from membership in the CLF after notifying the Board in writing on the earlier of the following:
(A) six months from the date of its written notice to the Board; or
(B) December 31, 2020.
Further, the April 29th IFR amended the NCUA's regulations to allow any credit union that remained a member after December 31, 2020, to withdraw from membership immediately upon notifying the Board in writing of its intent to do so. The Board noted that such an immediate withdrawal period would expire on December 31, 2021. After December 31, 2021, the termination requirements of current paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section would be reinstated and apply to all members. The Board believed that this flexibility was necessary to encourage the greatest number of eligible credit unions to join the CLF.
The March 24th IFR extended the termination of membership provisions described above until January 1, 2023. Pursuant to self-executing language in the April 29th IFR and the March 24th IFR, the provisions expired on January 1, 2023, and were removed from § 725.6 of the NCUA's regulations by the
Federal Register
in 2023. Thus, this proposed rule would not affect these provisions.
N. Agent Member Borrowing Under § 725.17(b)(2)(iv)
The April 29th IFR amended § 725.17 to add new paragraph (b)(2)(iv), which clarified that an agent may apply for a CLF advance based on the applicant agent's own liquidity needs. Pursuant to the extensions provided by the CAA, the Board's March 24th IFR amended paragraph (b)(2)(iv) further to provide that an agent may apply for a CLF advance based on the applicant agent's own liquidity needs, for the period beginning April 29, 2020, and ending on December 31, 2021. The March 24th IFR provided further that, after this period, an agent is prohibited from submitting an application for an extension for its own liquidity needs. Given the provision in current paragraph (b)(2)(iv) ended by its own terms on December 31, 2021, this proposal would amend § 725.17 to remove the paragraph from the NCUA's regulations.
O. Applications for Extensions of Credit Under § 725.17(a) and (b)
Current § 725.17(a) provides that a Regular member may apply for a CLF advance to meet its liquidity needs by filing an application on a CLF-approved form, or by any other method approved by the CLF. Current § 725.17(b)(1) provides in relevant part that an Agent member may apply for a CLF advance by filing an application on a CLF-approved form, or by any other method approved by the CLF. Footnote 4 at the end of paragraph (b)(1) provides further that if the Agent is an Agent group, the
(
printed page 65486)
application must be filed by the Agent group representative, and any CLF advance will be made to the Agent group representative. To streamline the NCUA's CLF regulations and eliminate outdated and unnecessary provisions, the Board is proposing to merge the language in paragraphs (a) and (b)(1) into a revised paragraph (a) and to also incorporate into revised paragraph (a) the text of footnote 4. Proposed § 725.17(a) would provide that a Regular member or Agent member may apply for a CLF advance to meet its liquidity needs by filing an application on a CLF-approved form, or by any other method approved by the CLF. Proposed paragraph (a) would provide further that if the Agent is an Agent group, the application must be filed by the Agent group representative and the advance will be made to the representative.
P. Agent Member Borrowing Under §§ 725.18 and 725.19
The April 29th IFR made conforming changes to §§ 725.18 and 725.19 to clarify the requirements applicable to a CLF advance to an agent for such agent's own needs. In particular, the IFR amended § 725.18(a) to provide that, prior to CLF approval of each application of a regular member for a CLF advance or an agent member for a CLF advance for such agent member's own need, the CLF shall consider the creditworthiness of such member. The Board's March 24th IFR clarified paragraph (a) to provide that, prior to CLF approval of each application of a regular member for a CLF advance or an agent member for a CLF advance for such agent member's own need (provided such agent may submit an application under § 725.17(b)(2)(iv)), the CLF shall consider the creditworthiness of such member. Given the provisions in  § 725.17(b)(2)(iv) lapsed on January 1, 2022, this proposal would amend current § 725.18(a) to remove the conforming and clarifying changes made by both the April 29th IFR and the March 24th IFR. Accordingly, current paragraph (a) would provide that, prior to CLF approval of each application of a regular member for a CLF advance, the CLF shall consider the creditworthiness of such member.
In addition, the April 29th IFR amended § 725.18(d) to provide that a credit union (whether a regular member of the CLF, agent member, or a member natural person credit union) that does not meet the CLF's creditworthiness standards may be limited in or denied the use of advances for its liquidity needs. The March 24th IFR clarified paragraph (d) to provide that a credit union (whether a regular member of the CLF, agent member (provided such agent may submit an application under § 725.17(b)(2)(iv), or a member natural person credit union) which does not meet the CLF's creditworthiness standards may be limited in or denied the use of advances for its liquidity needs. Given the provisions in § 725.17(b)(2)(iv) lapsed on January 1, 2022, this proposal would amend current § 725.18(d) to remove the conforming and clarifying changes made by both the April 29th IFR and the March 24th IFR. Accordingly, current paragraph (d) would provide that a natural person credit union (whether a regular member of the CLF or a member natural person credit union) which does not meet the CLF's creditworthiness standards may be limited in or denied the use of advances for its liquidity needs.
The April 29th IFR also made conforming changes to § 725.19(a) to provide that each CLF advance and each agent loan shall be secured by a first priority security interest in collateral of the credit union with a net book value at least equal to an amount as required by the CLF's collateral table, published at
www.NCUA.gov
,
or by guarantee of the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund (NCUSIF). The amendments to paragraph (a) also reduced the amount of collateral required for certain assets used to secure each CLF advance and each agent loan. Section 725.19 previously required that each CLF advance and each agent loan be secured by a first priority security interest in collateral of the credit union with a net-book value at least equal to 110 percent of all amounts due under the applicable CLF advance or agent loan, or by guarantee of the NCUSIF. The collateral table varies the required collateral percentages based upon different types of assets, and in some cases requires less than 110 percent. Depending on the types of assets a member has available to secure an advance request, lowering the collateral requirement for certain types of assets eased the collateral requirements and permitted a greater amount of borrowing overall. The Board replaced the 110 percent requirement with a requirement that a credit union collateralize a CLF advance or agent loan per the CLF collateral table posted on the NCUA's website,
www.NCUA.gov
.
This proposed rule would adopts as final the conforming changes to § 725.19(a) by the April 29th IFR.
The April 29th IFR also made conforming changes to § 725.19(b) to provide that the CLF may accept as collateral for each CLF advance to a regular member or to an agent member, for such agent member's own needs, a security interest in all assets of the member; provided, however, that the value of any assets in which any third party has a perfected security interest that is superior to the security interest of the CLF shall be excluded for purposes of complying with the requirements. Given the provisions in § 725.17(b)(2)(iv) lapsed on January 1, 2022, this proposal would amend current § 725.19(b) to remove the conforming changes made by the April 29th IFR. Accordingly, § 725.19(b) would provide that the CLF may accept as collateral for each CLF advance to a regular member, a security interest in all assets of the regular member; provided, however, that the value of any assets in which any third party has a perfected security interest that is superior to the security interest of the CLF shall be excluded for purposes of complying with the requirements.
Q. Collateral Requirements Under § 725.19(a)
Current § 725.19(a) provides that each CLF advance and each Agent loan shall be secured by a first-priority security interest in collateral of the credit union with a net value at least equal to an amount as required by the CLF's collateral margins table, published at
www.NCUA.gov
,
or by guarantee of the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund. To account for the CLF's preferred use of terminology with regard to the terms “net book value” and “collateral table,” the proposed rule would amend § 725.19(a) to instead use the more commonly used terms “net value” and “collateral margins table.” Accordingly, the proposal would amend § 725.19(a) to provide that each CLF advance and each agent loan shall be secured by a first-priority security interest in collateral of the credit union with a net value at least equal to an amount as required by the CLF's collateral margins table, published at
www.NCUA.gov
,
or by guarantee of the NCUSIF.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023
The Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023 (
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
) (Act) requires that a notice of proposed rulemaking include the internet address of a summary of not more than 100 words in length of a proposed rule, in plain language, that shall be posted on the internet website under section 206(d) of the E-Government Act of 2002 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
(
printed page 65487)
note) (commonly known as
regulations.gov
).
The proposed rule would adopt as final the revisions to the CLF rule made under two IFRs published on April 29, 2020, and March 24, 2021. The proposal would adopt the amendments made by these IFRs and, where appropriate, would remove provisions from the NCUA's regulations that have lapsed under the terms of the IFRs. The proposal would also remove or modify certain filing requirements and criteria the Board uses to approve CLF members. Finally, the proposal would amend the timing requirements related to pay adjustments to the capital stock subscription, clarify various regulatory provisions, and make necessary conforming edits.
The proposal and the required summary can be found at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
B. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, 14192
Pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
20
]
Executive Order 13563
(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
21
]
This proposed rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563
. OIRA has determined that this proposed rule is not a “significant regulatory action” as defined by section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
.
Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
22
]
This proposed rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
.
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
23
]
generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
24
]
For purposes of this analysis, the NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
25
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
This proposed rule would adopt certain IFR changes as final and remove certain criteria the Board requires to approve CLF members. These amendments would not impose any requirements on regulated entities, particularly not small entities. Accordingly, the NCUA certifies the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
D. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget control number. The PRA applies to rulemakings in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information-collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. The NCUA has determined that the changes addressed in this notice do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
E.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages certain agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests. The proposed rule would adopt as final the amendments made by two IFRs and, where appropriate, removes provisions from the NCUA's regulations that have lapsed under the terms of the IFRs. In addition, the proposed rule would remove certain criteria the Board requires to approve CLF members. Any effect on the states, on the relationship between the National Government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government does not rise to the level of material impact for purposed of
Executive Order 13132
.
F. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
The NCUA has determined that this proposed rule will not affect family well-being within the meaning of section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999,
Public Law 105-277
, 112 Stat. 2681 (1998) given that the proposed rule would implement changes already made to the NCUA's regulations through the April 29, 2020, and March 24, 2021 IFRs, and would remove certain criteria the Board requires to approve CLF members.

AGENCY:
National Credit Union Administration (NCUA).
ACTION:
Proposed rule.
SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) is proposing to amend the NCUA's regulations regarding incidental powers to clarify that federal credit unions (FCUs) are not required to seek an advisory opinion from the NCUA's Office of General Counsel before petitioning the Board to engage in an activity that does not fall within an FCU's preapproved incidental powers.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Introduction
A. Background
The Federal Credit Union Act (FCU Act) expressly grants FCUs the power to, among other activities, purchase, hold, and dispose of property; make loans to members; make certain investments; accept share, share draft, and share certificate accounts; and sell and cash negotiable instruments.
[
1
]
The accompanying incidental powers provision states that an FCU may “exercise such incidental powers as shall be necessary or requisite to enable it to carry on effectively the business for which it is incorporated.”
[
2
]
In 2001, the NCUA adopted regulations providing that FCUs could seek advisory opinions from the NCUA's General Counsel as to whether a proposed incidental powers activity fits into one of the preapproved categories of incidental powers under § 721.3 of the NCUA's regulations.
[
3
]
It also established a process for FCUs to petition the NCUA to approve new activities or categories of activities.
[
4
]
It is clear from the preamble to the 2001 rulemaking that seeking a legal opinion from the NCUA's General Counsel is optional.
[
5
]
A great deal of confusion has arisen, however, regarding whether FCUs are required to obtain an advisory opinion from the NCUA's Office of General Counsel before petitioning the Board.
The Board periodically amends rules to clarify confusing information. Consistent with confusion experienced by FCUs as a result of the language in § 721.4(a) regarding obtaining legal opinion letters, this proposed rule would remove the language regarding obtaining an advisory opinion before petitioning the Board. The Board invites comments on all aspects of this proposal.
B. Legal Authority
The Board has the legal authority to issue this proposed rule pursuant to its plenary rulemaking authority under the FCU Act and its specific rulemaking authority under the various acts the Board administers.
[
6
]
II. Proposed Rule
A. 721.1 What activities does this part cover?
Current § 721.1 provides, among other things, that part 721 describes how interested parties may request a legal opinion from the NCUA's Office of General Counsel on whether an activity is within an FCU's incidental powers or apply to add new activities or categories to the regulation. The section provides further that an activity determined to be an incidental power for an FCU in an NCUA legal opinion to an interested party, or as a result of an application by an interested party to add new activities or categories, is recognized as an incidental powers activity for all FCUs. For reasons explained in more detail in the part of the preamble on § 721.4, the NCUA is proposing to remove from § 721.1 the language regarding obtaining legal opinions from the NCUA. This information has caused confusion for the credit union industry in the past and is unnecessary. Accordingly, the proposal would amend § 721.1 to provide that part 721 authorizes an FCU to engage in activities incidental to its business as set out in part 721. The section would provide further that part 721 also describes how interested parties may apply to add new activities or categories to the regulation. The section would also provide that an activity approved as a result of an application by an interested party to add new activities or categories is recognized as an incidental powers activity for all FCUs. Finally, the section would provide that part 721 does not apply to the activities of corporate credit unions.
B. § 721.4 How may a credit union apply to engage in an activity that is not preapproved as within a credit union's incidental powers?
Current § 721.4(a) provides, among other things, that to engage in an activity that may be within an FCU's incidental powers but that does not fall within a preapproved category listed in § 721.3, an FCU may submit an application to the Board. Paragraph (a) also outlines what information an application must contain and states that before an FCU engages in the petition process it
should
seek an advisory opinion from the NCUA's Office of General Counsel as to whether a proposed activity fits into one of the authorized categories or is otherwise
(
printed page 65480)
within the FCU's incidental powers without filing a petition to amend the regulation.
[
7
]
The last sentence in paragraph (a) and its use of the word “should” has caused confusion for FCUs wishing to petition the Board to engage in a non-preapproved incidental power. FCUs are often unsure whether seeking an advisory opinion is mandatory or optional. As the NCUA made clear in its 2001 final rule regarding incidental powers, an FCU is not required to obtain an opinion from the NCUA's Office of General Counsel before petitioning the Board.
[
8
]
Moreover, credit unions are always able to ask the NCUA's Office of General Counsel questions on any provisions within the NCUA's regulations, not just with regard to part 721. It is commonly known throughout the credit union industry that credit unions, members, and other interested parties can contact the NCUA's Office of General Counsel, and the contact information for the office is easy to find and clearly displayed on the NCUA's website. Accordingly, consistent with other parts of the NCUA's regulations, the proposed rule would remove the last sentence of § 721.4(a) to clarify that FCUs are not required to obtain an advisory opinion from the NCUA's General Counsel's Office before submitting an application to the Board.
III. Regulatory Procedures
A. Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023
The Providing Accountability Through Transparency Act of 2023 (
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
) (Act) requires that a notice of proposed rulemaking include the internet address of a summary of not more than 100 words in length of a proposed rule, in plain language, that shall be posted on the internet website under section 206(d) of the E-Government Act of 2002 (
44 U.S.C. 3501 note
) (commonly known as
regulations.gov
). In summary, the proposed rule would amend the NCUA's regulations regarding incidental powers to clarify that FCUs are not required to seek a legal opinion from the NCUA's Office of General Counsel before petitioning the Board to engage in an activity that does not fall within an FCU's preapproved incidental powers.
The proposal and the required summary can be found at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
B. Executive Orders 12866, 13563, 14192

Executive Order 12866
(“Regulatory Planning and Review”), a determination must be made whether a regulatory action is significant and therefore subject to review by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA), within the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) in accordance with the requirements of the Executive Order.
[
9

(“Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review”) supplements and reaffirms the principles, structures, and definitions governing contemporary regulatory review established in
Executive Order 12866
.
[
10

This proposed rule was drafted and reviewed in accordance with
Executive Order 12866
and
Executive Order 13563

Executive Order 12866

Executive Order 14192
(“Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”) requires that any new incremental costs associated with new regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law, be offset by the elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior regulations.
[
11

This proposed rule is not an
Executive Order 14192
regulatory action because this rule is not significant under
Executive Order 12866
.
C. Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act
[
12
]
generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification.
[
13
]
For purposes of this analysis, the NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets.
[
14
]
The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
This proposed rule would amend the NCUA's incidental powers regulation to remove references to an optional process for FCUs wishing to apply to the Board to engage in an activity that does not fall within an FCU's preapproved incidental powers. This proposal would not impose any requirements on interested parties. The NCUA certifies the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small credit unions.
D. Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA) generally provides that an agency may not conduct or sponsor, and not withstanding any other provision of law, a person is not required to respond to, a collection of information, unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget control number. The PRA applies to rulemakings in which an agency creates a new or amends existing information collection requirements. For purposes of the PRA, an information-collection requirement may take the form of a reporting, recordkeeping, or a third-party disclosure requirement. The NCUA has determined that the changes described in this notice do not create a new information collection or revise an existing information collection as defined by the PRA.
E.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism

encourages certain agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests.
[
15
]
The proposed rule does not have substantial direct effects on the states, on the relationship between the National Government and the states, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. The proposed rule does not create or alter existing rights or requirements that apply to federally insured, state-chartered credit unions or affect the ability of state regulatory agencies to examine, supervise, or regulate such credit unions. Part 721 applies solely to FCUs. The NCUA has therefore determined that this proposed rule does not constitute a policy that has federalism implications for purposes of the executive order.
F. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families

SUMMARY:
The NCUA Board (Board) seeks comment on proposed amendments to its regulations governing fidelity bond and insurance coverage for federally insured credit unions (FICUs). The proposed rule would eliminate certain prescriptive procedural mandates and simplify requirements for coverage amounts and deductibles. The intended effect is greater flexibility for FICUs, simplified compliance, and reduced administrative costs without compromising safety and soundness.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Legal Authority and Background
The Board proposes to amend its regulations at part 713, which govern fidelity bond and insurance coverage for FICUs. The provisions of part 713 note the responsibility of a FICU's board of directors to maintain adequate insurance, set the minimum requirements for fidelity bond coverage and deductibles, and outline NCUA's process for approving bond forms.
A. Legal Authority
The Board has the legal authority to issue the proposed rule pursuant to its plenary rulemaking authority under the Federal Credit Union Act and its specific rulemaking authority related to statutory requirements mandating the bonding of FICU employees and officials to protect against losses. The NCUA's statutory authority for these rules is found at
12 U.S.C. 1761a
,
1761b(2)
,
1766(a)
,
1766(h)
, and
1789(a)(11)
.
B. Regulatory History
The Board established the current framework for fidelity bond and insurance coverage in a final rule published on May 27, 1999.
[
1
]
The 1999 rule created part 713 by redesignating and revising the requirements previously set forth in § 701.20. The primary purpose of the 1999 rule was to update and clarify the requirements related to fidelity bond coverage, for credit unions to better understand them and to enhance regulatory effectiveness.
Over the years, the Board has amended part 713 to keep pace with the evolving financial and technological environment. In a final rule published on October 26, 2005,
[
2
]
the Board modernized the regulation by increasing the minimum required coverage limits to account for inflation, asset growth, and increased risks from technology and insider fraud. The 2005 rule also increased the maximum permissible deductible from $200,000 to $1 million for certain credit unions.
The Board enacted a significant update to part 713 with a final rule published on July 24, 2019.
[
3
]
This amendment was prompted by an increase in losses to the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund resulting from bond issuers rescinding coverage when the signatory on the application was aware of fraudulent activity. To strengthen oversight by boards of directors and mitigate this risk, the 2019 rule amended § 713.2 to require a FICU's board of directors to do the following:
Review all applications for bond purchase or renewal;
Approve submission of any such application by board resolution; and
Delegate a non-employee board member to sign the agreement updating bond coverage, with the individual signing the agreement rotating to prevent the same signatory on consecutive renewals.
To better protect the National Credit Union Share Insurance Fund from losses related to liquidations, the 2019 rule amended § 713.3 to require that additional coverage be offered after a FICU is liquidated, which if purchased would provide a 12-month window enabling a claim to be filed under the bond for losses discovered after liquidation. In the 2019 rule, the Board amended § 713.4 by introducing a 10-year expiration period for any Board-approved bond form, to ensure the form remained current. This change was instituted after the Board discovered that some fidelity bonds issued on previously approved forms contained
(
printed page 65476)
outdated provisions, unapproved additions, or were being misinterpreted. The 2019 rule likewise amended § 704.18, which provides fidelity bonds requirements for federally insured corporate credit unions, to add these requirements for fidelity bond purchases and renewals made by corporate credit unions.
On October 27, 2021, the Board published a final rule
[
4
]
that made a technical amendment to § 713.6 as part of a broader update to the NCUA's supervisory ratings, which added the “S” component to the CAMELS rating system.
II. Proposed Rule
The Board is proposing several amendments to parts 704 and 713 to reduce regulatory burden, eliminate overly prescriptive requirements, and streamline the regulation while still requiring FICUs to maintain adequate fidelity bond coverage to protect against loss. The following discussion details the proposed changes and the Board's rationale. The Board invites comments on all aspects of this proposal.
A. Streamlining Procedural Requirements
The Board proposes to amend provisions in §§ 704.18, 713.2, and 713.4 that impose specific procedural requirements related to fidelity bonds. The Board believes these to be unnecessarily prescriptive and that their removal will reduce administrative burden on FICUs and bond issuers without compromising safety and soundness.
First, the Board proposes to amend § 713.2(b) by removing the requirement that the FICU's full board of directors review all applications for purchase or renewal of fidelity bond coverage. The Board believes that this requirement is unduly burdensome. The 2019 rule added this requirement in part to strengthen board oversight of fidelity bond purchases and renewals. The Board now believes that FICU boards can retain effective oversight by reviewing coverage annually, as § 713.2 required before 2019 and would continue to require under the proposed rule.
However, as noted in the 2019 rule, the Board was and remains concerned about the risk of a FICU's fidelity bond being revoked based on its signatory's knowledge of fraud or other potential claims under the bond, and thus believes it should retain some procedural safeguards. Accordingly, the Board is proposing to revise § 713.2(b) to authorize a FICU board to delegate, or otherwise authorize, review and approval of applications for purchase and of renewals to an individual member of the board or the supervisory or audit committee of the FICU. The proposed rule would also authorize a FICU board to similarly delegate or otherwise authorize the final signature to a member of the board, supervisory, or audit committee who is not also an employee of the FICU. This limitation is meant to mitigate against the risk cited in the 2019 rule that a manager or chief executive officer would be more likely than a board member to be engaged in, or know of, fraud or other potential claims. By continuing to bar people in those positions from authorizing new or renewed bonds, NCUA is seeking to limit the possibility that a bond will be revoked, while recognizing that FICU boards may benefit from delegating these administrative functions to appropriate individuals. Under the proposed rule, a FICU board would still be able to review and approve fidelity bond purchases and renewals, despite the new option to delegate this task. The proposed rule is also intended to be flexible procedurally. That is, a FICU board may specifically delegate this authority to an individual member of the board or supervisory or audit committee, or such an individual may be deemed duly authorized by virtue of their assigned duties or areas of responsibility.
Likewise, the Board is proposing to remove language in § 713.2(b) that prohibits a member of the FICU's board of directors from signing consecutive fidelity bond purchase or renewal agreements. The requirement was added in the 2019 rule for the reasons just noted for the board approval requirement. However, the Board finds that this is an overly prescriptive requirement that creates an undue burden, particularly for smaller FICUs that may have a limited number of non-employee board members available to serve as a signatory. Accordingly, the Board is proposing to remove this rotation requirement.
Second, the Board proposes to eliminate § 713.4(d) in its entirety. This paragraph establishes an automatic 10-year expiration period for the Board's approval of all fidelity bond forms. The statutory authority in
12 U.S.C. 1766(h)
grants the Board the power to approve the “form” of the bond but does not specify a temporal limit for that approval. The creation of an automatic 10-year expiration cycle is a substantive requirement not found in the statute. This provision was added in 2019 to reduce occurrences of Board-approved bond forms becoming outdated or conflicting with post-approval statutory or regulatory changes. The Board now believes this automatic sunset provision creates an unnecessary and recurring administrative burden for both FICUs and bond issuers who must seek re-approval for forms that may still be suitable. A FICU board would remain responsible for ensuring that it uses only NCUA-approved forms and should contact NCUA if they need to confirm the validity of specific forms. The proposed change does not diminish the Board's authority to review bond forms at any time and rescind approvals as appropriate. Removing § 713.4(d) will eliminate a recurring burden while retaining the Board's ability to ensure all approved forms remain current.
Finally, the Board proposes to make parallel changes to § 704.18 for corporate credit unions. Specifically, the Board proposes to revise § 704.18(b)(2) to provide the same delegation option and limitation proposed for § 713.2(b). The 2019 rule added these requirements to the corporate credit union regulation for the same reasons that supported the changes to part 713. Accordingly, the Board finds it appropriate to propose the same changes in § 704.18(b)(2) as for § 713.2(b). Likewise, the Board is proposing to revise § 704.18(c)(3) to remove the 10-year expiration provision that it is proposing to remove from § 713(d). The reasons for removing this provision from part 713 apply equally to corporate credit unions—that is, the change would reduce burden on FICUs and fidelity bond carriers who would otherwise need to have all their forms reapproved by NCUA even if they remain suitable. As with § 713.2(a), § 704.18(b)(1) would continue to require a corporate credit union's board to review coverage carefully, which would keep its oversight intact.
The Board invites public comment on these proposed changes.
B. Simplifying Coverage Requirements
The Board also proposes changes to § 713.5 to simplify the rules governing the minimum amount of fidelity bond coverage under a FICU's bond. The change is intended to eliminate redundant or advisory language and remove inflexible formulas.
First, the Board proposes removing two paragraphs from § 713.5, which specify the minimum required dollar amount of fidelity bond coverage. These paragraphs use the word “should,” which creates uncertainty for FICUs as to whether the provision is a requirement or a recommendation, leading to potential confusion regarding
(
printed page 65477)
compliance. Changing the minimum requirements stated in § 713.5(a) through use of ambiguous thresholds for additional coverage is not the best reading of the Board's statutory authority to prescribe a required “amount” for “reasonable coverage.”
The proposal would eliminate paragraph (b), which states a FICU's board of directors “should purchase” additional coverage beyond the regulatory minimum as circumstances warrant. A FICU's board of directors already has a fundamental fiduciary duty to ensure the institution operates in a safe and sound manner, which includes securing insurance coverage that is adequate for its specific risk profile. This paragraph is purely advisory and restates a basic principle of corporate governance. Its removal simplifies the regulation without diminishing underlying responsibilities of the FICU's board of directors.
In addition, the proposal would eliminate paragraph (c), which states that FICUs “should maintain increased coverage” based on a specific formula tied to the amount of daily cash on hand or money in transit. The Board believes this provision is both overly prescriptive and ambiguous. Moreover, a rigid formula focused on only two specific criteria may not be the most relevant measure of risk for all FICUs in a modern financial environment. The existing requirement in § 713.2(a) for the board of directors to conduct an annual review based on potential risks contains a sufficiently effective, flexible, principles-based approach to determining a FICU's amount of fidelity bond coverage.
The Board invites comment on these proposed changes. The Board also specifically requests comment on one aspect of current § 704.18. The Board notes that § 704.18(d)(2) contains a “duty” for a corporate credit union's board to provide adequate protection for its unique circumstances by obtaining, when necessary, coverage above the minimum required amounts. While this provision is stated as a mandate and not guidance, the Board requests comment on eliminating this provision. The reason for removing this provision would differ from the reason for removing the guidance in part 713. The Board is interested in public feedback on whether the part 704 duty is too vague to offer a corporate credit union board enough direction on when or whether NCUA would expect it to obtain extra coverage voluntarily.
C. Making Technical Corrections
The Board additionally proposes to make a conforming change to § 704.18(c)(3) for corporate credit unions, in a manner more consistent with the parallel provision of § 713.4(c) for FICUs. The separation of current § 704.18(c)(3) into new subsections (i) and (ii) would be to make clear there are two distinct prohibited scenarios. No substantive effect is intended by this technical conforming amendment.
The Board similarly proposes to make a conforming change to § 713.4(c) for FICUs, to correct an inconsistency with the parallel provision of § 704.18(c)(3) for corporate credit unions. The two clauses found in the proposed § 704.18(c)(3)(i) and (ii) are separated by the word “and,” while the same clauses found in the current § 713.4(c) are separated by the word “or.” However, these provisions were always intended to create identical prohibitions, and have both been treated as the same in practice since the 2019 amendments. To eliminate this textual discrepancy, the Board now proposes to use “or” in both § 704.18(c) and § 713.4(c), which is best read in a way consistent with present practice that prohibits credit unions from using any of the bond documents described. No substantive effect is intended by this technical conforming amendment.

D. The Regulatory Flexibility Act
The Regulatory Flexibility Act generally requires an agency to conduct a regulatory flexibility analysis of any rule subject to notice and comment rulemaking requirements, unless the agency certifies that the rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. If the agency makes such a certification, it shall publish the certification at the time of publication of either the proposed rule or the final rule, along with a statement providing the factual basis for such certification. For purposes of this analysis, the NCUA considers small credit unions to be those having under $100 million in assets. The Board fully considered the potential economic impacts of the regulatory amendments on small credit unions.
To the extent that the proposed rule would have any economic impacts, they will be deregulatory in nature. The proposed rule would eliminate certain prescriptive procedural mandates and simplify requirements for coverage amounts and deductibles. The intended effect is greater flexibility for FICUs, simplified compliance, and reduced administrative costs without compromising safety and soundness. While the proposed changes could create an economic benefit for FICUs, they are unlikely to be significant for purposes of the Regulatory Flexibility Act. Accordingly, the NCUA certifies the proposed rule would not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
E.
Executive Order 13132
on Federalism
Executive Order 13132
encourages certain regulatory agencies to consider the impact of their actions on state and local interests. The NCUA, an agency as defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(5)
, complies with the order to adhere to fundamental federalism principles. The proposed rule would apply to all FICUs, including state-chartered credit unions. The NCUA expects that any effect on states or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government will be minor. The proposed changes would mainly clarify the existing regulations and guidance in this area, eliminating certain prescriptive provisions but not fundamentally altering the calculation of or provision of insurance or fidelity bond coverage for FICUs. The proposed changes are not intended to affect the division of responsibilities between the NCUA and state regulatory authorities with oversight of federally insured, state-chartered credit unions. The NCUA welcomes comments on ways to eliminate, or at least minimize, any potential impact in this area.
F. Assessment of Federal Regulations and Policies on Families
The NCUA has determined that the proposed rule would not affect family well-being within the meaning of section 654 of the Treasury and General Government Appropriations Act, 1999. The proposed rule relates to fidelity bond coverage that protects credit unions against losses due to fraud, dishonesty, and theft committed by credit union employees or volunteers; accordingly, any effect on family well-being is expected to be indirect.

AGENCY:
Federal Maritime Commission.
ACTION:
Sixty-day notice; request for comments.
SUMMARY:
As part of our continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, and as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, the Federal Maritime Commission (Commission or FMC) invites comments on the continuing information collections related to ocean common carrier and marine terminal operator agreements and related forms, FMC-150 and FMC-151. This notice announces a renewal of an existing collection and includes updates to the collection based on the increase in number of responses and burden hours for respondents; the transition from use of the Monitoring Report Form (FMC-151) to individualized reporting requirements under the Periodic Reporting Requirements provision; monthly submissions of the global vessel sharing agreements; and a new electronic platform to submit agreement filings, required reports, and other agreement-related collections electronically.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted on or before December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The Commission is accepting comments using the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
www.regulations.gov
.
The docket for this notice, which includes copies of applicable forms and submitted comments, can be found at
www.regulations.gov
under FMC-2026-0430. Follow the instructions provided for submitting comments.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Stephanie Rice, (202) 794-1067,
srice-hartung@fmc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The Commission invites the general public and other Federal agencies to comment on any aspect of the continuing information collection listed in this notice, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
). We are particularly interested in receiving comments on: (1) the necessity and utility of the proposed information collection for the proper performance of the agency's functions; (2) the accuracy of the estimated burden; (3) ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected; and (4) the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology to minimize the information collection burden.
Comments submitted in response to this notice will be included or summarized in our request for Office of Management and Budget (OMB) approval of the relevant information collection. All comments are part of the public record and subject to disclosure. Please do not include any confidential or inappropriate material in your comments.

Abstract:
The Commission administers subtitle IV of title 46 of the United States Code (the Shipping Act or the Act).
46 U.S.C. 40301
(a)-(c), identifies certain agreements by or among ocean common carriers (carriers) and marine terminal operators (MTOs) that fall within the jurisdiction of that Act. Section 5 of the Act,
46 U.S.C. 40302
, requires that carriers and MTOs file those agreements with the Federal Maritime Commission. Section 6 of the Act,
46 U.S.C. 40304
,
40306
, and
41307
(b)-(d), specifies the Commission actions that may be taken with respect to filed agreements, including requiring the submission of additional information. Section 40104 authorizes the Commission to require that carriers and MTOs, among other persons, file periodic or special reports. Requests for periodic or special reports are meant to assist the Commission in fulfilling its statutory mandate of overseeing the activities of the ocean transportation industry. These reports are necessary so that the Commission can monitor agreement parties' activities to determine how or if their activities will have an impact on competition.
Type of Review:
Extension with change.
Current Actions:
The estimated number of responses and burden hours for the collection have increased due to a number of factors. The biggest change is attributed to the transition from use of the Monitoring Report Form (FMC-151) to individualized reporting requirements under the Periodic Reporting Requirements provision of
46 CFR 535.701(d)
. Global vessel sharing agreements, which are now monitored under Alternative Period Reporting under
46 CFR 535.703(d)
, are required to submit monitoring data monthly. The Commission has increased its monitoring activities for MTO agreements. The FMC has reduced the estimated time to complete the Information Form (FMC-150) from 75 hours to 3 hours. The FMC has also now added to the burden estimate the time it takes to file Voluntary Guidelines for service contracts with the Commission. It is unclear why this activity was previously excluded from the burden calculation. Agreement filings, required reports, other agreement-related collections and Forms FMC-150 and FMC-151 have been included with the agency's modernization initiative and will be included within the ServiceNow platform.
Needs and Uses:
The Commission uses the information filed by agreement parties to monitor their activities as required by the Shipping Act. Under
46 U.S.C. 41307
, the Commission must determine whether an agreement will result, or has resulted, in a substantial reduction in competition within the prevailing market leading to an unreasonable reduction in transportation service or an unreasonable increase in transportation costs, or “substantially lessen[s] competition in the purchasing of certain covered services.” In such cases, the Commission would take action to seek to enjoin the agreement in the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.

This information will be collected as required by the regulations at Part 535.

The types of respondents are marine terminal operators, vessel-operating common carriers, and other parties to FMC-filed agreements.

title: Authorization of Emergency Use for Four Animal Drugs for the Prevention and Treatment of New World Screwworm; Availability
abstract: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA or the Agency) is announcing the issuance of four Emergency Use Authorizations (EUA or Authorization) under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) for new animal products. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Elanco US Inc. for application on or around wounds for the prevention of infestations caused by New World screwworm (Cochliomyia hominivorax; NWS) larvae (myiasis) in sheep, cattle, goats, swine, camelids, and the following captive and captured wildlife species: cervids, American bison, bighorn sheep, and Sonoran pronghorn. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Zoetis Inc. for the treatment of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs and puppies. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Bimeda Animal Health Ltd. for the prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in cattle. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Sergeant's Pet Care Products LLC for the treatment and prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs, puppies, cats and kittens 2 pounds of body weight or greater and 4 weeks of age and older. The Authorizations contain, among other things, conditions on the emergency use of the authorized products. The Authorizations follow the August 18, 2025, determination by the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) that there is a significant potential for a public health emergency that has a significant potential to affect national security or the health and security of U.S. citizens living abroad and that involves NWS. On the basis of such determination, the Secretary of HHS declared on August 18, 2025, that circumstances exist justifying the authorization of emergency use of animal drugs to treat or prevent NWS myiasis in animals. The Authorizations, which include an explanation of the reasons for issuance, are reprinted in this document.
dates: The Authorizations are effective on their dates of issuance: August 7, 2026, August 13, 2026, August 27, 2026, and September 3, 2026, respectively.

FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Elanco US Inc. for application on or around wounds for the prevention of infestations caused by New World screwworm (
Cochliomyia hominivorax
; NWS) larvae (myiasis) in sheep, cattle, goats, swine, camelids, and the following captive and captured wildlife species: cervids, American bison, bighorn sheep, and Sonoran pronghorn. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Zoetis Inc. for the treatment of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs and puppies. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Bimeda Animal Health Ltd. for the prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in cattle. FDA has issued one EUA for an animal product as requested by Sergeant's Pet Care Products LLC for the treatment and prevention of infestations caused by NWS (myiasis) in dogs, puppies, cats and kittens 2 pounds of body weight or greater and 4 weeks of age and older. The Authorizations contain, among other things, conditions on the emergency use of the authorized products. The Authorizations follow the August 18, 2025, determination by the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) that there is a significant potential for a public health emergency that has a significant potential to affect national security or the health and security of U.S. citizens living abroad and that involves NWS.
