(e)
Proration of awards.
Investment advisers that submit competitive bids in the names of controlled accounts are responsible for prorating any awards at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin using the same percentage that we announce. * * *
5.
Section 356.20 is amended by revising paragraphs (a), (d)(1) and (2) to read as follows:
§ 356.20
How does the Treasury determine auction awards?
(a)
Determining the range and amount of awarded competitive bids
—(1)
Awarding bids.
After the competitive auction closes, we award noncompetitive bids that were submitted prior to the noncompetitive auction close, subject to the noncompetitive bidding limitations and restrictions described in this part. Then we award competitive bids at the lowest yields, discount rates, or discount margins, through successively higher yields, discount rates, or discount margins, up to the amount required to meet the offering amount. When necessary, we prorate bids at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin as described below. If the amount of noncompetitive bids would absorb all or most of the offering amount, we will award competitive bids in an amount sufficient to provide a fair determination of the yield, discount rate, or discount margin for the securities we are auctioning.
(2)
Awarding bids at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin.
Generally, the total amount of bids at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin exceeds the offering amount remaining after we award the noncompetitive bids and the competitive bids at the lower yields, discount rates, or discount margins. In order to keep the total amount of awards as close as possible to the announced offering amount, we award a percentage of the bids at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin. We derive the percentage by dividing the remaining par amount needed to fill the offering amount by the par amount of the bids at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin and rounding up to the next hundredth of a whole percentage point, for example, 17.13%.
*
*
*
*
*
(d) * * *
(1)
Single-price auctions.
Both noncompetitive and competitive bidders receive the price equivalent to the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin at which bids were awarded. For inflation-protected securities, the price for awarded securities is the price equivalent to the high real yield.
(2)
Multiple-price auctions
—(i)
Competitive bids.
Competitive bidders receive the price equivalent to each yield, discount rate, or discount margin at which their bids were awarded.
(ii)
Noncompetitive bids.
Noncompetitive bidders receive the price equivalent to the weighted average yield, discount rate, or discount margin of awarded competitive bids.
6.
Section 356.21 is revised to read as follows:
§ 356.21
How are awards at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin calculated?
(a)
Awards to submitters.
We generally prorate bids at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin under § 356.20(a)(2) of this part. For example, if 80.15% is the
(
printed page 65459)
announced percentage at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin, we award 80.15% of the amount of each bid at that yield, discount rate, or discount margin. A bid for $100 million at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin would be awarded $80,150,000 in this example. We always make awards for at least the minimum to bid, and above that amount we make awards in the appropriate multiple to bid. For example, Treasury bills may be issued with a minimum to bid of $100 and multiples to bid of $100. Say we accept an $18,000 bid at the high discount rate, and the percent awarded at the high discount rate is 88.27%. We would award $15,900 to that bidder, which is an upward adjustment from $15,888.60 ($18,000 × .8827) to the nearest multiple of $100. If we were to award 4.65% of bids at the high discount rate, for example, the award for a $100 bid at that rate would be $100, rather than $4.65, in order to meet the minimum to bid for a bill issue.
(b)
Awards to customers.
The same prorating rules apply to customers as apply to submitters. Depository institutions and dealers, whether submitters or intermediaries, are responsible for prorating awards for their customers at the same percentage that we announce. For example, if 80.15% is the announced percentage at the high yield, high discount rate, or high discount margin, then each customer bid at that yield, discount rate, or discount margin must be awarded 80.15%.
7.
Section 356.23 is amended by revising paragraphs (a), (b) introductory text, (b)(1), (b)(2), (b)(5), and (b)(6) to read as follows:
§ 356.23
How are the auction results announced?
(a) After the conclusion of the auction, we will make the auction results available on our website.
(b) The auction results may include such information as:
(1) The amounts of bids we recognized and awarded;
(2) The range of awarded yields, discount rates, or discount margins.

46 CFR Part 551
[FMC-2026-0463; Docket No. 26-14]
AGENCY:
Federal Maritime Commission.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
The Federal Maritime Commission (Commission) proposes to adjust or meet unfavorable shipping conditions created by the Government of Spain. The Commission proposes a per-voyage fee on all Spanish vessels of $200,000 and restrictions on the import of certain Spanish goods into the United States. The Commission also proposes using additional statutory authority to impose these remedies because the Government of Spain has unduly impaired the access of U.S. flag vessels to trade between foreign ports. The Commission herein offers an opportunity for a public hearing. The Commission invites public comment on all aspects of this proposed rule.
DATES:
Comments and related material must be received by the Commission on or before December 14, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
To view background documents or comments received, you may use the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
www.regulations.gov
under FMC-2026-0463. See the “Public Participation and Request for Comments” portion of the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section for further instructions on submitting comments. This notice of proposed rulemaking with its plain-language, 100-word-or-less proposed rule summary will be available in this same docket.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
David Eng, Secretary; Phone: (202) 523-5725; Email:
secretary@fmc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
A. Legal Authority
The Federal Maritime Commission (Commission) is charged with investigating and prescribing regulations to adjust or meet conditions unfavorable to shipping in the foreign trade of the United States which arise out of or result from the laws or regulations of a foreign country.
46 U.S.C. 42101(a)
. The Commission must also investigate when a foreign government is unduly impairing the access of a vessel documented under the laws of the United States to ocean trade between foreign ports and take appropriate action to remedy any such violation.
46 U.S.C. 41108(d)
. The Commission is empowered to remedy foreign government actions that impair the access of U.S. flag vessels to ocean trade between foreign ports by
Chapter 423 of Title 46, United States Code.
The remedies provided by Chapter 421 and Chapter 423 of Title 46 authorize the Commission to charge fees to foreign-flagged vessels entering U.S. ports and limit the import into the United States of amounts or types of cargo.
B. Investigation
The Commission initiated this investigation in December 2024 under Title 46, Chapter 421 of the United States Code to determine whether the Government of Spain (Spain) is creating general or special conditions unfavorable to shipping in U.S. foreign trade by barring certain vessels from its ports, including vessels transporting cargo under the United States Maritime Administration's (MARAD) Maritime Security Program (MSP). Docket No. 24-30; FMC-2024-0022. Initial reports that prompted this investigation indicated that Spain had refused port access in November 2024 to three MSP vessels on the grounds that they were carrying cargo bound for or coming from Israel. Spain reportedly cited European Union (EU) regulations as the basis for these port refusals.
[
1
]
The Commission published a notice of investigation and request for comments in the
Federal Register
on December 6, 2024.
Investigation into Conditions Affecting Shipping in the Foreign Trade and Denial of Entry of Vessels into Spanish Ports,
89 FR 96973
(Dec. 6, 2024) (December 2024 notice). That request resulted in over 8,000 comments from the public and interested parties. Many comments expressed views about Spain's policy based on views about Israel. That is not part of this investigation, which is focused only on maintaining the reliability and efficiency of the U.S. ocean shipping supply chain, including whether Spain is refusing docking privileges to certain vessels, and if so, how Spain's refusal of docking privileges is affecting shipping in U.S. foreign trade.
The Commission reviewed these comments and also ordered information to be supplied under oath as necessary to further the investigation.
46 U.S.C. 42104(a)
. Materials the Commission ordered to be supplied under oath will not be disclosed to the public.
46 U.S.C. 42105
.
The Commission published a second notice and request for comments in the
Federal Register
on December 22, 2025.
Investigation Into Conditions Affecting Shipping in the Foreign Trade and Denial of Entry of Vessels Into Spanish Ports; Request for Additional Comments,
90 FR 59826
(Dec. 22, 2025) (December 2025 notice). The evidence the Commission received up to that point confirmed that the unfavorable conditions identified in this investigation still existed, and the Commission provided 60 additional days for commenters to weigh in. The Commission also described its authority to prescribe remedies and solicited comment on possible remedies, including remedies focused on vessels with links to Spain, cargo from Spain that might be appropriately limited, or other possible remedies. The second notice resulted in only one comment that was not relevant to the purposes of the Commission's investigation.
II. Public Comments
The Commission received over 8,000 comments in response to the December 2024 notice. The Commission received only one comment in response to the December 2025 notice. The Commission reviewed these comments and considered the issues they raised.
Many of the responses to the December 2024 notice and the lone comment on the December 2025 notice did not raise issues relevant to this investigation. For instance, the one comment responding to the Commission's December 2025 notice urged the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration to approve an economic fishery disaster
(
printed page 65516)
declaration.
[
2
]
Many of the responses to the December 2024 notice focused on concerns about possible human rights violations. These issues are beyond the scope of this investigation. The Commission is investigating Spain's denial of docking privileges to certain vessels and whether such denials are creating conditions unfavorable to shipping in the foreign trade. Because of the volume of comments, the Commission's analysis focuses on comments raising relevant issues within the scope of the Commission's investigation.
A. Government of Spain
[
3
]
Spain submitted a comment in response to the Commission's December 2024 notice but not the December 2025 notice. In its comment, Spain argued that the Commission does not have power to compel Spain's participation in this proceeding, the Commission does not have jurisdiction over Spain given sovereign immunity, and the appropriate remedy is for the Commission to pursue a diplomatic solution through the U.S. Secretary of State. Moreover, Spain argued that it must follow Spanish, EU, and international laws that require it to prevent the transit of defense and dual-use goods through its ports and Spain is doing so in a non-discriminatory manner. Spain's arguments do not address the questions posed by the Commission, and Spain's unquestioned sovereignty to act within its borders does not affect the Commission's authority to investigate and regulate conditions unfavorable to U.S. foreign shipping under Chapter 421.
First, the Commission cannot compel Spain to participate in this proceeding. The Commission's power to remedy unfavorable conditions to shipping in foreign trade is the power to take action within the jurisdiction of the United States. The Commission can deny vessels entry into the United States, impose fees on vessels coming to the United States, and take other appropriate actions to adjust or meet unfavorable shipping conditions.
46 U.S.C. 42106
. The Commission cannot force Spain to take any action or repeal any Spanish or EU law or regulation. Likewise, Spain cannot infringe on U.S. sovereignty by demanding the Commission take or refrain from any action.
Further, Spain's compliance with Spanish, EU, and international law is not a defense to a Chapter 421 investigation. Chapter 421 presupposes that Spain's actions are consistent with its laws and regulations. Section 42101 obligates the Commission to prescribe regulations meeting unfavorable conditions that “arise out of or result from laws or regulations of a foreign country.” This statutory language shows Congress assumed that the unfavorable conditions arise from compliance with foreign laws or regulations, not non-compliance or illegal behavior. The Commission's investigation is into whether the conditions created by Spain result in unfavorable conditions affecting shipping in the foreign trade, not whether Spain was required by its own legal system to create those conditions.
Spain's claims that it is enforcing its laws in a non-discriminatory manner without regard to flag is also not a defense against an investigation of whether Spain has created unfavorable conditions in the foreign trade. Spain claims that it did not reject docking authorization to certain vessels on the basis of a vessel's flag or port of origin, but that it only rejected the transit of the individual containers. Spain, however, failed to support these claims in its response, and they are inconsistent with the evidence received in this investigation. The evidence shows that Spain rejected docking privileges for U.S. flag vessels and did not merely deny offloading or transshipment of specific containers. Moreover, the argument that it did not discriminate based on flag or port of origin does not rebut a finding that Spain's actions created unfavorable conditions. Selectively enforcing laws or regulations to deny docking privileges to specific vessels can create, and has created, unfavorable conditions even if Spain allows access to other vessels of the same flag or origin.
Finally, it is true, as Spain contends, that a diplomatic solution may resolve this investigation. Spain is uniquely positioned to make that occur. But until that time, Spain continues to create unfavorable shipping conditions. The Commission is charged with meeting or adjusting those conditions while they persist. The Commission can rescind any final remedies once a diplomatic solution has been reached, but does not intend to delay the proposed remedies based on a hypothetical solution.
[
4
]
B. Members of Congress
[
5
]
The Commission received a comment from two then-current members and one former member of Congress. These members opposed the Commission's investigation, but their comment did not address the questions posed in the Commission's December 2024 notice or discuss the Commission's statutory authority. The members argued that Spain's actions are legitimate actions of a sovereign state, Spain is right to follow its affirmative legal obligations to block weapons that may facilitate violations of the Geneva Convention, Spain's actions do not threaten the reliable international ocean shipping system, and U.S. agencies should not punish its allies for enforcing international obligations. The members' arguments that Spain's actions do not threaten international ocean shipping were not supported by evidence submitted to the Commission. Their remaining arguments are beyond the scope of the Commission's investigation or outside the Commission's authority to investigate.
C. Maritime Labor Unions
[
6
]
The Commission received a comment submitted on behalf of maritime labor unions.
[
7
]
The unions supported the Commission's investigation and argued that Spain's port denials undermine fair trade and create unfavorable conditions for U.S. shipping in the foreign trade. The comment contended that MSP vessels are essential for maintaining the security and reliability of U.S. foreign trade and defense readiness, and that Spain's actions jeopardize the free flow of commerce and disrupt shipping operations. The unions affirmed their support for promoting the economic and national security interest of the U.S. by delivering timely cargo on behalf of the American people, encouraged the Commission to use every available tool to compel a reversal of Spain's policy, and argued that Spain's actions set a dangerous precedent for the treatment of U.S. vessels abroad. The unions urged the Commission to protect the right of U.S. flag vessels to operate freely in international trade and offered their support in any way necessary.
(
printed page 65517)
D. Former State Department Diplomat
[
8
]
A self-identified former State Department diplomat who worked on Middle East issues opposed the Commission's investigation. He argued that any remedies contemplated under Chapter 421 would be unwarranted given the current circumstances and contended that an investigation is unwarranted and inappropriate. This commenter argued that Spain's actions were legally obligated given that cargo carried on U.S. Government ships contributes to violations of the Geneva Convention and international law. Spain's compliance with domestic and international law, however, is not a defense to a Chapter 421 investigation because the Commission's authority is premised on the conditions arising out of the “laws or regulations of a foreign country.” That these conditions are arising out Spain's laws or regulations is necessary for a Chapter 421 investigation. This commenter concluded that the United States should cease arming Israel and should not stand in the way of Spain's legally and morally necessary arms embargo. These issues are beyond the scope of this investigation.
E. Mass Comments
The Commission received thousands of mass comments with almost identical language. The Commission used federal comment deduplication tools to identify representative comments for consideration. The Commission included all of these mass comments in the online rulemaking docket. Most of the mass comments opposed the Commission's investigation for reasons already discussed and discussed further below.
[
9
]
The commenters raised Spain's legal obligation to follow Spanish, EU and international law,
[
10
]
the sovereign right of Spain to enforce an arms embargo, and the Commission's lack of authority to exercise jurisdiction over Spain.
[
11
]
The mass comments also argued that the United States is obligated by law to stop arming Israel, that this investigation is a waste of government resources and tax dollars, and that the International Court of Justice's (ICJ) preliminary ruling against Israel binds the United States and requires it to stop arming Israel. These issues, and others raised in the mass comments, were not responsive to the Commission's December 2024 notice and do not address the focus of the Commission's investigation. Arguments about obligations to human rights treaties and ICJ rulings do not provide evidence about the impact of Spain's port denials on the efficiency and reliability of the ocean shipping supply chain or whether Spain's actions are creating unfavorable shipping conditions. Although the volume of the comments opposing Commission action in this regard was high, the Commission finds the analysis in these comments unpersuasive.
One set of mass comments supported the Commission's investigation.
[
12
]
This set of mass comments argued that Spain's refusal of docking privileges undermines equitable trade and critical logistics networks, and that Spain has jeopardized bilateral trade and NATO defense efforts. This set of mass comments urged the Commission to impose remedies such as fines or vessel bans to reaffirm the importance of fair and open maritime commerce. This set of mass comments is relevant to the investigation because it addresses whether Spain's actions have impacted the efficiency and reliability of the ocean shipping supply chain. This set of mass comments does not provide new evidence for the Commission to consider, but it does reinforce the Commission's concerns about Spanish actions creating unfavorable shipping conditions.
F. Palestinian Youth Movement
[
13
]
The Commission received a set of mass comments created by the Palestinian Youth Movement (PYM). The PYM did not submit a comment itself, but many commenters followed a template created by the PYM. These commenters argued that Spain's blocking of specific ships is not only within Spain's purview as a sovereign country but is a legal obligation. Any remedies contemplated in Chapter 421 of United States Code, Title 46 would be unwarranted under the current circumstance according to these commenters. They argued the cargo carried on Maersk ships, provided by the U.S. Government, contributes to war crimes, crimes against humanity, the crime of genocide, violations of the 4th Geneva Convention and Additional Protocols, and violations of international legal norms. These commenters concluded that the United States should cease arming Israel and should not stand in the way of Spain's legally and morally necessary arms embargo. The Commission's investigation focuses on whether Spain's actions result in unfavorable conditions affecting shipping in the foreign trade, and Spain complying with its own law in taking those actions is presupposed by the statute.
III. Investigation Results
The Commission's investigation provided conclusive evidence that Spain's actions have created unfavorable shipping conditions in the foreign trade resulting from its laws or regulations. Spain has publicly denied docking privileges to multiple vessels and publicly stated it will deny docking privileges to certain vessels in the future. Those vessels had to reroute to non-Spanish ports and omit Spanish ports from future voyages. Spain's policy of port denials is ongoing. Confidentially submitted evidence confirms that Spain's policy has created unfavorable conditions. The Commission concludes that Spain's actions create unfavorable shipping conditions in the foreign trade resulting from its laws or regulations.
The Commission's investigation returned public and non-public evidence of Spain's actions. In May 2024, Spain publicly announced a policy of preventing vessels from docking at its ports and Spain's transport minister identified a vessel that had been refused docking privileges as the
Marianne Danica.
[
14
]
In November 2024, Spain's foreign ministry said two vessels participating in MSP, the
Maersk Seletar
and the
Maersk Denver,
“will not stop in Spain.” Those vessels did not dock in Spain. Another MSP vessel, the
Maersk Hartford,
with a stop planned at a Spanish port later that month also did not dock in Spain. Spain publicly reinforced and expanded this policy in September 2025.
[
15
]
Public vessel tracking data confirms Spain has created unfavorable conditions. The
Maersk Seletar
and
Maersk Denver
signaled Algeciras, Spain as their destination during voyages in early November 2024 and then changed their destinations while crossing the Atlantic Ocean to Tangier, Morocco. Both then docked at Tangier, Morocco. Public vessel tracking data show that both vessels no longer call at
(
printed page 65518)
Spanish ports and last did so in January of 2025. The
Maersk Hartford
was destined for a Spanish port in November 2024 but public vessel tracking data confirms it rerouted to Morocco mid-voyage.
[
16
]
The
Maersk Hartford
last visited Spain in January 2025 and has since visited Morocco regularly. Since November 2024, vessel tracking data shows that the U.S. flag fleet of Maersk Line Limited (MLL)
[
17
]
has almost entirely avoided stopping in Spain with only six visits occurring across 2026 as opposed to the multiple monthly visits prior to November 2024. Vessel tracking data shows 7.25
[
18
]
port calls per month in Spain by MLL vessels on average prior to November 2024. Since July 2025, MLL vessel calls have almost ceased at Algeciras, and MLL vessel calls at Tangier in Morocco have replaced much of this traffic. MLL vessel calls at Tangier now average 4.17 per month, replacing many of the MLL vessel calls to Algeciras. The larger population of MSP vessels also now mostly avoid calling at Algeciras.
Confidentially submitted information confirms that Spain's public announcements and non-public actions have created unfavorable conditions. It confirms that Spain's public policy of preventing certain vessels, including MSP vessels, from docking at Spanish ports is creating unfavorable shipping conditions. It confirms that almost all MSP vessels no longer dock at Spanish ports because of Spain's policy of port denials, and not for other reasons.
[
19
]
It confirms that this prevents MSP vessels from trading between Spanish ports and other foreign ports.
Based on this record, the Commission concludes that Spain has created conditions unfavorable to shipping in the foreign trade through its laws or regulations. Spain has publicly announced and enforced a policy that has prevented MSP vessels from docking at Spanish ports. MSP vessels were turned away in at least three instances from Spanish ports. Publicly, Spain has only reinforced and expanded this public policy since those vessels were turned away in November 2024. Almost all MSP vessels no longer dock at Spanish ports. This policy prevents U.S. flag vessels from carrying goods destined for Spanish ports and prevents them from picking up Spanish goods for carriage to non-Spanish ports. This policy creates conditions that directly impact the purposes for which Congress created the Commission. The exclusion of MSP vessels, vessels necessary for the national defense and the domestic and foreign commerce of the United States,
[
20
]
prevents these vessels from providing shipping services essential for maintaining waterborne domestic and foreign commerce, especially when called upon to serve as naval and military auxiliary vessels in a time of national emergency.
[
21
]
46 U.S.C. 42101
,
citing
46 U.S.C. 50101
. Further, the Spanish policy impairs the efficient, competitive, and economical transportation of goods in the ocean commerce of the United States by preventing U.S. flag vessels from transporting goods destined for, or coming from, Spain.
46 U.S.C. 40101(2)
. The policy directly conflicts with the Commission's purpose of encouraging the development of an economically sound and efficient liner fleet of U.S.-flagged vessels capable of meeting national security needs and supporting commerce, as it prevents exactly those vessels from carrying goods to or from Spain.
46 U.S.C. 40101(3)
. Finally, the policy undermines the Commission's ability to promote a competitive and efficient system for the carriage of goods by water in the foreign commerce of the United States since MSP vessels can no longer compete for cargos destined for, or coming from, Spain.
46 U.S.C. 40101(4)
. This record supports the Commission's conclusion that Spain's laws or regulations are creating conditions unfavorable to shipping in the foreign trade.
IV. Section 41108(d)
The Commission commenced this investigation pursuant to its Chapter 421 authority to remedy unfavorable conditions, but the evidence also demonstrates that Spain has prevented U.S. flag vessels from docking at its ports, and by doing so prevented these vessels from delivering goods to Spanish ports from other foreign ports and from loading Spanish goods for delivery in foreign ports. This supports the conclusion that Spain's actions have potentially impaired the access of U.S. flag vessels to ocean trade between foreign ports. As a result, the Commission, through this notice, is providing an opportunity for Spain to request a hearing pursuant to
46 U.S.C. 41108(d)
.
The record shows that Spain denied access to its ports to three MSP vessels in November 2024. Spain denied docking privileges to the
Maersk Seletar
and the
Maersk Denver
in November 2024. Later in November 2024, Spain did not permit another MSP vessel, the
Maersk Hartford,
to dock at its ports. Spain's policy of denying docking privileges to these vessels, which are documented under the laws of the United States, still prevents them from exporting goods to Spain and from carrying Spanish goods to foreign ports. This continues to impair the ability of these vessels to engage in ocean trade between foreign ports. MSP vessels cannot compete fairly against non-MSP vessels for cargo destined for Spain or to carry Spanish exports.
Section 41108(d) gives the Commission power to impose remedies authorized by sections 42304 and 42305 of Title 46 of the United States Code, but that section requires that the Commission do so only after notice and opportunity for a hearing. Because the Commission's investigation has focused on Chapter 421 violations to this point, the Commission has not yet provided Spain with an opportunity for a hearing concerning section 41108(d). Through this notice, the Commission informs Spain that it intends to consider, and potentially impose remedies for, Spain's actions that impair the ability of U.S. flag vessels to ocean trade between foreign ports. The Commission also, through this notice, provides Spain with the opportunity to request a hearing before the Commission. Should Spain request a hearing, its representatives should use the Further Contact
(
printed page 65519)
Information provided at the beginning of this notice to file such a request with the Commission.
V. Proposed Remedies
The Commission proposes two sets of remedies to meet or adjust the unfavorable shipping conditions created by Spain in the foreign trade of the United States. First, the Commission proposes to levy fees on Spanish-flagged vessels entering U.S. ports.
46 U.S.C. 42106(4)
,
42304(a)(4)
. Second, the Commission proposes to limit imports into the United States of some or all categories of Spanish goods. The Commission intends to exercise its authority to restrict the type of cargo carried to U.S. ports and work with relevant U.S. government agencies to enforce these restrictions.
46 U.S.C. 42106(4)
,
42109
.
A. Per Voyage Fees
First, the Commission proposes imposing fees on a per-voyage basis on Spanish-flagged vessels calling at U.S. ports. One of the Commission's prior uses of this authority came during an investigation into Japanese harbor services monopolies and Japan's licensing of terminal operators and stevedores.
[
22
]
In that investigation, the Commission imposed a $100,000 fee per-voyage on vessels operated by Japanese carriers in a 1997 final rule. That investigation differed because there were many Japanese carriers and many Japanese-flagged vessels entering U.S. ports, whereas there are relatively few Spanish-flagged vessels that call at U.S. ports. Still, the Commission now proposes similar remedies to those that led to a bilateral resolution in that investigation. The Commission proposes a per-voyage fee on Spanish-flagged vessels of $200,000, which is the approximate adjustment for inflation between 1997 and 2026.
46 U.S.C. 42106(4)
,
42304(a)(4)
. This remedy alone will not fully meet or adjust the unfavorable conditions created by Spain, but it has been effective before and the Commission proposes to use it again.
B. Trade Category Import Restrictions
Second, the Commission reviewed the Harmonized Tariff Schedule (HTS) to choose Spanish goods that could be limited from import to appropriately meet or adjust the unfavorable shipping conditions created by Spain. The HTS of the United States is a U.S. nomenclature system used to classify traded goods based on their material composition, product name, and/or intended function. The HTS is based on the international harmonized system, which is the global system of nomenclature applied to most world trade in goods. The international harmonized system maps exactly with the U.S. version to the 6-digit level while the HTS (U.S.) further stratifies traded goods into even more specific categories. The HTS is designed so that each article falls into only one category. It is divided into chapters, each of which has a 2-digit number. Each product category within the various chapters is designated by 4, 6, 8, or 10 digits. The 4-digit categories are called “headings.” The 6-, 8- and 10-digit classifications are called “subheadings.”
The Commission proposes limiting the import of trade categories from Spain to appropriately meet or adjust the unfavorable shipping conditions created by Spain's actions.
[
23
]
The Commission emphasizes that this is a proposed list of trade categories that the Commission may limit, and that the Commission may choose a lesser remedy from these options. The Commission may choose to broadly limit imports, impose more targeted limitations, limit only certain of the trade categories described below, or some combination of these options. The Commission is soliciting public comment to help it decide the appropriate remedy to meet or adjust the unfavorable shipping conditions created by Spain. These unfavorable conditions have grave consequences for the efficiency and reliability of the international ocean shipping supply chain, as well as the ability of the Commission to promote the growth and development of U.S. exports, encourage the development of a liner fleet of U.S. vessels capable of meeting national security needs and supporting commerce, and supporting the U.S. merchant marine. These purposes are frustrated by Spain preventing U.S. vessels from importing U.S. goods into Spain and exporting Spanish goods to foreign ports. The unfavorable conditions created by Spain that deny U.S. vessels access to Spanish ports and Spanish goods require a significant mix of remedies to meet or adjust them. Therefore, the Commission has proposed to limit meaningful volumes of Spanish imports to approximate the damage done to U.S. carriers and the liner fleet of U.S. vessels capable of meeting national security needs.
1. Perfumery and Cosmetics
The Commission proposes limiting imports of HTS chapter 33, Perfumery and Cosmetics. Perfumes and Toilet Waters (HTS 33.0300) imports were valued at nearly $700 million in 2025. At the Chapter level (2-digit HTS 33) Essential Oils Etc.; Perfumery, Cosmetic Etc. Preps, represents nearly $940 million in imports to the United States from Spain in 2025. The Commission proposes limiting imports of all goods falling under the HTS 33 chapter.
2. Oils and Fats
The Commission proposes limiting imports of HTS chapter 15, Oils and Fats. United States imports from Spain under this category at the two-digit level in 2025 were $1.15 billion (Animal, Vegetable or Microbial Fats and Oils Etc.). At the four-digit level, the United States imports $836.9 million from Spain under HTS 15.09 (Olive Oil & Its Fractions, Not Chemically Modified). The Commission proposes limiting imports of all goods falling under the HTS 15 chapter.
3. Ceramics
The Commission proposes limiting imports of HTS chapter 69, Ceramics. United States imports from Spain under this category in 2025 at the two-digit level were $634.7 million (Ceramic Products). At the four-digit level, the United States imports $523.7 million under HTS 69.07 (Ceramic Tiles and Mosaic Cubes) from Spain. The Commission proposes limiting imports of all goods falling under the HTS 69 chapter.
4. Articles of Stone
The Commission proposes limiting imports of HTS chapter 68, Articles of Stone. United States imports from Spain under this category in 2025 totaled $270.6 million (Articles of Stone, Plaster, Cement, Asbestos, Mica Etc.). At the 4-digit level, the United States imports $176.9 million under HTS 68.10 (Articles of stone, plaster, cement, and related products) from Spain. The Commission proposes limiting imports of all goods falling under the HTS 68 chapter.
(
printed page 65520)
5. Sugar and Confectionaries
The Commission proposes limiting imports of HTS chapter 17, Sugar and Confectionaries. U.S. imports from Spain under this category in 2025 sum to $138.8 million (sugar and confectionary products). The majority of this trade takes place under the category specific to a single 6-digit code, 17.0490 (sugar confection including white chocolate, no cocoa). The Commission proposes limiting imports of all goods falling under the HTS 17 chapter.
VI. Public Participation and Request for Comments
The Commission invites public comment on all aspects of this proposed rule, including the regulatory text and the preliminary regulatory analyses. The most helpful comments would reference a specific portion of the proposal, explain the reason for any recommended change, and include supporting data.
Please note that all comments received are considered part of the public record and will be made available for public inspection at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Such information includes personally identifiable information (“PII”) (such as your name and address). Any PII that is submitted is subject to being posted to the publicly accessible
https://www.regulations.gov
site without redaction. The Commission will not accept anonymous comments.
The Commission may withhold from public viewing information provided in comments that it determines may impact the privacy of an individual, is offensive, or raises copyright or other legal concerns. For additional information, please read the Privacy Act notice that is available via the link in the footer of
https://www.regulations.gov
.
How do I submit confidential business information?
The Commission may provide confidential treatment for identified confidential information to the extent allowed by law. If you would like to request confidential treatment, pursuant to
46 CFR 502.5
, you must submit the following, by email, to
secretary@fmc.gov
:
A transmittal letter that identifies the specific information in the comments for which protection is sought and demonstrates that the information is a trade secret or other confidential research, development, or commercial information.
A confidential copy of your comments, consisting of the complete filing with a cover page marked “Confidential-Restricted,” and the confidential material clearly marked on each page.
A public version of your comments with the confidential information excluded. The public version must state “Public Version—confidential materials excluded” on the cover page and on each affected page and must clearly indicate any information withheld.
VII. Rulemaking Analysis
Administrative Law Matters
Notice and comment procedures are not required because this final rule falls within the Administrative Procedure Act's (APA) exception for “foreign affairs” functions under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1)
.
[
24
]
The Commission, however, is voluntarily electing to issue a notice of proposed rulemaking and solicit public comment.
Because this rule falls within the APA's foreign affairs function exemption, it is exempt from
Executive Order 14192
[
25
]
and from interagency review under
Executive Order 12866
.
[
26
]
Paperwork Reduction Act
This amendment does not contain any collection of information requirements as defined by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (
44 U.S.C. 3501-3520
).
See
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
.
Executive Order 12988
(Civil Justice Reform)
This rule meets the applicable standards in
Executive Order 12988
(Civil Justice Reform) to minimize litigation, eliminate ambiguity, and reduce burden.
National Environmental Policy Act
The Commission has determined that the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA) does not apply to this action. NEPA only applies to “major federal actions.” The terms “major” and “Federal action” each have independent force. NEPA applies only when both of these two criteria are met. The proposed rulemaking, if finalized, would be a “Federal action” but not “major” and therefore not subject to NEPA. The Commission anticipates little to no environmental impact if the proposed changes are adopted. Proposed import restrictions merely restrict Spanish goods from import, but limited Spanish imports are expected to mostly be replaced by similar goods from other nations. Further, the fungibility of cargo containers means that carriers can easily replace lost Spanish cargo volume with volume of other cargo. Given this, the Commission has determined that there will be little to no impact if the proposed rule is adopted, and therefore NEPA does not apply to this action.

§ 551.2
Remedies to Meet or Adjust Conditions Unfavorable to Shipping in the Foreign Trade Created by the Government of Spain.
(a)
Conditions unfavorable to shipping in the foreign trade.
The Federal Maritime Commission (Commission) after investigation has identified the following conditions unfavorable to shipping in the foreign trade of the United States created by the laws or regulations of the Government of Spain (Spain):
(1) Spain announced a policy of preventing certain vessels from docking at Spanish ports.
(2) Spain prevented U.S. flag vessels from docking at Spanish ports on at least three occasions.
(3) Spain expanded and formalized its policy of preventing certain vessels from docking at Spanish ports.
(b)
Definitions
—(1)
Spanish vessel
means a vessel registered under the Spanish flag, documented or registered under the laws of Spain.
(2)
Covered goods
means goods falling within the trade categories listed below that are exported from Spain and intended for import into the United States.
(i) HTS 33—Perfumery and Cosmetics
(ii) HTS 15—Oils and Fats
(iii) HTS 69—Ceramics
(iv) HTS 68—Articles of Stone
(v) HTS 17—Sugar and Confectionaries
(c)
Assessment of fees.
A fee of two hundred thousand dollars is assessed each time a Spanish vessel enters any port of the United States from any foreign port or place.
(
printed page 65521)
(d)
Refusal of clearance by the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.
If any Spanish vessel subject to this section fails to pay any fee within the prescribed period, the Commission may request the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security to refuse clearance required by
46 U.S.C. 60105
to that vessel or any other Spanish vessel. If any vessel, regardless of country of registration, transports any covered goods to a United States port and offloads those covered goods, the Commission may request the Secretary of Homeland Security to refuse clearance required by
46 U.S.C. 60105
to that vessel until the covered goods are reloaded onto that vessel.
(e)
Denial of entry to or detention at United States ports by the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security.
If any Spanish vessel fails to pay any fee required by this section within the prescribed period or if any vessel transports any covered goods destined for the United States, the Commission may request that the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security:
(1) Deny entry for purpose of oceanborne trade, of any designated Spanish vessel or any vessel carrying covered goods to any port or place in the United States or the navigable waters of the United States; or
(2) Detain any designated Spanish vessel or any vessel carrying covered goods to any port or place in the United States or the navigable waters of the United States.
(f)
Adjustment in fees and goods to meet retaliatory measures.
Upon a finding by the Commission that U.S. carriers or shippers have been subjected to discriminatory fees, restrictions, services disruptions, denial of access to ports, or other retaliatory measures by Spain, or any agency, organization, or person under the authority or control thereof, the level of fee set forth in paragraph (c) of this section shall be increased and additional chapters of HTS goods shall be added to the definition of covered goods. The increase and additions shall be based on the economic harm to U.S. carriers or shippers as a result of such retaliatory actions, provided that the total fee under this section shall not exceed the limits for Commission fees set by statute and regulation.

AGENCY:
National Endowment for the Arts.
ACTION:
Notice of meetings.
SUMMARY:
Pursuant to the Federal Advisory Committee Act, as amended, notice is hereby given that 51 meetings of the Arts Advisory Panel to the National Council on the Arts will be held by teleconference or videoconference.
DATES:
See the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section for individual meeting times and dates. All meetings are Eastern time and ending times are approximate:
ADDRESSES:
National Endowment for the Arts, Constitution Center, 400 7th St. SW, Washington, DC 20506.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Further information with reference to these meetings can be obtained from Daniel Beattie, Office of Guidelines & Panel Operations, National Endowment for the Arts, Washington, DC 20506;
ogpo@arts.gov
or call 202-682-5688.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The closed portions of meetings are for the purpose of Panel review, discussion, evaluation, and recommendations on financial assistance under the National Foundation on the Arts and the Humanities Act of 1965, as amended, including information given in confidence to the agency. In accordance with the determination of the Chair of April 30, 2026, these sessions will be closed to the public pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 10
.

AGENCY:
Executive Office for Immigration Review, United States Department of Justice.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
In the Notice section of today's
Federal Register
, the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), a component within the United States Department of Justice (DOJ or Department), has published a notice of a new system of records titled “Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program Records” and numbered JUSTICE/EOIR-006. This system of records is exempt from U.S.C. 552a(c)(3) and (d) pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a
(k)(2). EOIR proposes to exempt this system of records from certain provisions of the Privacy Act in order to protect law enforcement sensitive materials maintained in the system. For the reasons provided below, the Department proposes to amend its Privacy Act regulations by exempting records in this system from certain provisions of the Privacy Act. Public comment is invited.
DATES:
Comments must be received by November 16, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may send comments by any of the following methods:
Email:
privacy.compliance@usdoj.gov
.
To ensure proper handling, please reference the CPCLO Order No. in the subject line of the message.
Fax:
202-307-0693.
Mail:
United States Department of Justice, Office of Privacy and Civil Liberties, ATTN: Privacy Analyst, Two Constitution Square, 145 N St. NE, Suite 8W-300, Washington, DC 20530. All comments sent via regular or express mail will be considered timely if postmarked on the day the comment period closes. To ensure proper handling, please reference the CPCLO Order No. in your correspondence.
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
http://www.regulations.gov
.
When submitting comments electronically, you must include the CPCLO Order No. in the subject box. Please note that the Department is requesting that electronic comments be submitted before midnight Eastern Daylight Savings Time on the day the comment period closes because
http://www.regulations.gov
terminates the public's ability to submit comments at that time. Commenters in time zones other than Eastern Time may want to consider this so that their electronic comments are received.
(
printed page 65513)
Posting of Public Comments:
Please note that all comments received are considered part of the public record and made available for public inspection online at
http://www.regulations.gov
and in the Department's public docket. Such information includes personally identifying information (such as your name, address, etc.) voluntarily submitted by the commenter. If you want to submit personal identifying information (such as your name, address, etc.) as part of your comment, but do not want it to be posted online or made available in the public docket, you must include the phrase “PERSONAL IDENTIFYING INFORMATION” in the first paragraph of your comment. You must also place all personal identifying information that you do not want posted online or made available in the public docket in the first paragraph of your comment and identify what information you want redacted.
If you want to submit confidential business information as part of your comment, but do not want it to be posted online or made available in the public docket, you must include the phrase “CONFIDENTIAL BUSINESS INFORMATION” in the first paragraph of your comment. You must also prominently identify confidential business information to be redacted within the comment. If a comment has so much confidential business information that it cannot be effectively redacted, all or part of that comment may not be posted online or made available in the public docket.
Personal identifying information and confidential business information identified and located as set forth above will be redacted and the comment, in redacted form, may be posted online and placed in the Department's public docket file. Please note that the Freedom of Information Act applies to all comments received. If you wish to inspect the agency's public docket file in person by appointment, please see the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
paragraph, below.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Justine Fuga, Senior Component Official for Privacy, Office of the General Counsel; Executive Office for Immigration Review, 5107 Leesburg Pike, Suite 2600, Falls Church, VA 22041;
Justine.Fuga@usdoj.gov
;
EOIR.Privacy.Intake@usdoj.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The primary mission of EOIR is to adjudicate immigration cases by fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly interpreting and administering the Nation's immigration laws. Under delegated authority from the Attorney General, EOIR conducts immigration court proceedings, appellate reviews, and administrative hearings. Individuals who are subjects of EOIR immigration proceedings may be represented by counsel.
Within EOIR's Office of the General Counsel (OGC), under the supervision of a designated anti-fraud officer, the Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program (Fraud Program) investigates complaints of immigration fraud, immigration scams, and the unauthorized practice of immigration law within EOIR proceedings. The Fraud Program refers complaints of fraud to appropriate law enforcement and disciplinary authorities; and it provides training for EOIR personnel, outreach materials, and education for the public on these issues.
See
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)
.
The anti-fraud officer serves as a point of contact relating to concerns about possible fraud involving EOIR proceedings, particularly with respect to matters relating to fraudulent applications or documents affecting multiple removal proceedings, applications for relief from removal, appeals, or other proceedings before EOIR.
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)(i)
. The Fraud Program coordinates with investigative authorities of the Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security, and other appropriate agencies with respect to the identification of and response to reported fraud.
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)(ii)
. The Fraud Program also collaborates with the EOIR disciplinary counsel and with other appropriate authorities with respect to instances of fraud, misrepresentation, or abuse pertaining to an attorney or accredited representative providing representation to clients in EOIR immigration proceedings.
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)(iii)
.
The Fraud Program maintains a system of records in connection with its work receiving, tracking, managing, investigating, and responding to reports of suspected immigration fraud, abuse, and unauthorized practice of immigration law. The Fraud Program refers complaints to appropriate Federal, state, local, territorial, or tribal law enforcement and disciplinary authorities for further investigation into potential violations of civil and/or criminal law. When referring complaints, the Fraud Program will provide authorities with copies of records maintained in the system. The records include information pertaining to complainants, witnesses, and subjects of investigations of alleged fraud and individuals (EOIR adjudicators or personnel, or members of the public) reporting or observing alleged fraud. Such records contain law enforcement sensitive information and are properly exempt from various provisions of the Privacy Act pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a(k)(2)
.
II. Privacy Act Exemptions
The Privacy Act allows Federal agencies to exempt eligible records in a system of records from certain provisions of the Act, including those that provide individuals with a right to request access to and amendment of records about the individual. If an agency intends to exempt a particular system of records, it must first issue a rulemaking pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(1)-(3)
, (c), and (e).
The Department proposes to modify
28 CFR part 16
to amend the Privacy Act exemptions for the new system of records, Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program Records, JUSTICE/EOIR-006. Specifically, in section 16.83, the Department proposes to add paragraph (g) claiming certain records within the new system of records are exempt from
5 U.S.C. 552a(c)(3)
and
(d)
and
(2)
pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a(k)(2)
. The exemption is justified because access to or an accounting for disclosures of records contained in this system of records could inform the subject of the investigation of an actual or potential criminal, civil, or regulatory violation or the existence of that investigation; of the nature and scope of the information and evidence obtained by the investigation as to the subject's activities; of the identity of confidential sources, witnesses, and law enforcement personnel; and of information that may enable the subject to avoid detection or apprehension. These factors would present a serious impediment to effective law and regulatory enforcement where they prevent the successful completion of the investigation; endanger the physical safety of confidential sources, witnesses, and law enforcement personnel; and/or lead to the improper influencing of witnesses, the destruction of evidence, or the fabrication of testimony.
These exemptions apply only to the extent that information in this system of records is subject to exemption pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a
(k)(2). To the extent that information in a record pertaining to an individual does not relate to official Federal investigations and/or law enforcement matters, the exemption does not apply. In addition, where compliance would not appear to interfere with or adversely affect the overall law or regulatory enforcement process, the applicable exemption may be waived by EOIR.
(
printed page 65514)
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563—Regulatory Review
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 552a(k)
, this proposed action is subject to formal rulemaking procedures by giving interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rulemaking process “through submission of written data, views, or arguments,” pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
. The purpose of this proposed rule is to exempt certain records within this system from the requirements of
5 U.S.C. 552a(c)(3)
and
(d)
to protect law enforcement sensitive information contained within the system of records. This proposed rule does not raise novel legal or policy issues, nor does it adversely affect the economy, the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, user fees, loan programs, or the rights and obligations of recipients thereof in a material way. The Office of Management and Budget has determined that this rule is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
, section 3(f), and accordingly this rule has not been reviewed by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs within the Office of Management and Budget pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
This proposed rule will only impact Privacy Act-protected records, which are personal and generally do not apply to an individual's entrepreneurial capacity, subject to limited exceptions. Accordingly, the Chief Privacy and Civil Liberties Officer, in accordance with the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
), has reviewed this regulation and by approving it certifies that this regulation will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (Subtitle E-Congressional Review Act)
The Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) of 1996,
5 U.S.C. 801
et seq.,
requires the Department to comply with small entity requests for information and advice about compliance with statutes and regulations within the Department's jurisdiction. Any small entity that has a question regarding this document may contact the person listed in
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
paragraph, above. Persons can obtain further information regarding SBREFA on the Small Business Administration's web page at
https://www.sba.gov/​advocacy
.
This proposed rule is not a major rule as defined by
5 U.S.C. 804
of the Congressional Review Act.
Executive Order 13132
—Federalism
This proposed rule will not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship between the national government and the States, or on distribution of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government. Therefore, in accordance with
Executive Order 13132
, it is determined that this rule does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a Federalism Assessment.
Executive Order 12988
—Civil Justice Reform
This proposed regulation meets the applicable standards set forth in sections 3(a) and 3(b)(2) of
Executive Order 12988
to eliminate drafting errors and ambiguity, minimize litigation, provide a clear legal standard for affected conduct, and promote simplification and burden reduction.
Executive Order 13175
—Consultation and Coordination With Indian Tribal Governments
This proposed rule will have no implications for Indian Tribal governments. More specifically, it does not have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal government and Indian tribes. Therefore, the consultation requirements of
Executive Order 13175
do not apply.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995
This proposed rule will not result in the expenditure by State, local and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100,000,000, as adjusted for inflation, or more in any one year, and it will not significantly or uniquely affect small governments. Therefore, no actions were deemed necessary under the provisions of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995.
Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995,
44 U.S.C. 3507(d)
, requires the Department to consider the impact of paperwork and other information collection burdens imposed on the public. This system of records may include copies of the official records of proceedings (ROPs) in immigration cases before EOIR, which are comprised in part by EOIR and DHS forms subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act. A list of active EOIR forms and their OMB Control Numbers can be found on the EOIR website at
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​eoir-forms
.
A list of active DHS forms and their OMB Control Numbers can be found on the DHS website at
https://www.dhs.gov/​find-dhs-forms
.

title: Privacy Act of 1974; Systems of Records
abstract: Pursuant to the Privacy Act of 1974 and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular No. A-108, notice is hereby given that the Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR), a component within the United States Department of Justice (DOJ or Department), proposes to develop a new system of records notice titled "Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program Records," and numbered JUSTICE/EOIR-006. This system of records assists the EOIR Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program (Fraud Program) in receiving, tracking, and managing complaints of suspected immigration fraud, abuse, and unauthorized practice of immigration law, and in referring complaints to Federal, state, and local law enforcement and disciplinary authorities when appropriate. Fraud Program records were previously included within a different system of records, JUSTICE/EOIR-001. See 69 FR 16179 (May 11, 2004). However, JUSTICE/EOIR-001 was recently modified and now only partially covers Fraud Program records. See JUSTICE/EOIR-001, Adjudication and Appeal Records of the Office of the Chief Immigration Judge and Board of Immigration Appeals, 90 FR 42265 (Aug. 29, 2025). Accordingly, EOIR proposes to establish a new system of records encompassing all Fraud Program records.

(May 11, 2004). However, JUSTICE/EOIR-001 was recently modified and now only partially covers Fraud Program records.
See
JUSTICE/EOIR-001, Adjudication and Appeal Records of the Office of the Chief Immigration Judge and Board of Immigration Appeals,
90 FR 42265
(Aug. 29, 2025). Accordingly, EOIR proposes to establish a new system of records encompassing all Fraud Program records.
DATES:
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 552a(e)(4)
and
(11)
, this notice is effective upon publication, subject to a 30-day period in which to comment on the routine uses, described below. Routine uses will become effective after the 30-day comment period. Please submit any comments by November 16, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
The public, OMB, and Congress are invited to submit any comments by mail to the United States Department of Justice, Office of Privacy and Civil Liberties, ATTN: Privacy Analyst, Two Constitution Square (2CON), 145 N Street NE, Suite 8W.300, Washington, DC 20530; by facsimile at 202-307-0693; or by email at
privacy.compliance@usdoj.gov
. To ensure proper handling, please reference the above CPCLO Order No. on your correspondence.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Justine Fuga, Senior Component Official for Privacy, Office of the General Counsel; Executive Office for Immigration Review, 5107 Leesburg Pike, Suite 2600, Falls Church, VA 22041;
Justine.Fuga@usdoj.gov
;
EOIR.Privacy.Intake@usdoj.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The primary mission of EOIR is to adjudicate immigration cases by fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly interpreting and administering the Nation's immigration laws. Under delegated authority from the Attorney General, EOIR conducts immigration court proceedings, appellate reviews, and administrative hearings. Individuals and aliens who are subjects of EOIR immigration proceedings may be represented by counsel.
Within EOIR's Office of the General Counsel (OGC), under the supervision of a designated anti-fraud officer, the Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program (Fraud Program) investigates complaints of immigration fraud, immigration scams, and the unauthorized practice of immigration law within EOIR proceedings. The Fraud Program refers complaints of fraud to appropriate law enforcement and disciplinary authorities; and it provides training for EOIR personnel, outreach materials, and education for the public on these issues.
See
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)
.
The anti-fraud officer serves as a point of contact relating to concerns about possible fraud involving EOIR proceedings, particularly with respect to matters relating to fraudulent applications or documents affecting multiple removal proceedings, applications for relief from removal, appeals, or other proceedings before EOIR.
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)(i)
. The Fraud Program coordinates with investigative authorities of the Department of Justice, Department of Homeland Security, and other appropriate agencies with respect to the identification of and response to reported fraud.
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)(ii)
. The Fraud Program also collaborates with the EOIR disciplinary counsel and with other appropriate authorities with
(
printed page 65603)
respect to instances of fraud, misrepresentation, or abuse pertaining to an attorney or accredited representative providing representation to clients in EOIR immigration proceedings.
8 CFR 1003.0(f)(2)(iii)
.
This system of records is used by the Fraud Program in connection with its work receiving, tracking, managing, investigating, and responding to reports of suspected immigration fraud, abuse, and unauthorized practice of immigration law, and referring complaints to Federal, state, local, territorial, or tribal law enforcement and disciplinary authorities when appropriate. The system consists primarily of electronic records. Records received in hard copy are digitized and the hard copies are disposed of following quality control checks of the digital copies, in accordance with authorized agency records information management practices. Records are stored on the DOJ EOIR Microsoft Azure Cloud in agency shared drives and disposed of in accordance with applicable record retention schedules. As such, EOIR has prepared this system of records notice to account for the changes to JUSTICE/EOIR-001, resulting in the need for a system of records specific to the Fraud Program system of records.
Finally, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a(k)(2)
, EOIR claims that information in this system is exempt from
5 U.S.C. 552a(c)
and
(d)
. Rules will be promulgated in accordance with the requirements of
5 U.S.C. 553(b)
, (c), and (e) and will be published and codified in the
Federal Register
at
28 CFR 16.83
.
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 552a(r)
, the Department has provided a report to OMB and Congress on this new system of records.
