PURPOSE(S) OF THE SYSTEM:
The purpose of this system is to maintain records of the Fraud Program in connection with its work receiving, tracking, managing, investigating, and responding to reports of suspected immigration fraud, abuse, and unauthorized practice of immigration law, and referring complaints to law enforcement and disciplinary authorities when appropriate. The records in the system are also used to generate statistical reports, informational materials for public awareness concerning immigration fraud issues, and internal materials to train EOIR personnel in identifying and reporting suspected fraud.
CATEGORIES OF INDIVIDUALS COVERED BY THE SYSTEM:
This system includes records pertaining to complainants, witnesses, and subjects of investigations of alleged fraud; EOIR adjudicators and personnel reporting, observing, or investigating alleged fraud; individuals who are subjects of EOIR immigration proceedings; attorneys, representatives, and organizations practicing before EOIR adjudicators; and law enforcement and disciplinary authorities to which the Fraud Program refers complaints.
CATEGORIES OF RECORDS IN THE SYSTEM:
The system includes the following categories of electronic records: Fraud Program case files, related data, and education and training materials.
Fraud Program case files consist of: complaints of fraud, including the complainant's contact information; evidentiary records submitted with complaints or collected during the course of investigating and substantiating complaints, including copies of relevant portions of official records of immigration proceedings and digital audio recordings of immigration hearings; correspondence, witnesses statements, memoranda, and notes collected or created in the course of investigating and substantiating complaints; correspondence with law enforcement and disciplinary authorities to which a complaint may be referred.
Fraud Program data contained in the records in this system consists of: complaints, including case number and status; the date a complaint or case was reported or closed; names and contact information of complainants, witnesses, subjects, and law enforcement or disciplinary authorities; and date of birth, age, sex, and physical descriptors of the complainants, witnesses, or subjects, as well as their alien registration number (A-number), and/or EOIR ID numbers. Fraud Program data is used to generate statistical reports.
This system includes general educational materials, including the Fraud Program Newsletter, created by the Fraud Program for purposes of informing and raising internal and/or public awareness concerning immigration-related fraud issues. The system also includes internal training materials and presentations developed by the Fraud Program to train EOIR personnel on identifying and reporting suspected fraud.
RECORD SOURCE CATEGORIES:
Records in this system are generated or provided by members of the public; EOIR personnel; and law enforcement or disciplinary authorities.
ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND THE PURPOSES OF SUCH USES:
In addition to those disclosures generally permitted under
5 U.S.C. 552a(b)
, all or a portion of the records contained in this system of records may be disclosed as a routine use pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a(b)(3)
under the circumstances or for the purposes described below, to the extent such disclosures are compatible with the purposes for which the information in the record was collected:
(1) To the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), including but not
(
printed page 65604)
limited to the Disciplinary Counsel(s) for the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), Homeland Security Investigations, and Fraud Detection and National Security Directorate, to investigate and respond to complaints of fraud;
(2) To Federal agencies, including but not limited to the Federal Trade Commission and DHS, involved in statistical analysis of data, and publication and/or reporting of aggregated or de-identified information designed to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of immigration proceedings at those agencies or to better meet EOIR's mission of adjudicating cases fairly, expeditiously, and uniformly interpreting and administering the Nation's immigration laws.
(3) Where a record, either alone or in conjunction with other information, indicates a violation or potential violation of law—criminal, civil, or regulatory in nature—to the appropriate federal, state, local, territorial, tribal, or foreign law enforcement authority or other appropriate entity charged with the responsibility for investigating or prosecuting such violation or charged with enforcing or implementing such law.
(4) To any person or entity that EOIR has reason to believe possesses information regarding a matter within the jurisdiction of EOIR, to the extent deemed to be necessary by EOIR in order to elicit such information or cooperation from the recipient for use in the performance of an authorized activity, such as to assist EOIR in evaluating and substantiating claims of immigration-related fraud or abuse or unauthorized practice of immigration law.
(5) In an appropriate proceeding before a court, grand jury, or administrative or adjudicative body, when the Department or an adjudicator determines that the records are relevant to the proceeding; or when the records are relevant to a proceeding and the DOJ or any subcomponent thereof is authorized to appear in it; or when any of the following is a party to litigation or has an interest in litigation: DOJ or any components thereof; any DOJ employee in his or her official capacity; any DOJ employee in his or her individual capacity where DOJ has agreed to represent the employee; or the United States where DOJ or any component thereof determines that litigation is likely to affect it or any of its subdivisions.
(6) To an actual or potential party to litigation or the party's authorized representative for the purpose of negotiation or in connection with settlement, plea bargaining, or discovery proceedings, whether formal or informal.
(7) To the news media and the public, including disclosures pursuant to
28 CFR 50.2
, unless it is determined that release of the specific information in the context of a particular case would constitute an unwarranted invasion of personal privacy.
(8) To contractors, grantees, experts, consultants, students, and others performing or working on a contract, service, grant, cooperative agreement, or other assignment for the agency, when necessary to accomplish an agency function related to this system of records.
(9) To designated officers and employees of state, local, territorial, or tribal law enforcement or detention agencies in connection with the hiring or continued employment of an employee or contractor, where the employee or contractor would occupy or occupies a position of public trust as a law enforcement officer or detention officer having direct contact with the public or with prisoners or detainees, to the extent that the information is necessary to the recipient agency's decision.
(10) To appropriate officials and employees of a federal agency or entity that requires information relevant to a decision concerning the hiring, appointment, or retention of an employee; the assignment, detail, or deployment of an employee; the issuance, renewal, suspension, or revocation of a security clearance; the execution of a security or suitability investigation; the letting of a contract, or the issuance of a grant or benefit.
(11) To a former employee of the Department for purposes of responding to an official inquiry by a Federal, state, or local government entity or professional licensing authority; in accordance with applicable Department regulations; or facilitating communications with a former employee that may be necessary for personnel-related or other official purposes where the Department requires information and/or consultation assistance from the former employee regarding a matter within that person's former area of responsibility.
(12) To Federal, state, local, territorial, tribal, foreign, or international licensing agencies or associations which require information concerning the suitability or eligibility of an individual for a license or permit.
(13) To a Member of Congress or staff acting upon the Member's behalf when the Member or staff requests the information on behalf of, and at the request of, the individual who is the subject of the record.
(14) To the National Archives and Records Administration (NARA) for purposes of records management inspections conducted under the authority of
44 U.S.C. 2904
and
2906
.
(15) To appropriate agencies, entities, and persons when (i) the Department suspects or has confirmed that there has been a breach of the system of records; (ii) the Department has determined that as a result of the suspected or confirmed breach there is a risk of harm to individuals, the Department (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security; and (iii) the disclosure made to such agencies, entities, and persons is reasonably necessary to assist in connection with the Department's efforts to respond to the suspected or confirmed breach or to prevent, minimize, or remedy such harm.
(16) To another Federal agency or Federal entity, when the Department determines that information from this system of records is reasonably necessary to assist the recipient agency or entity in (i) responding to a suspected or confirmed breach, or (ii) preventing, minimizing, or remedying the risk of harm to individuals, the recipient agency or entity (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security, resulting from a suspected or confirmed breach.
(17) To any Federal Office of the Inspector General, or similar publicly identified official of a federal agency who has the official mission and duty to detect and deter waste (the squandering of money or resources even if not explicitly illegal), fraud (the attempt to obtain something of value through willful misrepresentation), and abuse (behaving improperly or unreasonably, or misusing one's position or authority), as necessary for the purpose of identification and elimination of such waste, fraud, and abuse related to Federal programs, employees, contractors, grantees, inmates, or beneficiaries.
(18) To such recipients and under such circumstances and procedures as are mandated by federal statute, regulation, or treaty.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR STORAGE OF RECORDS:
All electronic records in this system are stored in electronic media via a configuration of government servers and in accordance with Federal and Department information security standards. Records received in hard
(
printed page 65605)
copy are digitized. Digitized copies undergo quality control checks to confirm the digitization of the records was complete and accurate before the original hard copy is disposed of in accordance with authorized agency record information management practices. Records in this system are maintained in accordance with applicable laws, rules, and policies on protecting individual privacy and operating in a Federal Risk and Authorization Management Program (FedRAMP) certified cloud-storage environment. Stored records are organized by complainant name, complaint or case number, complaint or case type and date, complaint or case status, and/or the name of the subject of the complaint or case.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETRIEVAL OF RECORDS:
Records may be retrieved by complainant name, complaint or case type, complaint or case numbers, date the complaint or case was reported or closed, and/or the name of the subject of the complaint or case. Records may only be retrieved by authorized DOJ personnel on a need-to-know basis.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETENTION AND DISPOSAL OF RECORDS:
Records are retained in accordance with EOIR Agency Records Control Schedule DAA-0582-2017-0001. The Immigration Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program Case Files and Data are temporary records retained for 15 years after cutoff (DAA-0582-2017-0001-0001 and DAA-0582-2017-0001-0002). The Fraud and Abuse Prevention Program Newsletters are temporary records disposed of 5 years after cutoff (DAA-0582-2017-0001-0003). The Fraud and Abuse Prevention Working Files are temporary records with a retention period of 3 years after cutoff (DAA-0582-2017-0001-0004). Fraud Program Items Closed without Action are temporary records retained for 3 years after cutoff (DAA-0582-2017-0001-0005).
ADMINISTRATIVE, TECHNICAL, AND PHYSICAL SAFEGUARDS:
Records in this system are safeguarded in accordance with applicable laws, rules, and policies that protect individual privacy, including automated system security and access policies of EOIR and the Department. Access to records is limited to Department personnel who have an official need for access in order to perform their duties. Electronic records are maintained and backed up on secure servers and networks that may only be accessed by authorized personnel. Physical records are stored in locked filing cabinets or locked offices until they are digitized and disposed of, as described above. Access to records may be restricted depending on a user's role and responsibility within the system. internet connections are protected by multiple firewalls. Security personnel conduct periodic vulnerability scans using DOJ-approved software to ensure security compliance, and security logs are enabled for all computers to assist in troubleshooting and forensics analysis during incident investigations. Users of individual computers can only gain access to the data by authorized user identification and authentication processes. Records are safeguarded in accordance with appropriate laws, rules, and policies based on the classification and handling restrictions of the record.
RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURES:
All requests for access to records must be made in writing and include a general description of the records sought and identifying information about the record subject, including but not limited to, the record subject's full name, date of birth, place of birth, and alien registration number (A-number), where applicable.
See
28 CFR 16.41
;
28 CFR part 16 Appendix I
. If the A-number is not known, or the case occurred before 1988, the date of an Order to Show Cause, country of origin, and location of the immigration hearing must be provided.
See
28 CFR part 16 Appendix I
.
All requests for access to records may be submitted by mail to EOIR's Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) Service Center at 5107 Leesburg Pike, Suite 2600, Falls Church, VA 22041, by email at
EOIR.FOIARequests@usdoj.gov
,
or online through the EOIR FOIA Public Access Link, available at
https://foia.eoir.justice.gov/​app/​Home.aspx
. Additional information for submitting requests to the FOIA Service Center can be found at
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​foia-submit-a-request
. The envelope and letter or email subject should be clearly marked “Privacy Act Access Request.”
The request must describe the records sought in sufficient detail to enable Department personnel to locate them with a reasonable amount of effort. The request should include a general description of the records sought and must include the requester's full name, current address, and date and place of birth. The request must be signed and either notarized or submitted under penalty of perjury. Although no specific form is required, individuals may use Form EOIR-59, Certification and Release of Records, available at
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​eoir-forms
.
More information regarding EOIR's procedures for accessing records is available at
https://www.justice.gov/​eoir/​freedom-information-act-foia
. General information about the Department's procedures for accessing records in accordance with the Privacy Act can be found at
28 CFR part 16 Subpart D
, “Access to and Amendment of Individual Records Pursuant to the Privacy Act of 1974, and Other Privacy Protections.”
CONTESTING RECORD PROCEDURES:
Individuals seeking to contest or amend records maintained in the system should direct their requests to EOIR at the address indicated in the “RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURES” paragraph above. All requests to contest or amend records must be in writing and the envelope, letter, or email subject should be clearly marked “Privacy Act Amendment Request.” All requests must state clearly and concisely what record is being contested, the reasons for contesting it, and the proposed amendment to the record. For general information regarding the Department's procedures for amending or contesting records in accordance with the Privacy Act can be found at
28 CFR 16.46

Individuals may be notified if a record in this system of records pertaining to them is requested via the procedures identified in the “RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURES” paragraph, above.

In this notice of proposed rulemaking, the OJP proposes to exempt this system of records from certain provisions of the Privacy Act in order to comply with the confidentiality provisions of 34 U.S.C. 10231 and 34 U.S.C. 30303 and the requirement of 34 U.S.C. 10134 that the data are to be used solely for statistical or research purposes. Consistent with the data use requirements set forth in 34 U.S.C. 10134, no adverse determinations are made from these records as to any identifiable individual. For the reasons provided below, the Department proposes to amend its Privacy Act regulations by establishing an exemption for records in this system from certain provisions of the Privacy Act. Public comment is invited.

Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
In the Notice section of today's
Federal Register
, the Office of Justice Programs (OJP), a component within the United States Department of Justice (DOJ or Department), has published a notice of a new system of records, Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) Statistical Data, JUSTICE/OJP-017, for the statistical data collections that BJS conducts under
34 U.S.C. 10132
. In this notice of proposed rulemaking, the OJP proposes to exempt this system of records from certain provisions of the Privacy Act in order to comply with the confidentiality provisions of
34 U.S.C. 10231
and
34 U.S.C. 30303
and the requirement of
34 U.S.C. 10134
that the data are to be used solely for statistical or research purposes. Additionally, data are to be used for authorized purposes under the Prison Rape Elimination Act of 2003 (PREA;
44 U.S.C. 3563
) and the
(
printed page 65511)
Death in Custody Reporting Act of 2013 (DCRA;
Pub. L. 113-242
). Consistent with the data use requirements set forth in
34 U.S.C. 10134
, no adverse determinations are made from these records as to any identifiable individual. For the reasons provided below, the Department proposes to amend its Privacy Act regulations by establishing an exemption for records in this system from certain provisions of the Privacy Act. http://www.regulations.gov
.

http://www.regulations.gov

Please note that all comments received are considered part of the public record and made available for public inspection online at
http://www.regulations.gov
and in the Department's public docket. Such information includes personally identifying information (such as your name, address, etc.) voluntarily submitted by the commenter. If you want to submit personal identifying information (such as your name, address, etc.) as part of your comment, but do not want it to be posted online or made available in the public docket, you must include the phrase “PERSONAL IDENTIFYING INFORMATION” in the first paragraph of your comment. You must also prominently identify confidential business information to be redacted within the comment. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
BJS is a Federal statistical agency and is a principal source of official statistics on crime and justice. BJS's mission is to collect, analyze, and disseminate information on crime, criminal offenders, victims of crime, and the operation of justice systems at all levels of government. “BJS Statistical Data” is a new system of records that includes information collected under BJS's authority from sources including survey respondents and from administrative records that are routinely maintained by other entities including Federal, state, local, and tribal criminal justice or governmental agencies and offices. The purpose of this system of records is to maintain data collected under BJS's authority through questionnaires, paper and electronic surveys, interviews, focus groups, and administrative records to support its statistical mission. BJS regularly obtains records with names, dates of birth, addresses, social security numbers, and other identification numbers, to complete its statistical work.
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563—Regulatory Review
In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 552a(k)(4)
, this proposed action is subject to formal rulemaking procedures by giving interested persons an opportunity to participate in the rulemaking process “through submission of written data, views, or arguments,” pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
. The purpose of this system of records is to maintain data collected under BJS's authority through questionnaires, paper and electronic surveys, interviews, focus groups, and administrative records maintained and provided by Federal, state, local, and tribal criminal justice or governmental agencies. This proposed action does not raise novel legal or policy issues, nor does it adversely affect the economy, the budgetary impact of entitlements, grants, user fees, loan programs, or the rights and obligations of recipients thereof in a material way. The Office of Management and Budget has determined that this rule is not a “significant regulatory action” under
Executive Order 12866
, section 3(f), and accordingly this rule has not been reviewed by the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs within the Office of Management and Budget pursuant to
Executive Order 12866
.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
This proposed rule will only impact Privacy Act-protected records, which are personal and generally do not apply to an individual's entrepreneurial capacity, subject to limited exceptions. Accordingly, the Chief Privacy and Civil Liberties Officer, in accordance with the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. 605(b)
), has reviewed this regulation and by approving it certifies that this regulation will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities.
Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 1996 (Subtitle E-Congressional Review Act)
The Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act (SBREFA) of 1996,
5 U.S.C. 801
et seq.,
requires the Department to comply with small entity requests for information and advice about compliance with statutes and regulations within the Department's jurisdiction. Any small entity that has a question regarding this document may contact the person listed in
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
paragraph, above. Persons can obtain further information regarding SBREFA on the Small Business Administration's web page at
https://www.sba.gov/​advocacy
.
This
(
printed page 65512)
proposed rule is not a major rule as defined by
5 U.S.C. 804
of the Congressional Review Act.

—Federalism

Executive Order 13132
, it is determined that this rule does not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation of a Federalism Assessment.
Executive Order 12988
—Civil Justice Reform

Executive Order 12988
to eliminate drafting errors and ambiguity, minimize litigation, provide a clear legal standard for affected conduct, and promote simplification and burden reduction.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Office of Government Ethics (OGE) is issuing this final rule to update the name of an existing departmental component that was previously designated for purposes of the one-year post-employment conflict of interest restriction for senior employees.
DATES:

Kimberly L. Sikora Panza, Associate Counsel; Telephone: 202-482-9300; Email:
usoge@oge.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Substantive Discussion; Revision of Existing Departmental Component
The Director of OGE (Director) is authorized by
18 U.S.C. 207(h)
to designate distinct and separate departmental or agency components in the executive branch for purposes of
18 U.S.C. 207(c)
, the one-year post-employment conflict of interest restriction for senior employees. Under
18 U.S.C. 207(h)(2)
, component designations do not apply to persons employed at a rate of pay specified in or fixed according to subchapter II of
5 U.S.C. chapter 53
(the Executive Schedule). Component designations are listed in appendix B to 5 CFR part 2641.
The representational bar of
18 U.S.C. 207(c)
usually extends to the whole of any department or agency in which a former senior employee served in any capacity during the year prior to termination from a senior employee position. However,
18 U.S.C. 207(h)
provides that whenever the Director “determines that an agency or bureau within a department or agency in the executive branch exercises functions which are distinct and separate from the remaining functions of the department or agency and that there exists no potential for use of undue influence or unfair advantage based on past Government service,” the Director shall by rule designate that agency or bureau as a separate component of that department or agency. As a result, a former senior employee who served in a designated component of a parent department or agency is barred from communicating to or making an appearance before any employee of that component, but is not barred as to any employee of the parent, of another designated component, or of any other agency or bureau of the parent that has not been designated. Likewise, a former senior employee who served in a “parent” department or agency is not barred by
18 U.S.C. 207
(c) from making communications to or appearances before any employees of any designated component of that parent, but is barred as to employees of that parent or of other components that have not been separately designated.
The Director regularly reviews the component designations listed in appendix B to part 2641, and in consultation with the department or agency concerned, makes adjustments as are necessary. Pursuant to the procedures prescribed in
5 CFR 2641.302(e)
, the Department of Transportation has requested that OGE revise the name of one component currently listed in appendix B to part 2641. Specifically, the Department of Transportation requested that OGE revise Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation to read “Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation.” The revision is requested because the Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation was legally renamed the Great Lakes St. Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation as part of the 2021 Consolidated Appropriations Act (Section 512 of Division AA of
P.L. 116-260
), signed into law on December 27, 2020. The Department of Transportation advised that there have been no substantive changes to this component, and that the component name update is purely a technical change. OGE is therefore amending the Department of Transportation listing in appendix B to reflect the current name of this component.
The designation of Saint Lawrence Seaway Development Corporation in appendix B to part 2641 was effective as of January 1, 1991.
See
56 FR 3961
. The component name change being made in this rule, which does not affect the underlying component designation date, is effective on October 15, 2026, the date this rule is published in the
Federal Register
.
II. Matters of Regulatory Procedure
Administrative Procedure Act
Pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553
, as the Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I find that good cause exists for waiving the general requirements for notice of proposed rulemaking, opportunity for public comment, and a 30-day delayed effective date. As the change effectuated by the final rule is a minor, technical amendment to the current regulation, notice and comment is unnecessary. Furthermore, it is important and in the public interest that the component name change, which reflects the current organization of the concerned
(
printed page 65450)
department be published in the
Federal Register
and take effect as promptly as possible.
Regulatory Flexibility Act
As Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I certify under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (
5 U.S.C. chapter 6
) that this rule will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small entities because it affects only Federal departments and agencies and current and former Federal employees.
Paperwork Reduction Act
The Paperwork Reduction Act (
44 U.S.C. chapter 35
) does not apply to this rule because it does not contain information collection requirements that require the approval of the Office of Management and Budget.
Unfunded Mandates Reform Act
For purposes of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (
2 U.S.C. chapter 25
, subchapter II), this rule will not significantly or uniquely affect small governments and will not result in increased expenditures by State, local, and tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector, of $100 million or more (as adjusted for inflation) in any one year.
Congressional Review Act
The rule is not a major rule as defined in
5 U.S.C. chapter 8
, Congressional Review of Agency Rulemaking.
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563
In promulgating this rule, the Office of Government Ethics has adhered to the regulatory philosophy and the applicable principles of regulation set forth in
Executive Order 12866
, Regulatory Planning and Review (
58 FR 51735
, Oct. 4, 1993) and
Executive Order 13563
, Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review (
76 FR 3821
, Jan. 21, 2011). Executive Orders 13563 and 12866 direct agencies to assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select the regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity).
Executive Order 13563
emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, of reducing costs, of harmonizing rules, and of promoting flexibility.
This rule has not been reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget under
Executive Order 12866
because it is not a “significant” regulatory action for the purposes of that order.
Executive Order 12988
As Acting Director of the Office of Government Ethics, I have reviewed this rule in light of section 3 of
Executive Order 12988
, Civil Justice Reform, and certify that it meets the applicable standards provided therein.
Executive Order 13175
The Office of Government Ethics has evaluated this rule under the criteria set forth in
Executive Order 13175
and determined that tribal consultation is not required as this rule has no substantial direct effect on one or more Indian tribes, on the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian tribes, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal Government and Indian tribes.

SUMMARY:
The U.S. Department of Transportation (Department or DOT) is delaying the effective date of its September 3, 2026 final rule, titled “Cause of Airline Delay and Cancellation Categories under Section 511(b) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024,” until February 1, 2027.
DATES:
The effective date of the final rule published on September 3, 2026 (
91 FR 56588
) is delayed until February 1, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Robert Nazareth, Bureau of Transportation Statistics, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590, 202-934-2413,
robert.nazareth@dot.gov
(email). You may also contact Blane Workie, Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590, 202-366-9342 (phone), 202-366-7152 (fax),
blane.workie@dot.gov
(email).
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Delay of Effective Date
On September 3, 2026, the Department published a final rule with an effective date of October 19, 2026 to implement the requirements of Section 511(b) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024. That final rule amended an existing Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) reporting regulation at
14 CFR 234.4
. Under
14 CFR 234.4
, reporting carriers must file a report of the causes of reportable flight cancellations and delays within 15 days of the end of the month for which data are reported.
[
1
]
The September 2026 final rule mandated that ten specific types of events be excluded from the BTS “Air Carrier” causal code for carriers to report delays and cancellations, consistent with statutory requirements. The air carrier code is reserved for circumstances that are within the carrier's control. The final rule created a new reporting category to capture these 10 specific events, ensuring that the data reported to the Department and shared with the traveling public accurately reflects the statutory distinction between carrier-controllable events and the specific exclusions identified by Congress. In the final rule, the Department explained that the rule would require revisions to a BTS information collection under OMB Control No. 2138-0041 and approval by OMB of those revisions.
On September 21, 2026, Airlines for America (A4A) requested that the Department extend the effective date of the final rule, which sets forth when airlines must report under the revised cancellation and delay causal reporting categories, to February 1, 2027 so that the changes to reporting under the final rule would start for flights beginning January 1, 2027.
[
2
]
A4A explained that the requested delay of the effective date would provide necessary additional time for the Department to update the BTS technical reporting directive, which provides reporting instructions to carriers; for industry stakeholders to update their systems to ensure that the data is collected, reported, and ingested properly; and for BTS to update its own systems. A4A also stated that a new calendar year would be the “natural and logical” date for the Department to begin applying the updated categories.
For the reasons requested by A4A, the Department agrees that it is appropriate to delay the effective date of the final rule until February 1, 2027. In particular, the Department agrees that applying the reporting requirement to cancellations and delays starting with the new calendar year will provide clearer information for consumers and industry. In addition, the delayed effective date will provide the Department with additional time to obtain necessary approvals for the revised information collection under the Paperwork Reduction Act.
As noted previously, carriers must submit reports on the causes of flight cancellations and delays to BTS within 15 days of the end of the month for which data are reported. Accordingly, the delay of the effective date for the reporting requirement to February 1, 2027 will apply to the reporting of delays and cancellations of flights occurring on or after January 1, 2027. Airlines must file their reports with BTS for the entire month of January 2027 in a manner reflecting the changes in causal reporting described in the final rule.
Good Cause for This Final Rule
The Administrative Procedure Act provides an exception to its notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures when an agency for good cause finds that the requirement is impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.
[
3
]
The Department's final rule titled “Cause of Airline Delay and Cancellation Categories under Section 511(b) of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024” would be effective on October 19, 2026 absent a delay of the rule's effective date. DOT only recently became aware of air carriers' need to delay the final rule. There is not sufficient time to propose and seek comment on the delayed effective date before the rule would have come into effect. Accordingly, notice-and-comment procedures are impracticable because they cannot be completed prior to the rule's scheduled effective date.
Signed in Washington, DC.
Edward Strocko,
Acting Director, Bureau of Transportation Statistics.

Proposed Project: Assessment of Communities Talk To Prevent Alcohol and Other Drug Misuse (Formerly Assessment of the Underage Drinking Prevention Initiative OMB No. 0930-0288)—Revision
The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, Center for Substance Abuse Prevention (SAMHSA/CSAP) is requesting a revision from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for information collection regarding the
Assessment of Communities Talk to Prevent Alcohol and Other Drug Misuse
, which is implemented by the Substance Use Disorder Prevention Engagement Initiatives (SUDPEI) within CSAP.
Communities Talk
activities are grassroots activities that raise awareness of the public health dangers of substance misuse and engage communities in evidence-based prevention, particularly to individuals aged 12-25 years old. In this survey, substance use disorder (SUD) questions refers to any alcohol or drugs used in the 12 months prior to the survey and the language “alcohol and other drug misuse” will be used to ask questions about SUDs throughout the survey. Alcohol misuse includes any underage use of alcohol. Other drug use includes use of marijuana, cocaine (including crack), heroin, hallucinogens, inhalants, methamphetamine, and any misuse of prescription stimulants, tranquilizers or sedatives (
e.g.
, benzodiazepines), and pain relievers.

SAMHSA/CSAP will be responsible for collecting, compiling, analyzing, and reporting on information requested in this survey.
SAMHSA supports nationwide
Communities Talk
activities every year. Collecting data on each round of
Communities Talk
activities and using this information to inform policy and measure impact connects with SAMHSA's Strategic Plan.
Communities Talk
activities are intended to work at the grassroots level to raise awareness of the public health dangers of drinking alcohol and other drug misuse and to engage communities in evidence-based prevention. Notably,
Communities Talk
activities provide a forum for communities to discuss ways they can best prevent drinking alcohol and other drug misuse by reducing the availability of alcohol and other drugs, and by creating community norms that discourage demand.
SAMHSA will use the information collected to document the implementation efforts of this nationwide initiative, determine if the federally sponsored
Communities Talk
activities lead to additional activities within the community that are aimed at preventing and reducing drinking alcohol and other drug misuse, identify what these activities may possibly include, and help plan for future rounds of
Communities Talk
events. SAMHSA intends to post online a summary document of each round of
Communities Talk
activities and present findings at national conferences attended by CBOs and colleges and universities that have hosted these activities and might host future activities. Similarly, SAMHSA plans to share findings with the Interagency Coordinating Committee on the Prevention of Underage Drinking. Agencies within this committee encourage their grantees to participate as the activity hosts. Additionally, the information collected will support performance measurement for SAMHSA programs under the Government Performance Results Act (GPRA).
Data Collection Component
SAMHSA/CSAP will use a web-based method, such as Qualtrics, to collect data through the Organizer Survey. The web-based application will comply with the requirements of Section 508 of the Rehabilitation Act to permit accessibility to people with disabilities.
On an annual basis, the Organizer Survey will be completed by an estimated 500
Communities Talk
activity organizers and will require only one response per respondent. It will take an average of 15 minutes (0.25 hours) to review the instructions and complete the survey. This burden estimate is based on comments from three 2019
Communities Talk
activity organizers who reviewed the survey and provided comments on how long it would take them to complete it.

AGENCY:
Internal Revenue Service (IRS), Treasury.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking and notice of public hearing.
SUMMARY:
This document contains proposed regulations that would amend regulations regarding an individual taxpayer's eligibility for a premium tax credit (PTC), the computation of a PTC, and an individual's tax liability due to excess advance payments of the PTC. The proposed regulations would affect taxpayers who enroll themselves or a family member in individual health insurance coverage through a Health Insurance Exchange and may be allowed a PTC for this coverage. This document also provides a notice of a public hearing on these proposed regulations.
DATES:
Electronic or written comments must be received by November 30, 2026. A telephonic public hearing on this proposed regulation has been scheduled for December 8, 2026, at 10 a.m. ET. Requests to speak and outlines of topics to be discussed at the public hearing must be received by November 30, 2026. If no outlines are received by November 30, 2026, the public hearing will be cancelled. Requests to attend the public hearing must be received by 5 p.m. ET on December 4, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
Commenters are strongly encouraged to submit public comments electronically. Submit electronic submissions via the Federal eRulemaking Portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
(indicate IRS and REG-101576-26) by following the online instructions for submitting comments. Requests for the public hearing must be submitted as prescribed in the “Comments and Public Hearing” section. Once submitted to the Federal eRulemaking Portal, comments cannot be edited or withdrawn. The Department of the Treasury (Treasury Department) and the IRS will publish for public availability any comments submitted to the IRS's public docket. Send paper submissions to: CC:PA:01:PR (REG-101576-26), Room 5503, Internal Revenue Service, P.O. Box 7604, Ben Franklin Station, Washington, DC 20044. We encourage commenters to include supporting facts, research, and evidence in their
(
printed page 65495)
comments. When doing so, commenters are encouraged to provide citations to the published materials referenced, including active hyperlinks. Likewise, commenters who reference materials which have not been published are encouraged to upload relevant data collection instruments, data sets, and detailed findings as a part of their comment. Providing such citations and documentation will assist us in analyzing the comments.

Concerning the proposed regulations, Mia Romano at (202) 317-4718; concerning submissions of comments or the public hearing, please contact Publications and Regulations Section at (202) 317-6901 (not toll-free numbers) or by email at

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Authority
This notice of proposed rulemaking contains proposed amendments that would amend the Income Tax Regulations (
26 CFR part 1
) under section 36B of the Internal Revenue Code (Code), as amended by sections 71119 and 71301 through 71305 of
Public Law 119-21
, 139 Stat. 72, 306-315, 321-325, (July 4, 2025), commonly known as the One, Big, Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA). Section 36B(h) provides an express delegation of authority for the Secretary of the Treasury or the Secretary's delegate (Secretary) to prescribe such regulations as may be necessary to carry out section 36B, including regulations that provide for the coordination of the Premium Tax Credit (PTC) allowed under section 36B with the program for advance payment of the Premium Tax Credit (APTC) under section 1412 of the Affordable Care Act (ACA).
[
1
]
The proposed regulations are also issued under the authority of section 7805(a) of the Code, which authorizes the Secretary to prescribe all needful rules and regulations for the enforcement of the Code including all rules and regulations as may be necessary by reason of any alteration of law in relation to internal revenue.
Background
I. Definition of “Qualified Health Plan”
Section 36B provides a PTC to applicable taxpayers who meet certain eligibility requirements, and who enroll, or enroll another member of the applicable taxpayer's family, as defined in § 1.36B-1(d)(1), in a qualified health plan (QHP) through a Health Insurance Exchange (Exchange). Under section 36B(c)(3)(A) and § 1.36B-1(c), the term “qualified health plan” has the same meaning as in section 1301(a) of the Affordable Care Act (
42 U.S.C. 18021(a)
) but does not include a catastrophic plan described in section 1302(e) of the Affordable Care Act (
42 U.S.C. 18022(e)
). Individuals must, in general, enroll in a QHP during the open enrollment period for the coverage year, but Exchanges provide special enrollment periods (SEP) for enrollments during a coverage year if certain conditions are met.
Section 71303(b) of the OBBBA amends section 36B(c)(3)(A) to provide that, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027, the term “qualified health plan” does not include any plan enrolled in through an Exchange that fails to provide a pre-enrollment verification process described in section 36B(c)(3)(A)(ii). Section 71304(a) of the OBBBA further amends section 36B(c)(3)(A) to provide that, for plan years beginning after December 31, 2025, the term “qualified health plan” does not include any plan enrolled in during a SEP described in section 36B(c)(3)(A)(iii) (relating to a SEP based on a change in an individual's expected household income).
II. Disallowing PTC During Periods of Medicaid Ineligibility Due to Alien Status
Under section 36B(c)(1)(A) and § 1.36B-2(b)(1), a taxpayer is, in general, not an applicable taxpayer eligible for a PTC unless the taxpayer's household income, as defined in section 36B(d)(2) and § 1.36B-1(e), for the taxable year, is at least 100 percent but not more than 400 percent of the Federal Poverty Level (FPL), as defined in § 1.36B-1(h), for the taxpayer's family size. Prior to the OBBBA amendments, section 36B(c)(1)(B) treated a taxpayer with household income below 100 percent of the FPL for the taxpayer's family size as an applicable taxpayer if the taxpayer or a member of the taxpayer's family was an alien lawfully present in the U.S. and not eligible for the Medicaid program due to immigration status, and the taxpayer met the other applicable taxpayer requirements. Section 71302(a) of the OBBBA removed section 36B(c)(1)(B) effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Thus, for taxable years after December 31, 2025, a taxpayer who is a lawfully present alien with household income below 100% of the FPL for the taxpayer's family size and who is ineligible for Medicaid due to his or her alien status is not eligible for the PTC.
III. Failure To Demonstrate Community Engagement
Under section 36B, a PTC is allowed only for months that are “coverage months” for a taxpayer or a member of the taxpayer's family. Section 1.36B-3(c)(1)(iii) provides that a month is not a coverage month for an individual if the individual is eligible for the full calendar month for minimum essential coverage (within the meaning of § 1.36B-2(c)) other than coverage described in section 5000A(f)(1)(C) of the Code (relating to coverage in the individual market). Under section 5000A(f)(1)(A) and § 1.5000A-2, the term “minimum essential coverage” includes coverage under Government-sponsored programs such as Medicaid.
Section 1.36B-2(c)(2)(i) provides that, for purposes of determining whether a month is a coverage month for an individual, an individual generally is considered eligible for Government-sponsored minimum essential coverage if the individual meets the criteria for coverage under a Government-sponsored program described in section 5000A(f)(1)(A) as of the first day of the first full month the individual may receive benefits under the program. Government-sponsored programs typically require individuals who meet the criteria for eligibility under the program to complete certain requirements to receive benefits under the program. Under § 1.36B-2(c)(2)(ii), an individual who fails, by the last day of the third full calendar month following the event that establishes eligibility for the Government-sponsored minimum essential coverage, to complete the requirements to obtain that coverage is generally treated as eligible for the coverage as of the first day of the fourth calendar month following the event that establishes eligibility.
Notwithstanding these provisions relating to eligibility for Government-sponsored minimum essential coverage, including Medicaid, § 1.36B-2(c)(2)(v) provides that, in general, an individual is treated as not eligible for Medicaid for a period of coverage under a QHP if, when the individual enrolls in the QHP,
(
printed page 65496)
an Exchange conducts an eligibility determination or assessment (within the meaning of
45 CFR 155.302(b)
) and determines or assesses the individual to be not eligible for Medicaid. However, § 1.36B-2(c)(2)(v) also provides that this rule does not apply for an individual who, with intentional or reckless disregard for the facts, provides incorrect information to an Exchange for the year of coverage.
Under the section 36B regulations, a reckless disregard of the facts occurs if the taxpayer makes little or no effort to determine whether the information provided to the Exchange is accurate under circumstances that demonstrate a substantial deviation from the standard of conduct a reasonable person would observe. Likewise, a disregard of the facts is intentional if the taxpayer knows that information provided to the Exchange is inaccurate.
See, e.g.,
§ 1.36B-2(c)(2)(v).
Section 71119(a) of the OBBBA added subsection (xx) to section 1902 of the Social Security Act (
42 U.S.C. 1396a
) relating to an individual's eligibility for medical assistance under a State plan (or waiver of such plan) under title XIX of the Social Security Act (commonly referred to as the Medicaid statute). In general, section 1902(xx) of the Social Security Act provides that States must require, as a condition of Medicaid eligibility, that “applicable individuals” (generally, individuals eligible for Medicaid's “adult group” or certain individuals eligible for medical assistance under demonstration programs authorized under section 1115 of the Social Security Act (
42 U.S.C. 1315
)) demonstrate “community engagement” for at least one month (and up to three consecutive months, as specified by a State) immediately preceding the month during which the applicable individual applies for Medicaid. “Community engagement” is generally defined in section 1902(xx)(2) of the Social Security Act (
42 U.S.C. 1396a(xx)(2)
) as working not less than 80 hours in a month, completing not less than 80 hours of community service in a month, participating in a work program for not less than 80 hours in a month, being enrolled in an educational program at least half-time, or a combination of these activities adding up to not less than 80 hours a month. Applicable individuals can also demonstrate community engagement by meeting certain income requirements. Once enrolled, applicable individuals are subject to ongoing community engagement requirements.
Some individuals are either excepted or excluded from community engagement requirements under section 1902(xx) of the Social Security Act (
42 U.S.C. 1396a(xx)
). States must implement community engagement requirements no later than January 1, 2027, unless the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services grants the state a good faith effort exemption to delay implementation under section 1902(xx)(11)(A) of the Social Security Act (
42 U.S.C. 1396a(xx)(11)(A)
), not to extend beyond December 31, 2028.
For purposes of the definition of coverage month under section 36B(c)(2)(B), section 1902(xx)(7)(B) of the Social Security Act (
42 U.S.C. 1396a(xx)(7)(B)
) provides that an individual is deemed to be eligible for minimum essential coverage under section 5000A(f)(1)(A)(ii) (the Medicaid program under title XIX of the Social Security Act) for a month if the individual would have been eligible for Medicaid but for a failure to meet the requirement to demonstrate community engagement under
42 U.S.C. 1396a(xx)(1)
.
IV. Definition of Coverage Month
Section 1.36B-3(c)(1) provides that a month is a coverage month for an individual if, (i) as of the first day of the month, the individual is enrolled in a QHP through an Exchange; (ii) the taxpayer pays the taxpayer's share of the enrollment premium by the unextended due date for the taxpayer's income tax return for the taxable year, the full premium for the month is paid by advance credit payments, or the amount of the premium paid (including by advance credit payments) for the month is sufficient to avoid termination of the individual's coverage for that month under one of the scenarios described in § 1.36B-3(c)(4); and (iii) the individual is not eligible for the full calendar month for minimum essential coverage (within the meaning of § 1.36B-2(c)) other than coverage described in section 5000A(f)(1)(C) of the Code (relating to coverage in the individual market).
Section 71303(a) of the OBBBA adds sections 36B(c)(5) and 36B(c)(6) effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027.
Section 36B(c)(5)(A) generally provides that a month is not a coverage month for an individual unless the Exchange through which the individual enrolls in QHP coverage verifies for such month using applicable enrollment information provided or verified by the applicant, the individual's eligibility (i) to enroll in the plan through the Exchange, and (ii) for any APTC for the coverage. Section 36B(c)(5)(B) specifies the applicable enrollment information that Exchanges must verify. This includes, to the extent relevant, household income and family size, whether the individual is an eligible alien, “any health coverage status or eligibility for coverage”, and place of residence, along with information not specifically identified in section 36B(c)(5) that the Secretary (in consultation with the Secretary of Health and Human Services) determines to be necessary to the verification prescribed in section 36B(c)(5)(A). Section 36B(c)(5)(E) also allows the Secretary to provide verification waivers for individuals who enroll in a QHP during a SEP based on a change in family size.
Section 36B(c)(6) provides that the term “coverage month” does not include, with respect to any individual covered by a QHP, any month for which the Exchange through which the individual enrolled does not meet the requirements of
45 CFR 155.305(f)(4)(iii)
, as published in the
Federal Register
on June 25, 2025 (
90 FR 27074
). These Exchange requirements relate to individuals who fail to reconcile their APTC with the PTC that they are allowed on the tax return for a prior enrollment year and, consequently, are determined ineligible for APTC. The prior enrollment year is the year of QHP coverage for which the Exchange would use tax data to verify household income and family size.
Section 1312 of the Affordable Care Act (
42 U.S.C. 18032
) provides that an individual is not eligible to enroll in a QHP unless the individual resides in the State that established the Exchange through which the individual is seeking to enroll. In addition, an individual is not eligible to enroll in a QHP if the individual is not, or is not reasonably expected to be for the entire period for which enrollment is sought, a citizen or national of the U.S., or an alien lawfully present in the U.S. These enrollment eligibility requirements are described in greater detail under
45 CFR 155.305(a)
.
Sections 1411 and 1412 of the Affordable Care Act (
42 U.S.C. 18081
and
18082
) in relevant part, require the establishment of a program for determining eligibility for enrolling in a QHP and for APTC.
V. Computation of PTC for Families With Individuals Not Lawfully Present and Individuals Lawfully Present But Not Eligible Aliens
Section 1.36B-3(a) provides that the premium assistance credit amount is the sum of the premium assistance amounts determined under § 1.36B-3(d) for all coverage months for individuals in the taxpayer's family. Under § 1.36B-3(d)(1), the premium assistance amount
(
printed page 65497)
for a coverage month is the lesser of (i) the enrollment premiums, which are the premiums for the month reduced by any amounts that were refunded or unpaid as of the unextended due date for filing the taxpayer's income tax return for the taxable year, for one or more QHPs in which a taxpayer or a member of the taxpayer's family enrolls; or (ii) the excess of the adjusted monthly premium for the applicable benchmark plan over 
                    1/12
                     of the product of a taxpayer's household income and the applicable percentage for the taxable year. The adjusted monthly premium for the applicable benchmark plan is defined in § 1.36B-3(e) and the applicable percentage is defined in § 1.36B-3(g).
For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2027, section 36B(e)(1)(A) provides that if one or more individuals in a taxpayer's family (including the taxpayer) are aliens not lawfully present (within the meaning of section 36B(e)(2)), the enrollment premiums and adjusted monthly premiums for the applicable benchmark plan otherwise taken into account in determining the taxpayer's PTC must be reduced by the portion of such premiums attributable to the individuals who are aliens not lawfully present. In addition, section 36B(e)(1)(B) and § 1.36B-3(l) provide that in determining the taxpayer's applicable percentage, (i) the percentage the taxpayer's household income bears to the FPL for the taxpayer's family size is determined by excluding aliens who are not lawfully present from family size and (ii) by treating household income as equal to the product of the taxpayer's household income and a fraction, the numerator of which is the FPL for the taxpayer's family size determined by excluding aliens who are not lawfully present, and the denominator of which is the FPL for the taxpayer's family size determined by including aliens who are not lawfully present.
Section 71301(a) of the OBBBA amended section 36B(e)(1) to expand the applicability of section 36B(e)(1) to the QHP coverage of individuals in a taxpayer's family (including the taxpayer) who are aliens lawfully present in the U.S. but are not eligible aliens. Section 71301(a) of the OBBBA also adds a definition of the term “eligible alien” to section 36B(e)(2). The OBBBA section 71301 amendments to section 36B are effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026.
VI. Multiple Families Enrolled in One Policy
Section 1.36B-3(h) provides that if a QHP covers more than one family under a single policy, each applicable taxpayer covered by the plan may claim a PTC, if otherwise allowable. In addition, in determining for a month the lesser of the enrollment premiums or the excess of the benchmark plan premium over 
                    1/12
                     of the product of household income and the applicable percentage, the enrollment premiums for the month are allocated to each taxpayer in proportion to the premiums for each taxpayer's applicable benchmark plan.
VII. Excess APTC Repayment Limitation
Section 36B(f)(1) provides that, if APTC is paid for the QHP coverage of a taxpayer or another member of the taxpayer's family, the taxpayer's PTC allowed under section 36B is reduced by the amount of the APTC. Under section 36B(f)(2), if the taxpayer's APTC exceeds the PTC that would have been allowed had no APTC been paid, the taxpayer must increase tax liability for the taxable year of the coverage. For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2026, the tax liability increase was equal to the excess of the APTC over the PTC (excess APTC), unless a repayment limitation in section 36B(f)(2)(B) applied to the taxpayer and the amount of the repayment limitation was less than the excess APTC. This excess APTC repayment limitation is reflected in § 1.36B-4(a)(3)(ii). In addition, § 1.36B-4(a)(3)(iii) provides the excess APTC limitation that must be used by taxpayers who claim a section 162(l) deduction for their QHP premiums. Section 71305 of the OBBBA removed the section 36B(f)(2)(B) repayment limitation for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Thus, for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, a taxpayer's tax liability for the taxable year of the coverage is increased by the full amount of the excess APTC.
VIII. Reporting of QHP Information by Exchanges
Section 36B(f)(3) and § 1.36B-5 require Exchanges to report to taxpayers and the IRS certain information relating to QHP enrollment. This information is reported to taxpayers on IRS Form 1095-A,
Health Insurance Marketplace Statement.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), part of the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), is responsible for the Form 1095-A reporting for Exchanges that use the Federal eligibility and enrollment platform (Federally-facilitated Exchanges, or FFEs, and State-based Exchanges on the Federal platform, or SBE-FPs). States with their own platforms (State-based Exchanges or SBEs) are responsible for the Form 1095-A reporting for individuals who enroll in their State-based Exchange. Among the items Exchanges must report are (i) enrollment premiums for the plan or plans enrolled in (excluding the portion of the premiums allocable to benefits in excess of essential health benefits), and (ii) for plans for which APTC is paid, the premium for the applicable benchmark plan for purposes of computing advance credit payments and the amount of the advance credit payments.
Explanation of Provisions
The proposed regulations would amend the regulations under section 36B to reflect the amendments to section 36B made by sections 71301 through 71305 of the OBBBA. The proposed regulations would also amend the regulations under section 36B to reflect section 71119(a) of the OBBBA's addition of subsection (xx)(7)(B) to section 1902 of the Social Security Act (
42 U.S.C. 1396a
) regarding an individual's eligibility for Medicaid for purposes of determining whether a month is a coverage month under section 36B(c)(2)(B).
I. Change to the Definition of “Qualified Health Plan”
To reflect the amended definition of the term “qualified health plan” in section 36B(c)(3)(A) provided by sections 71303(b) and 71304(a) of the OBBBA, the proposed regulations would amend the definition of “qualified health plan” in § 1.36B-1(c). The proposed regulations would provide that the term “qualified health plan” does not include any plan enrolled in through an Exchange if the Exchange fails to provide a pre-enrollment verification process through which an applicant may, beginning not later than August 1 of the year prior to the enrollment year, verify with the Exchange the applicant's household income and eligibility for enrollment in a plan for the plan year beginning in the subsequent year. For the pre-enrollment verification process that Exchanges must provide, see
45 CFR part 155
and any successor or other applicable regulations as may be promulgated.
In addition, the proposed regulations would amend the definition of “qualified health plan” in § 1.36B-1(c) to provide that, for the purposes of section 36B, the term “qualified health plan” does not include any plan enrolled in during a SEP provided by an Exchange on the basis of the percentage that the individual's expected household income bears to the FPL for the individual's family size (income-based SEP), and not in connection with the occurrence of an event or change in
(
printed page 65498)
circumstances specified by the Secretary of Health and Human Services for such purposes.
II. Determination of “Applicable Taxpayer”
To reflect the OBBBA's removal of section 36B(c)(1)(B), which allowed a taxpayer with household income less than 100 percent of the FPL for the taxpayer's family size to be treated as an applicable taxpayer if the taxpayer is a lawfully present alien not eligible for the Medicaid program due to immigration status, the proposed regulations would remove the reiteration of that rule in § 1.36B-2(b)(5).

IV. Changes to the Definition of “Coverage Month”
a. General Verification Rule
As noted previously, section 71303(a) of the OBBBA, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027, adds section 36B(c)(5) to provide that a month is not a coverage month for a taxpayer unless the Exchange through which the taxpayer or another member of the taxpayer's family enrolls in QHP coverage, using applicable enrollment information, verifies the individual's eligibility (i) to enroll in the plan through the Exchange, and (ii) for any APTC for the coverage. Because section 36B(c)(5)(A) requires, for coverage month purposes, verification of an individual's eligibility to enroll in a QHP and for any APTC, if relevant, verification is required for any individual for whom a month is to be treated as a coverage month. Therefore, this requirement applies regardless of whether the enrollee requests APTC for their coverage. Exceptions associated with changes in family size are further explained below in section IV.b of this proposed rule.
Section 36B(c)(5)(B)(ii) specifies that applicable enrollment information includes whether an individual is an eligible alien, but section 36B(c)(5)(B) does not expressly identify citizenship, status as a national of the U.S., or lawful presence as applicable enrollment information. In addition to eligible aliens, U.S. citizens, nationals of the U.S., and other aliens who are lawfully present are also eligible to enroll in a QHP and an Exchange also verifies these statuses for enrollment eligibility.

Consistent with this proposed rule, a month would not be a coverage month for an individual if the Exchange through which the individual enrolled fails to verify the individual's place of residence and that the individual is a U.S. citizen, a national of the U.S., or an alien lawfully present in the U.S.

Similarly, a month of enrollment may be a coverage month for an individual who does request APTC but for whom no APTC is paid, provided the Exchange verifies enrollment eligibility information. However, months of enrollment would not be coverage months for an individual if the Exchange is unable to verify an individual's eligibility to enroll in the QHP. For example, if the Exchange enrolls an individual in coverage while verification is pending, but the Exchange is subsequently unable to verify the individual's eligibility to enroll in the QHP, then the months of enrollment before the individual was removed from the coverage would not be coverage months for that individual.
In addition, the proposed regulations would provide that a month for which APTC is paid for an individual is not a coverage month for the individual if the Exchange through which the individual enrolled fails to verify relevant applicable enrollment information. The Treasury Department and the IRS believe the language in section 36B(c)(5)(B) “any health coverage status or eligibility for coverage” is referring to eligibility for minimum essential coverage, other than individual market coverage. This is consistent with the function of section 36B(c)(5)(A), which provides rules regarding when a month is not a coverage month for an individual, and with section 36B(c)(2)(B), under which a month is not a coverage month for an individual if the individual is eligible for minimum essential coverage other than individual market coverage.
Therefore, the proposed regulations would provide that a month for which APTC is paid for an individual is not a coverage month for the individual unless the Exchange through which the individual enrolled verifies all of the following items: the prescribed verification items related to enrollment such as residency, and whether the individual is a U.S. citizen, national of the U.S., or an alien lawfully present in the U.S.; the household income and family size of the taxpayer who is expected to file an income tax return for the year of coverage reconciling the APTC for the individual's coverage with the PTC allowed for the coverage; whether the individual is eligible for minimum essential coverage, other than individual market coverage; and, if the individual is a lawfully present alien, whether the individual is an eligible alien as defined in section 36B(e)(2)(B). In sum, for a month for which APTC is paid to be a coverage month, the Exchange must verify the applicable enrollment information for both eligibility to enroll in a QHP and eligibility for APTC.

b. Changes To Verified Information During a Plan Year
The Treasury Department and the IRS anticipate that forthcoming CMS proposed regulations would provide that once an Exchange learns of a change in circumstances relating to a QHP enrollee, the Exchange will, in general, seek to verify that information before adjusting the enrollee's current enrollment, including the amount of APTC being paid for the coverage, when applicable. Once an Exchange has verified the relevant applicable enrollment information for an individual for a plan year, section 36B(c)(5) will not cause a month to fail to be a coverage month for the individual for the remainder of the plan year provided the Exchange follows the procedures in the CMS regulations for eligibility and verification relating to enrollee-reported changes in circumstances.
For example, assume all items in section 36B(c)(5)(B) have been verified for an individual and the individual is enrolled in a QHP and is determined to be eligible for APTC in the amount of $250 per month beginning in January of a plan year. In June of the plan year, the individual informs the Exchange that the individual's projected household income will be less than previously projected and verified, which would make the individual eligible for more than $250 of APTC per month. If the Exchange maintains the current amount of $250 of APTC per month and increases APTC only after it verifies the new lower household income amount, the section 36B(c)(5) verification requirements will be met for this individual. However, if the enrollee informs the Exchange that the enrollee's projected household income will be more than previously projected and verified, which would make the enrollee eligible for less than $250 of APTC per month, section 36B(c)(5) does not prevent the Exchange from immediately implementing the lower APTC amount, prior to verification of the new information.

V. Eligible Alien Requirement and Conforming Amendments to PTC Computation
The proposed regulations would amend § 1.36B-3 to reflect the OBBBA's expansion of the limitation on aliens' eligibility for the PTC in section 36B(e)(1) to encompass individuals in a taxpayer's family who are aliens lawfully present in the U.S., but who are not eligible aliens, as defined in section 36B(e)(2)(B). The OBBBA section 71301 amendments to section 36B are effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026. Specifically, the proposed regulations would amend § 1.36B-3 to provide that, in determining the premium assistance amount under § 1.36B-3(d)(1), a taxpayer must reduce both the enrollment premiums under § 1.36B-3(d)(1)(i) and the applicable benchmark plan premium under § 1.36B-3(d)(1)(ii) by the portion of the premiums attributable to any individual in the taxpayer's family enrolled in a QHP who is an alien not lawfully present in the U.S. or, if a lawfully present alien, is not an eligible alien. In addition, the proposed regulations would expand § 1.36B-3(l), which now applies to taxpayers with a family member who is an alien not lawfully present in the U.S., to also apply to taxpayers with a family member who is a lawfully present alien, but not an eligible alien.
The proposed regulations would also amend § 1.36B-3(h) relating to the manner in which, in computing the PTC, the enrollment premiums for a QHP are allocated among multiple families enrolled in the QHP. The proposed regulations would provide that if (1) a QHP covers more than one family on a single policy and (2) one or more of the families have individuals enrolled in the QHP who are aliens not lawfully present or, in the case of aliens who are lawfully present, are not eligible aliens, then taxpayers must allocate enrollment premiums in accordance with § 1.36B-3(h)(2). Because the actual enrollment premium is a single amount for the policy and is not family specific, an allocation is required to appropriately reflect the correct amount of enrollment premiums for each family when computing the PTC. Consequently, this allocation must exclude individuals enrolled in the QHP who are aliens not lawfully present or, in the case of aliens who are lawfully present, are not eligible aliens.
The proposed rule would provide that a taxpayer's allocation of the monthly enrollment premium equals the total monthly enrollment premium for the policy (including the premium attributable to any individuals not lawfully present or if lawfully present, not eligible aliens), multiplied by the ratio of the monthly applicable benchmark plan premium for the taxpayer's family, which is determined by excluding any alien who is not lawfully present, or a lawfully present alien but not an eligible alien, to the monthly applicable benchmark plan premium for all families enrolled in the policy, which is determined by including any alien who is not lawfully present or, if an alien lawfully present, is not an eligible alien. Using the applicable benchmark plan premium for all families enrolled in the policy, including any individuals who are not lawfully present or, if lawfully present aliens, are not eligible aliens, as the denominator ensures that the full monthly enrollment premium is consistently allocated across all families who share the same policy.
VI. Elimination of Excess APTC Repayment Limitation
The proposed regulations would revise § 1.36B-4(a)(3) to reflect the OBBBA amendment to section 36B(f)(2)(B), which eliminates the limitation on the amount of excess APTC that a taxpayer is required to repay for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. Consequently, when reconciling APTC on a taxpayer's Federal income tax return for such taxable year, the full amount by which APTC exceeds PTC allowed under section 36B increases the taxpayer's tax liability for that taxable year.

I. Regulatory Planning and Review—Economic Analysis
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits (including potential economic, environmental, public health and safety effects, distributive impacts, and equity).
Executive Order 13563
emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and benefits, reducing costs, harmonizing rules, and promoting flexibility.
The proposed regulations have been designated by the Office of Management and Budget's (OMB's) Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) as subject to review under
Executive Order 12866
pursuant to the Memorandum of Agreement (MOA, July 4, 2025) between the Treasury Department and the OMB regarding review of tax regulations. OIRA has determined that the proposed rulemaking is significant under section 3(f) of
Executive Order 12866
and subject to review under
Executive Order 12866
and section 1(b) of the MOA. Accordingly, the proposed regulations have been reviewed by OMB.
a. Need for Regulation
The OBBBA revised the eligibility and computational rules for an individual taxpayer's PTC, and these proposed regulations are necessary to comply with the OBBBA amendments to section 36B.
b. The Statute and the Proposed Regulations
The OBBBA amended section 36B of the Code. Additionally, the OBBBA amendment to section 1902 of the Social Security Act affects the section 36B “coverage month” determination.
Section 71301(a) expands the existing section 36B(e)(1) rule that excludes family members who are not lawfully present from PTC computations. The amendment, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2026, also excludes lawfully present alien family members who are not “eligible aliens.” The proposed regulations would require taxpayers to reduce the enrollment premiums and premiums for the applicable benchmark plan allocable to family members who are not lawfully present or who are aliens lawfully present but not eligible aliens, apply that reduction after any multiple family allocation of enrollment premiums, and exclude those individuals from certain household income calculations used for applicable percentage purposes.
Section 71302(a) removes the rule in section 36B(c)(1)(B) that previously treated certain taxpayers with household income below 100 percent of the applicable FPL as applicable taxpayers if they, or a family member, were lawfully present aliens not eligible for Medicaid because of immigration status, effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025. The proposed regulations would remove the corresponding regulatory provision.
Section 71119 added section 1902(xx)(7)(B) to the Social Security Act and provides, for section 36B coverage month purposes, that an individual is deemed eligible for Medicaid minimum essential coverage for a month if the individual would have been eligible for Medicaid but for a failure to meet a community engagement requirement under section 1902(xx)(1). The proposed regulations would provide that this deemed Medicaid eligibility starts when Medicaid would otherwise have begun, blocks use of the Exchange Medicaid ineligibility safe harbor in these cases, ends once Medicaid ineligibility arises for another reason, and preserves an anti-abuse rule for intentional or reckless misstatements.
Section 71303(a) adds section 36B(c)(5), effective for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2027. Section 36B(c)(5) makes Exchange verification a condition of having a coverage month and, under the related amendment to section 36B(c)(3)(A), of having a QHP for section 36B purposes. The proposed regulations would provide that a month is not a coverage month for an individual who enrolls in a QHP unless the Exchange verifies the individual's residence and citizenship, national status, or lawful presence for the month. For individuals for whom APTC is paid, the proposed regulations would also provide that a month is not a coverage month for an individual unless the Exchange verifies the individual's household income, family size, absence of other minimum essential coverage, and eligible alien status where relevant. The proposed regulations would further coordinate these tax rules with Exchange procedures for re-enrollment and changes in circumstances by tying tax consequences to whether Exchange verification requirements have been satisfied.
Section 71303(a) also adds section 36B(c)(6), which provides that a month is not a coverage month for an individual covered by a QHP if the Exchange fails to satisfy the applicable prior reconciliation requirements with respect to that individual.
