F. Reporting
The proposed amendments would establish new reporting requirements for certain registered funds.
[
111
]
We propose to amend Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP (together, the “forms”) to require certain registered funds to provide additional information about their cross trade-related purchase and sale activity. Specifically, we propose to amend the forms to require registered funds that engaged in cross trades of portfolio investments in reliance on rule 17a-7 during the preceding twelve-month period to disclose, for each asset type (or category of investment, in the case of Form N-MFP) during the reporting period and in U.S. dollars:
[
112
]
The aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund purchased under rule 17a-7;
[
113
]
The aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund purchased;
The aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund sold under rule 17a-7; and
The aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund sold.
[
114
]
The aggregate value would mean the value of portfolio investments purchased or sold, calculated on a gross basis, without netting any purchases and sales. When providing the aggregate value of portfolio investments purchased or sold under the items mentioned in the second and fourth bullets above, a registered fund should include all purchase or sale transactions, including any amounts purchased or sold in cross trades. The trading information would be reported for the preceding month.
[
115
]
This disclosure would follow the filing timelines, publication frequency, and reporting period of each form.
[
116
]
Currently, most registered funds report on Form N-CEN whether they relied on certain statutory and rule-based exemptions, including rule 17a-7.
[
117
]
While this information helps identify whether a registered fund made cross trades in the reporting period, it does not provide any additional information, such as the volume of cross trades by registered fund or asset class. Registered funds currently also are subject to requirements to disclose material information about cross trades in their financial statements.
[
118
]
This information is often in narrative form, which limits comparability, and may not provide a clear picture of the frequency, type, or amount of all cross trades by the registered fund or those that are not deemed material. As suggested by some respondents, reporting aggregated cross-trade information on Form N-PORT could provide additional transparency and visibility into registered funds' cross-trading practices.
[
119
]
The proposed reporting on the forms would provide information about the total and comparative volume of cross trades by asset class in a structured format that can be efficiently analyzed by the Commission staff and market participants across registered funds in a
(
printed page 65641)
way that is not currently available through reports on Form N-CEN or in registered fund financial statements.
Similarly, registered funds do not currently disclose the volume of trading activity that occurred during the reporting period, specifically, the aggregate value of portfolio investments that were purchased or sold. Registered funds are currently required to report information on the forms generally on an “as-of” basis, which provides information at a single point in time, but does not provide this specific information about the volume of investments the registered fund purchased or sold during the period.
[
120
]
This reporting requirement would enable the Commission and its staff and market participants to understand the proportion of a registered fund's overall trading activity that consists of cross trades, both in the aggregate and within specific asset classes, which would provide necessary context for understanding the volume, significance, and materiality of cross trades relative to total trading activity as well as trends in such activity over time. To provide better contextual information about how the volume of a registered fund's cross trades compares to its overall trading activity, the proposed reporting requirement would begin when a registered fund begins cross trading and apply for a 12-month period following any cross trades. During this period, the registered fund would be required to report information about its aggregate trading activity by asset class, even if it does not conduct cross trades for particular months within that period. This approach is designed to recognize that the volume and character of funds' trading activities can vary from month-to-month and also provide an appropriately lengthy period for data review. For example, if we were to instead require aggregate trading information only for months in which a fund conducts cross trades, the aggregate trading information for those months may not accurately reflect how the volume of a fund's cross-trading activity compares to its overall trading activities.
[
121
]
Since the volume of cross trades can reasonably be expected to grow under the proposed amendments, the proposed reporting requirement would assist in understanding and monitoring the effects of that growth and how it affects specific registered funds and asset classes. This reporting requirement would enhance transparency and facilitate more informed decision-making by providing information on cross-trading activity over time for a registered fund and across similar registered funds by asset class and reporting period.
The proposed reporting is also important because cross trades occur outside of the public markets and do not generate publicly observable market data, unlike transactions on registered exchanges or reported through post-trade transparency systems such as TRACE or RTRS. The lack of public information about specific transaction prices may negatively impact price discovery processes. In addition, the lack of public information about the volume of cross trades may distort perceptions of liquidity in a particular asset class or market. While the proposal would not provide the type of transparency available through systems like TRACE or RTRS, the proposed reporting on the forms would provide volume transparency by requiring reporting of the aggregate volume of cross trades, by asset class. If the volumes of cross trades are growing or substantial, this information may help market participants understand the potential effects of the cross trades on the reliability of other available information about trading in that asset class. In addition, the proposed reporting may inform any future Commission action about cross-trading data and whether it should be made available through post-trade transparency systems.
As with other information on the forms, the proposed disclosure would be filed in a structured data format. Standardized disclosure on a registered fund's cross trading and total trading activity would provide transparent, standardized, and comparable information regarding the extent to which the registered fund industry, and each individual registered fund, engages in cross trading, overall volumes, as well as the types of assets involved in such trading activities. This allows investors and other market participants to easily access and process the cross-trade information reported, either by analyzing the forms directly or through analyses prepared by third-party service providers, which may enable more informed investment decisions and promote greater accountability by the adviser. This reporting would also provide market participants with information to evaluate the potential effects of cross trades on perceptions of liquidity in a particular asset class or market.
The information we propose to be reported is designed to balance the burden of providing it with the Commission's and the public's need for the information. The proposal would only require registered funds that engaged in cross trades of portfolio investments in reliance on rule 17a-7 during the preceding twelve-month period to provide information about the aggregate value of cross trade-related purchases and sales grouped by asset type or category of investments. While more granular reporting, such as the price and volume of each trade or cross trade, or industry-wide reporting on total trading volumes, would provide valuable information, registered funds would then bear a more significant reporting burden. In addition, the proposed amendments work with existing recordkeeping obligations under the Investment Company Act, such as the requirement to maintain records of registered funds' portfolio transactions.
[
122
]
The proposed reporting may help mitigate the potential conflicts of cross trading by providing insight into such trading to the Commission and its staff, assisting them in carrying out their regulatory responsibilities, including any future Commission action as to cross trading, risk monitoring during periods of market stress, and regulatory oversight.

J. Transition Period
We propose to provide a tiered transition period for registered funds to come into compliance with the proposed amendments to rule 17a-7 and Forms N-PORT and N-MFP, if adopted, based on fund size. We propose to provide a 12-month transition period for larger entities and an 18-month transition period for smaller entities. For these purposes, larger entities would be registered funds that, together with other investment companies in the same “family of investment companies” (as such term is defined in Item B.5 of Form N-CEN), have net assets of $10 billion or more as of the end of the most recent fiscal year. Smaller entities would be registered funds that, together with other investment companies in the same family of investment companies, have net assets of less than $10 billion as of the end of the most recent fiscal year.

III. Economic Analysis
A. Introduction
The proposed amendments would expand the types of securities eligible for cross trades to include securities valued using observable level 2 inputs, provide two pricing options (NAV-based pricing or current-market pricing using one or more unaffiliated pricing sources), reallocate certain oversight responsibilities from the board to the fund's CCO through quarterly and annual reviews, and permit only
de minimis
payments to unaffiliated parties for necessary administrative services such as clearing and settlement. The amendments would also update recordkeeping requirements and add new structured reporting on Forms N-PORT and N-MFP requiring registered funds that engage in cross trades to report monthly cross-trade activity and aggregate purchase and sale activity by asset class.
As discussed above, cross trading is prohibited under section17(a). Examples of problematic practices include parking,
[
135
]
cherry-picking,
[
136
]
and dumping
[
137
]
securities between a registered fund and its affiliates. However, in circumstances where those conflicts can be effectively mitigated, economic theory suggests that internal execution can achieve the same allocative result as external execution, while consuming fewer real resources.
[
138
]
When a registered fund and its eligible affiliate have offsetting trading interest and a security can be reliably valued through independent pricing, dealer-intermediated execution (that is, execution routed externally through a broker-dealer acting in a principal or agency capacity) may not add any additional benefits to the transaction for either counterparty. Yet dealer intermediation requires greater consumption of real resources, including dealer labor, operational infrastructure, settlement processes, and adviser search costs. Under the current regulatory definition of readily available market quotations, level 2 securities generally cannot be cross traded. As a result, advisers must route trades through external intermediaries even in cases where an internal match could achieve a better economic outcome.
[
139
]
From a social-welfare perspective, this represents a productive inefficiency.
When accounts engage in a cross trade, the price reflects a single valuation derived from reliable, market-based inputs. If both sides have offsetting interest and rely on that same market-informed value, routing the trade externally would not add any meaningful price-setting or negotiation function. In such cases, dealer involvement can introduce additional transaction costs without altering the economic terms of the trade.
Permitting cross trading in level 2 securities under appropriate safeguards (independent valuation, conflict-of-interest controls, and CCO and board oversight) would allow advisers to use the more efficient execution method subject to conditions designed to protect the interests of each fund and its shareholders.
Cross trading may allow funds and certain affiliates to lower trading costs, avoid unnecessary market impact, and match complementary trading needs more effectively than in external markets. At the same time, cross trading can harm funds or other clients and create conflicts of interest because the adviser acts on behalf of multiple funds and affiliates whose interests might not always align.
[
140
]
As explained in section I.C, additional conflicts may also arise when an adviser's compensation varies across the participating funds or affiliates, for example, when advisory or performance-based fees differ, or when the adviser or its personnel have financial interests connected to an affiliate. Without appropriate safeguards, a registered fund could be disadvantaged relative to an affiliate.
[
141
]
The proposed amendments therefore would provide conditions, such as eligibility limits, pricing requirements, fee restrictions, adviser best-interest determinations, and structured CCO oversight, to help funds capture these efficiencies while mitigating conflicts.

(

proposed amendments to rule 17a-7 and the new Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP reporting requirement associated with these amendments, including the anticipated benefits and costs to registered investment companies, investment advisers, fund boards, and investors. To assess these effects, the economic analysis evaluates the proposed amendments relative to the current regulatory and market baseline. Accordingly, the discussion first describes the baseline, then examines the expected benefits and costs of the proposed amendments, then considers the potential effects on efficiency, competition, and capital formation, and finally evaluates the potential economic effects of certain reasonable alternatives. Many of these economic effects are difficult to quantify; where quantification is not practicable, the Commission instead provides a qualitative discussion of the potential economic consequences.

1. Regulatory Framework
Section 17(a) of the Investment Company Act generally prohibits certain transactions between a registered investment company and its affiliates, such as the sale or purchase of securities unless an exemption applies, or the transaction is otherwise permitted by SEC rules. Specifically, it is unlawful for an affiliated person (or an affiliate of such a person), acting as principal, to sell any security or other property to the investment company or purchase any security or other property from the investment company unless permitted by rule or exemption.
[
144
]
Rule 17a-7 provides a narrow exemption for certain purchase or sale transactions between investment companies and certain affiliates.
[
145
]
To qualify for the exemption under current rule 17a-7, the transaction must meet the following conditions: (1) The security involved must have market quotations that are readily available;
[
146
]
(2) The transaction must be executed at the independent current market price;
[
147
]
(3) The transaction must align with the investment policies of each participating fund, as disclosed in their registration statements and reports;
[
148
]
(4) No brokerage commission, fee, or other remuneration may be paid, except for customary transfer fees;
[
149
]
(5) The fund's board of directors, including a majority of disinterested directors, must adopt written procedures reasonably designed to ensure compliance with the rule; review and approve any changes to those procedures, and determine at least quarterly that all transactions were executed in accordance with the procedures;
[
150
]
(6) The board must meet the governance standards defined in rule 0-1(a)(7), which include requirements for board composition and independence;
[
151

and (7) The registered fund must permanently maintain a written copy of the procedures and any modifications; maintain detailed records of each transaction for at least six years (with the first two years in an easily accessible place), including a description of the security, the identity of the counterparty, terms of the transaction, and supporting documentation for the board's quarterly determinations.
[
152
]
Funds are also subject to existing requirements under rule 38a-1, which require them to adopt written compliance policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violation of the Federal securities laws, require CCO and board oversight, and require them to maintain related records. Although these requirements are not specific to cross trading, they require funds to have policies and procedures reasonably designed to prevent violations of section 17(a) of the Investment Company Act through cross trades that do not comply with rule 17a-7, to review the effectiveness of the policies and procedures at least annually, and report to the board at least annually. As a result, under the current regulatory framework funds already generate and maintain materials relating to compliance policies and procedures and reviews, and the proposed amendments would expand the amount of documentation required to be maintained by funds insofar as the new quarterly and annual cross-trade reviews interact with these existing obligations.
In the 1990s and early 2000s, Commission staff issued several no-action letters addressing cross trading of municipal securities in circumstances where market quotations were not readily available, stating that staff would not recommend enforcement action related to the use of evaluated prices under specific conditions.

a. Eligible Assets Under Rule 17a-7
Currently, cross trades are primarily limited to securities with prices that are publicly available and easy to verify. This typically includes exchange-listed equities (such as S&P 500 stocks), U.S. Treasury securities (typically on-the-run issues with readily available market quotations), and agency mortgage-backed securities (all securities that trade in active markets with transparent pricing). To quantify the scope of assets that are eligible for cross trading under rule 17a-7, Table 3 shows the aggregate gross value of assets held by mutual funds, ETFs, and closed-end funds, categorized by fair value level. Level 1 securities, which have quoted prices in active markets, are generally eligible for cross trading under rule 17a-7. Level 2 securities are typically valued using observable inputs other than quoted prices, such as quoted prices for similar assets, interest rates, yield curves, or credit spreads, and are often derived from pricing models or vendor evaluations. Level 2 securities do not meet the “readily available market quotation” standard under rule 2a-5 and therefore are typically ineligible for cross trading, although certain municipal bonds, which are often classified as level 2, have been the subject of cross trades in reliance on SEC staff no-action letters.

b. Cross-Trading Activity
No direct data on actual cross-trade executions are available; the existing available data derive from selected samples, proxy-based indicators, and industry surveys.
i. Equity Cross-Trading Activity
Several academic studies and industry surveys provide evidence on the frequency of equity cross trading among affiliated funds. A research paper found that between 1999 and 2010, a sample of 388 U.S. mutual fund families executed nearly half a million internal equity cross trades, representing 1.6% of daily trade orders (defined as the aggregation of all trades by a fund family in a given stock, on a given side (buy or sell), on a given day) and 3.1% of total trade value.

An academic study found that cross trades made up about 0.9% of all individual equity trade executions reported by mutual fund families in a sample of more than four million transactions from 1999 to 2010.

Pricing providers support the operational feasibility of cross trading by supplying pricing data used both to assess whether a security has a readily available market quotation where supplemental pricing information is relevant and, where applicable, to price the cross trade itself. According to a staff analysis of Form N-CEN filings, for funds with fiscal year ending in 2025, over 11,000 funds reported using pricing services, with the majority relying on multiple providers. C. Benefits and Costs
This section analyzes the expected benefits and costs of the proposed amendments to rule 17a-7, including their likely impact on registered funds, investors, and markets. The analysis identifies the main channels through which the amendments might produce economic benefits, such as reduced transaction costs and operational efficiencies, as well as the channels through which they could impose costs, including compliance, implementation, and data-vendor expenses. Because reliable data are limited, the discussion remains qualitative where quantification is not feasible. Where benefits or costs can be quantified, the relevant estimates are provided in section III.D. The analysis also considers potential distributional effects and highlights areas where the size of the benefits and costs may be uncertain. Because cross trading is optional, any benefits or costs discussed below would arise only to the extent a registered fund or adviser chooses to engage in cross-trading activity.
In evaluating the potential economic effects of the proposed amendments, the magnitude and timing of benefits and costs discussed below are likely to vary across registered funds and advisers of different sizes. For example, larger fund complexes are likely to have more cross-trading opportunities. In addition, larger complexes, whose valuation, technology, and compliance infrastructures tend to be more developed, may be able to update processes to comply with the proposed amendments more quickly and at lower incremental cost, while smaller registered funds may face higher fixed or upfront burdens relative to their scale. Differences in resources, systems, staffing, trading volumes, and cross-trading activity could therefore influence both how compliance costs are incurred and how any economic benefits and costs materialize over time.
In addition, different types of funds may experience the proposed amendments differently based on their existing regulatory frameworks and historical reliance on rule 17a-7. BDCs, for example, generally hold significant level 3 assets and do not file Form N-PORT.
[
197
]
Because level 3 assets would remain ineligible for cross trading under the proposal, the amendments may not materially expand the set of transactions available to BDCs, and are therefore less likely to confer meaningful benefits on BDCs relative to other types of funds. In addition, because BDCs do not report on Form N-PORT, they would not incur the proposal's new structured-reporting obligations. For municipal securities, the staff have not recommended enforcement action if cross trades are conducted at a price using an independent pricing service,
[
198
]
and the proposal would allow advisers to rely on pricing-service data as inputs under either NAV pricing or current-market pricing. Because these practices are already common in municipal cross trading, we do not expect distinct or additional costs with respect to pricing municipal-security cross trades relative to current practice.
1. Expansion of Eligible Securities To Include Level 2 Securities
Before the adoption of rule 2a-5, many registered funds cross traded fixed-income securities using broker-dealer quotes to satisfy rule 17a-7's “reasonable inquiry” requirement. Under the current rule, cross trading is permitted only for securities for which market quotations are readily available. After the adoption of rule 2a-5, this standard corresponds to securities valued using level 1 inputs because those securities have readily available market quotations as defined under rule 2a-5. As a result, some complexes discontinued cross trades in securities valued using level 2 inputs, while others continued to trade certain fixed-income securities, such as municipal bonds, based on staff no-action letters, even though such securities continued
(
printed page 65653)
to be valued using level 2 inputs for their daily NAV processes.
Under the proposed amendments, a security would be eligible for cross trading if it has readily available market quotations or would be valued using observable inputs.
[
199
]
This would expressly include securities valued using level 2 inputs and would continue implicitly to exclude securities valued using level 3 inputs. As a result, the universe of securities eligible for cross trading would broaden, while preserving the existing non-inclusion of securities that are valued using significant unobservable inputs.
a. Benefits
Allowing level 2 securities to be cross traded would enable registered funds to avoid the transaction costs they otherwise incur when accessing external markets.
[
200
]
These avoided costs may include bid-ask spreads, dealer markups, and other execution expenses. More generally, in this discussion the term “transaction costs” includes both express costs (such as commissions, mark-ups, and mark-downs) and implicit costs, such as execution quality and market-impact effects.
The magnitude of these benefits would depend on how often registered funds with an affiliated adviser have complementary trading needs in level 2 securities and the extent to which fund complexes opt to engage in cross trading to meet those needs. Some complexes might realize only limited efficiencies if matched trading needs arise infrequently, while others with higher volumes of fixed-income trading could observe more substantial reductions in transaction costs.
In addition to transaction-cost savings, expanding eligibility to level 2 securities could also provide several ancillary economic benefits. As noted in section I.C, cross trades eliminate the need for a third-party counterparty, which may reduce exposure to counterparty risk. Section I.C also explains that internal cross trading can, in some circumstances, provide greater execution speed or certainty relative to open-market transactions, particularly when coordinating large trades or in periods of market stress. Further, section I.C describes that cross trading can provide an alternative source of liquidity for buying and selling funds when few broker-dealers maintain inventory in a particular security. Finally, as discussed in section III.B.3 of the baseline, fixed-income index funds and ETFs often face predictable rebalance-driven trading needs; enabling internal crosses of level 2 securities may reduce tracking error by allowing these funds to execute benchmark-related adjustments without incurring external market frictions, such as transactions costs or delays.
We estimate that the total annual monetized benefits of permitting cross trades under the amended framework are $173 million (2026 dollars). This estimate reflects two components. First, for corporate-bond trades between two mutual funds, we use the SEC Staff White Paper data on the observed decline in quarterly cross trading following the implementation of rule 2a-5.

Average quarterly volumes fell from approximately $6.24 billion in the pre-rule period to about $0.85 billion post-rule, a reduction of roughly $5.39 billion. Applying post-rule transaction-cost spreads derived from the WRDS Bond Database to this decline yields an annual estimate of $49.91 million in forgone savings, which we express in 2026 dollars using the GDP price index.

This represents the cost investors bear when trades that previously could be crossed are instead executed in the market. Second, for other fixed-income securities, we rely on an industry survey on cross trading, which documents the volume of cross trades by asset class—including U.S. Treasuries, mortgage-related securities, other asset-backed securities, international fixed income, bank loans, and commercial paper—almost all of which are level 2 instruments.
