To estimate the resulting cost savings that funds currently realize, we apply the survey's “normal-market-conditions” bid-ask spreads to each asset class. Summing the estimated annual savings across all categories results in an aggregate benefit of $173 million, expressed in 2026 dollars. These benefits represent recurring reductions in transaction costs that funds avoid by matching trades internally rather than routing them to dealers in the open market.
b. Costs
Funds relying on the expanded eligibility to cross trade level 2 securities would need to meet the rule's requirements, which would generate associated compliance and operational costs. These costs may include reviewing and documenting pricing-vendor methodologies, updating valuation and compliance procedures to incorporate observable-input pricing for cross trades, and establishing internal controls to oversee such transactions. For complexes without any cross-trading infrastructure for level 2 securities, these steps would represent one-time expenditures needed to ensure that cross trades of level 2 securities could be executed and monitored appropriately. In practice, however, establishing a cross-trading program for level 2 securities would also entail ongoing costs, including recurring reviews of pricing sources, periodic CCO and compliance oversight, and maintenance of trade-level and board-level records required under the proposed amendments. These recurring obligations reflect the continuing nature of pricing and oversight activities described in the proposal and therefore should be understood as ongoing, not solely upfront, costs. The size of these costs would vary depending on how closely a fund's existing systems align with the processes needed for cross
(
printed page 65654)
trading level 2 securities. Registered funds that already obtain observable inputs for NAV purposes could in some cases rely on similar inputs to support cross-trade pricing, which would reduce, in some circumstances, the implementation costs associated with the cross trading of level 2 securities.
Currently, a decision to classify a security as level 2 or level 3 affects financial-statement disclosures and valuation oversight under rule 2a-5, but not whether the fund may enter into a transaction. Under the proposal, however, that classification would determine whether the security may be cross traded, which could, in some circumstances, influence how funds approach borderline classifications. Because determining whether observable inputs are sufficiently significant to support a level 2 classification can involve professional judgment under ASC820, some funds might have a potential incentive to view certain borderline securities as level 2 when they wish to cross trade them. Any such incentive would likely be constrained by existing safeguards, including audit review of fair-value classifications, testing and board oversight under rule 2a-5, and quarterly CCO review of eligibility, and it is uncertain how these factors would interact in practice.
Cross trades in level 2 securities can involve normal valuation dispersion due to differences in observable inputs, NAV timing, or pricing-vendor methodologies. Although advisers may execute a cross trade only after determining
ex ante
that each participating fund is at least as well off as under reasonably available market alternatives, valuation discrepancies can produce
ex post
differences in realized outcomes across funds compared to what might have occurred if the transaction had been executed in external markets, particularly for less liquid assets. These differences can reflect modest distributional shifts in value between the participating funds,
[
204
]
which arise from valuation dynamics rather than unequal treatment at execution. The proposed conditions are designed to prevent trades at prices that are disadvantageous relative to the market, and to ensure the use of fair and consistently applied pricing methods for off-market trades.
[
205
]
The conditions of the amendments—particularly the
ex-ante
best-interest determination, pricing requirements, and oversight provisions—are designed to contain the effects of such incentives and ensure that internal prices are applied consistently and without disadvantaging any fund. While underlying conflicts of interest exist regardless of the rule, expanding eligibility to level 2 securities increases the opportunity for advisers to act on such incentives because valuations for level 2 instruments rely on observable inputs that permit a wider range of plausible pricing outcomes than level 1 securities. In a principal-agent framework, this greater valuation discretion amplifies the potential for advisers to allocate internal prices in ways that advantage some funds at the expense of others. In addition, advisers may benefit reputationally when cross trades allow a fund or other client to avoid realizing losses that would have occurred had the position been liquidated in external markets, potentially improving reported performance. These incentives could, in the absence of effective controls, create risks that certain funds bear systematically less favorable pricing outcomes. The proposed conditions—including eligibility limits, pricing requirements, and oversight provisions—are intended to mitigate these risks, but to the extent they persist, they represent a potential cost of the proposed expansion. The amendments would also expand the set of transactions eligible for cross trading. As cross-trading volume increases, aggregate exposure to the associated conflicts would rise even if the risk of any individual transaction remains unchanged.
This proposed amendment could also impose costs related to reduced availability of independent pricing information for certain securities. To the extent advisers internalize a greater share of transactions, fewer trades would be reported in public markets, diminishing the volume of observable inputs available for pricing level 2—and, to a lesser extent, level 1—securities. Over time, this reduction in market data could reduce the reliability of the pricing inputs used in both the NAV-based and current-market-price approaches for cross trades. In the extreme, a feedback effect could occur in which reduced public trading leads to less informative prices, which in turn increases uncertainty around subsequent cross-trade valuations. The costs of reduced observable pricing could also extend beyond the funds that engage in cross trading. Internal transactions do not generate the public trade data used by other market participants, including registered funds that do not cross trade, insurance companies, pension plans, index and benchmark providers, and pricing services that rely on executed transactions in comparable securities. These participants could bear some of the resulting reduction in pricing quality without receiving any of the transaction-cost savings associated with internalization. The magnitude of this effect would depend on the share of trading in an asset class that is internalized. As discussed in section III.C.6, the proposed reporting requirements would provide information on internalization by funds over time and by asset class.
2. Pricing of Cross Trades
Under the current rule, cross trades must be priced according to a prescriptive pricing method that varies by asset type, for example, last-sale prices for listed equities or the average of the highest independent bid and lowest independent offer determined on the basis of reasonable inquiry for over-the-counter fixed-income securities. Historically, advisers generally satisfied the “reasonable inquiry” requirement for fixed-income cross trades by collecting multiple broker-dealer quotes. After the adoption of rule 2a-5, however, most fixed-income securities do not meet the definition of having readily available market quotations.
Under the proposed amendments, this prescriptive pricing requirement would be replaced with two pricing options: NAV pricing and current market pricing. If a fund elects to use current-market pricing, the adviser would also be required to periodically review whether the unaffiliated pricing sources continue to produce prices that reasonably represent current market conditions, and to maintain documentation of the pricing sources, their independence, and the results of those reviews. Because the revised framework permits advisers to draw from a broader range of pricing sources beyond broker-dealer quotes, the effects of this flexibility may be most significant for level 2 securities and for advisers with substantial fixed-income activity.
Both pricing options would be available regardless of the type of security being cross traded. In contrast to the current prescriptive hierarchy—
(
printed page 65655)
under which many fixed-income cross trades historically relied almost exclusively on multiple broker-dealer quotes—the proposed pricing framework would allow a substantially wider range of pricing sources. Advisers could draw on evaluated prices, intraday vendor data, electronic-platform indications, and other observable inputs that reflect contemporaneous market conditions, rather than being limited to broker-dealer quotes, which for cross-trading purposes may have been accommodation quotes in practice—because the quoting dealer never intended to execute with the fund, dealers had no incentive to provide actionable or accurate prices—and which could also be difficult to source and operationally burdensome for less-liquid fixed-income securities.
Because the proposal gives registered funds two alternative pricing methods, each fund would select the option it reasonably determines fits its valuation processes and operational needs. A fund's preferred pricing method may depend on considerations such as the markets in which the fund invests, the fund's trading strategy (including whether intraday execution is important), and the size and structure of the fund complex. Under either pricing method, advisers would retain flexibility to select the pricing source or valuation input they reasonably determine is appropriate for the security, and this flexibility may assist advisers in evaluating compliance with the rule's conditions because it allows them to rely on pricing sources and observable inputs that are already incorporated into their valuation workflows under rule 2a-5, reducing the operational frictions and data-collection steps that would arise if the rule required a single prescriptive source in all circumstances.
a. NAV Pricing
i. Benefits
Using NAV pricing could simplify operations when the fund's existing valuation process already produces a price for that day. A registered fund could rely on that value for cross trades rather than gathering broker-dealer quotes, thereby reducing operational steps. Because NAV pricing leverages processes that funds already use for valuation, advisers would be able to use the same infrastructure for cross-trade pricing, and improvements in those valuation processes could similarly extend to cross-trade pricing. These simplification benefits may be particularly relevant for level 2 securities, which constitute a large share of fixed-income fund portfolios and are typically valued using observable inputs other than quoted prices in active markets for the particular security. For these securities, NAV pricing allows advisers to rely on established valuation workflows and pricing-service methodologies already subject to rule 2a-5 oversight, reducing the need to obtain real-time quotes for instruments that rarely trade intraday. NAV pricing would also provide certainty, familiarity, and transparency to fund investors regarding how cross trades will be valued. Because NAV pricing reflects the next-computed NAV rather than intraday price levels, NAV pricing could introduce timing-related differences when markets move between the execution time and the NAV strike; these differences are usually modest under normal market conditions but may be more pronounced during periods of elevated intraday volatility. When a fund uses the same pricing service for both NAV valuation and any intraday evaluated prices, we expect NAV-based and intraday evaluated prices to diverge only modestly, because both are derived from the same observable inputs and methodologies. The size of these benefits would vary across complexes primarily based on differences in the availability and timeliness of valuation inputs on the trade date, and—in the case of closed-end funds—whether a daily NAV is computed.
ii. Costs
Allowing registered funds to use the next-computed NAV to price a cross trade would impose minimal incremental costs for registered funds that already strike daily NAVs, because they can rely on their existing valuation processes. However, using the next-computed NAV introduces a potential timing-related economic cost: a fund executes the trade at one point in time but receives a price determined later, creating intraday price-risk exposure for both counterparties. In financial economics, this timing mismatch is analogous to execution risk—the risk that market values move between the trade decision and the pricing timestamp. At the same time, some portfolio managers already execute market-on-close orders in ordinary trading, indicating that this type of timing-related risk is familiar and, in some circumstances, already managed within existing trading practices. Although the magnitude of this risk may be modest under normal market conditions, it may be more material during periods of elevated volatility and thus may represent a potential economic cost of NAV pricing under some circumstances. This timing risk is not symmetric across the two counterparties: if prices rise between trade execution and the NAV strike, the buying fund benefits at the expense of the selling fund, and if prices fall, the reverse is true; however, because subsequent price movements are unknowable at the moment the adviser places an NAV-priced cross trade, this asymmetry reflects an economic risk borne by both funds rather than a channel through which the adviser can intentionally time trades to favor one side. The proposed oversight conditions, including the CCO's quarterly and annual reviews, are intended to monitor whether any systematic patterns nonetheless arise. Because funds already record the price and supporting information for each cross trade under existing rule 17a-7, allowing funds to use the next-computed NAV would not introduce additional recordkeeping costs. And to the extent that broker-dealer quotes are non-actionable, uncompensated information requests, reducing reliance on such quotes is unlikely to impair broader broker-dealer relationships or execution quality for other transactions.
A fund that values a security at the bid price could, under NAV pricing, cross trade that security at the bid.
[
206
]
If a cross trade occurs at the bid price, the selling fund would receive a price below a mid-market execution, with the difference accruing to the buying fund. Unlike the timing-related effects discussed above, which may favor either participant depending on subsequent price movements, any directional effect would arise only when both participating funds value the security at bid and therefore may use NAV pricing; if one fund values the security at mid and the other at bid, the cross trade could not be priced using NAV pricing under the proposal and current-market pricing would be required instead. The use of current market pricing may produce a price closer to mid and mitigate this concern. In addition, for a cross trade to occur under the proposal, the adviser must determine that it is in the best interest of each registered fund, which likewise may mitigate concerns about selling funds receiving prices below mid-market executions. We cannot estimate how many registered funds value securities at bid or the
(
printed page 65656)
potential volume of affected trades. A selling fund may nevertheless benefit from avoiding market-impact costs, counterparty risk, liquidity risk, or other frictions associated with an open-market sale, which could offset some or all of the pricing difference in cases where both funds value at bid and the adviser determines that the NAV-priced trade is in each fund's best interest compared to reasonably available market alternatives.
NAV pricing could also give a fund's daily valuation of a security a transactional consequence it does not have today. Under the current framework, a stale or erroneous fair value affects a fund's reported NAV and the price at which its shares are issued and redeemed. Under NAV pricing, however, the same valuation would also determine the price of a cross trade with an eligible affiliate. If the valuation were later found to be incorrect, the fund would need to consider not only whether to correct its NAV under its existing error-correction policies, but also, depending on all the facts and circumstances, whether to reverse the trade or make the affected fund whole. We cannot estimate how often such circumstances might arise. The valuation processes required by rule 2a-5, including periodic testing of fair-value methodologies, are intended to reduce this risk.
NAV pricing also assumes that both participating funds assign the same value to a security. Affiliated funds may, at times, reach different valuations because they use different pricing vendors or methodologies or compute NAV at different times of day. In such cases, the funds would not be able to use NAV pricing and would instead need to price the transaction at current market price or decline the trade if current-market pricing is not reasonably available. Funds may therefore incur costs to establish procedures for identifying and considering valuation differences when funds otherwise would use NAV pricing to price a cross trade, and some otherwise beneficial cross trades may not occur. We expect such differences to be uncommon within fund complexes that apply consistent valuation policies, but we lack data on their frequency or magnitude.
b. Current Market Pricing
i. Benefits
The current market pricing method would allow registered funds to rely on a broader and more modern set of pricing inputs than under the current rule's hierarchy. In addition to actionable broker-dealer quotes, advisers could use intraday evaluated prices from unaffiliated pricing vendors,
[
207
]
and observable inputs made available through electronic trading platforms. This flexibility is particularly relevant for level 2 securities, which often lack quoted prices but have robust observable inputs—such as yield curves, spreads, or comparable-bond data—that vendors incorporate into evaluated prices. Allowing advisers to use these sources may avoid the need to solicit broker-dealer quotes as was historically the case for certain fixed-income securities under rule 17a-7, prior to the adoption of rule 2a-5, and may provide more contemporaneous prices in markets where dealer quotes are sparse or delayed. This approach can provide a more contemporaneous price than the next NAV computation, particularly when market conditions change during the trading day. Access to intraday pricing allows advisers to execute cross trades at the same point in time that they make trading decisions for other portfolio transactions, giving them a price that reflects prevailing market conditions rather than end-of-day valuations. This alignment with normal trading workflows may be important for fixed-income and equity trading decisions that are made and executed intraday. Using an intraday price can modestly reduce the risk that market movements between trade decision and end-of-day NAV introduce unintended gains or losses to one side of the cross trade. In addition, certain intraday pricing sources may include contextual information—such as bid- and asked-price data—that can assist an adviser in determining, for purposes of the best-interest analysis, that executing at the obtained price does not disadvantage the fund or its affiliate relative to executing in the market.
The benefits of intraday pricing depend on unaffiliated sources providing sufficiently frequent and reliable updates. Some pricing services offer intraday evaluated prices, but we lack information on the asset classes covered, the frequency of updates, and the quality of these values relative to end-of-day prices. Where reliable intraday prices are unavailable, an adviser seeking to execute a cross trade before the next NAV calculation may need to rely on other sources, such as broker-dealer quotes, which could limit expected operational savings. Advisers may also incur costs evaluating intraday-pricing products, which, unlike the end-of-day evaluated-price services used for NAV calculations, may not already be in established use.
Relative to the current baseline, in which advisers often must solicit multiple broker-dealer quotes to satisfy the pricing hierarchy for fixed-income cross trades, allowing advisers to rely on a wider range of current-market pricing sources—such as intraday evaluated prices and other observable inputs—may reduce operational costs and improve pricing accuracy by capturing more contemporaneous market information than periodically available quotes that the quoting broker-dealer knows will not be acted upon. This cost reduction would not stem from broker-dealer quotes being “expensive” but from reducing the staff time and operational effort required to solicit multiple quotes, particularly in less liquid fixed-income securities where dealers may be slow to respond. Although executable dealer quotes reflect actual tradeable levels, intraday evaluated prices and other observable inputs may provide a more up-to-date indication of prevailing market conditions when markets move between quote requests or when quotes are intermittent.
The periodic-review requirement would help ensure that prices derived from unaffiliated sources remain reliable over time, particularly in markets where liquidity and observable inputs fluctuate. By helping identify pricing that is stale, inconsistent, or outside the adviser's established tolerance thresholds (such as deviations from expected ranges based on observable inputs) more quickly, this requirement may improve the accuracy and integrity of cross-trade pricing and reduce the risk that funds transact at off-market levels. Because advisers would also need to document the pricing sources, their independence, and the results of these reviews, the requirement may further strengthen pricing discipline and transparency, albeit with some additional operational burden.
The magnitude of these benefits would depend on how frequently a registered fund trades securities whose market indications change throughout the day or whose evaluated pricing sources update frequently, as well as the degree to which the registered fund opts to use current market pricing in its cross trades.
The distribution of these benefits would vary across advisers and fund complexes. Advisers that trade frequently in fixed-income and other level 2 securities would generally experience the largest gains because
(
printed page 65657)
they currently incur higher costs obtaining broker-dealer quotes under the existing hierarchy, and because observable inputs such as evaluated prices and spreads are more commonly available for these instruments than for less liquid securities, even when such inputs reflect prior-day or periodically updated data rather than continuous intraday changes. Large complexes with diverse fixed-income strategies also may benefit more from the expanded set of permissible pricing sources. By contrast, advisers primarily invested in level 1 securities, where quoted prices are readily available and updated continuously, may experience fewer incremental benefits from the current market pricing option.
ii. Costs
Although the increased flexibility may reduce operational costs associated with soliciting multiple broker-dealer quotes, some funds may still incur vendor fees if they need additional evaluated-price feeds to implement the method for certain securities. In instances where the adviser reasonably determines that broker-dealer quotes represent current market price, these vendor-related costs could be avoided because the proposal would continue to permit their use. The adviser would also be required to periodically review whether the unaffiliated pricing sources produce reasonable results, which may entail staff time and analytical oversight. Because evaluated prices can differ across vendors or lag evolving market conditions, advisers might need additional monitoring to identify and address potential discrepancies. For level 2 securities, where evaluated prices may incorporate a range of observable inputs such as spreads, curves, and comparable-bond data, these discrepancies may arise more frequently, requiring advisers to perform additional periodic checks or cross-vendor comparisons to assess whether selected pricing sources remain reliable. Using an unaffiliated pricing source would not eliminate potential conflicts of interest. Pricing services may have incentives to accommodate clients on whose business they depend. Moreover, the adviser selects the pricing source, determines whether its price reasonably represents current market conditions, and may challenge or replace the obtained prices. Without effective controls, these functions could allow the adviser to influence the cross-trade price indirectly. The proposal's periodic review requirement and the CCO's review are intended to limit this risk, but any remaining ability to influence vendor-provided pricing would represent a potential cost of the method. Maintaining documentation of pricing sources, independence, and the results of periodic reviews would add to the operational workload. These costs could be partially mitigated because advisers already conduct certain vendor-pricing reviews for NAV valuation under rule 2a-5, and those processes may be leveraged for cross-trade pricing.
The proposed method would also give pricing services a more direct role in affiliated transactions. Today, an evaluated price is an input to a fund's fair-value determination and may be tested or adjusted under its rule 2a-5 valuation procedures. Under the proposal, that evaluated price could determine the price of a cross trade. Because pricing-service usage is concentrated—the five most frequently reported providers each serve around 4,000 or more funds—the proposal could increase funds' dependence on a small number of providers. This concentration could affect the terms on which services are offered and increase the consequences of service interruptions, pricing errors, or methodological weaknesses across multiple complexes. These effects may be mitigated because more than 5,000 funds obtain prices from at least four providers,
[
208
]
and because the current-market-pricing option does not require use of pricing-service data, allowing advisers to rely instead on broker-dealer quotes or observable information from electronic trading platforms. We cannot estimate the magnitude of these potential impacts.
3. Transaction Costs and Fees
Under the current rule, cross trades must involve only cash payment against prompt delivery, and no brokerage commission or fee may be paid other than undefined “customary transfer fees.” This ambiguity has created uncertainty regarding whether operational charges, such as settlement fees, custody fees, or platform charges, are permissible and may have led to divergent practices among complexes. At the same time, because the determination of what qualifies as
de minimis
depends on a fund's size and the context of the transaction, the proposal may allow some variation across complexes; however, these differences would reflect factual circumstances rather than interpretive uncertainty.
Under the proposed amendments, remuneration generally would be prohibited, except the proposal would permit
de minimis
payments to unaffiliated service providers (
i.e.,
not first- or second-tier affiliates) for clearing, settlement, custody, recording, or reporting the transaction. These payments would need to be small and operationally necessary for executing the transaction.
a. Benefits
By expressly allowing
de minimis
administrative payments to unaffiliated parties, the proposal could reduce operational steps by decreasing reliance on individualized interpretations of “customary transfer fees.” We do not anticipate that the proposal would materially increase or decrease the number or type of administrative fees charged, as these fees generally arise from ordinary settlement processes and the amendments are intended to clarify, rather than broaden, the range of permissible payments. Registered funds would spend less time reviewing routine settlement-related fees, although advisers would still need to exercise some judgment in confirming that a fee is
de minimis.
Reducing ambiguity around the “customary transfer fee” concept may also reduce compliance time spent evaluating whether a particular fee falls within that undefined category.
As discussed in section II.C, in some non-U.S. markets, funds are subject to mandatory settlement charges (such as stamp duties, transaction taxes, or local settlement fees). By allowing these existing charges to be treated as
de minimis
payments, the proposal may reduce a prior disincentive to engage in cross trades in certain non-U.S. markets where such fees are unavoidable. The proposed
de minimis
allowance would simply clarify that such existing charges may be paid when they arise as part of ordinary settlement processes. Likewise, permitting
de minimis
fees charged by electronic trading platforms—limited to clearing, settlement, custody, recording, or reporting—may similarly reduce a practical barrier to cross trading on platforms that impose administrative fees, while clarifying treatment of administrative charges associated with platforms that already facilitate settlement workflows.
The extent of these benefits would depend on how often a registered fund encounters small administrative fees when settling cross trades. Complexes that currently absorb operational inefficiencies to avoid potential non-compliance could experience greater improvements, while complexes that
(
printed page 65658)
already treat certain small fees as permissible might see more modest gains.
b. Costs
Under the proposal, the
de minimis
standard would apply on a per-trade basis. Although each payment is individually small, funds with higher volumes of cross trades may experience larger cumulative administrative outlays because the standard is applied to each transaction separately. These cumulative amounts would depend on a fund's trading volume and the markets in which it trades, but they would not alter the per-trade nature of the
de minimis
condition.
Because funds already need to review settlement-related fees under the existing “customary transfer fee” standard, the proposal would not introduce a new type of monitoring obligation; rather, it would shift that existing review to a clearer, more bounded
de minimis
framework. Registered funds would need to monitor administrative fees to confirm they remain
de minimis
and relate only to clearing, settlement, custody, recording, or reporting of the transaction. We expect that monitoring under a
de minimis
standard would be no more burdensome, and in many cases clearer, than evaluating whether a fee is “customary,” because the proposal limits permissible payments to specific administrative categories and ties the analysis to a fact-bounded, transaction-specific threshold rather than an open-ended industry-custom standard. Monitoring for compliance with the
de minimis
standard may require personnel of the fund or its service providers to review invoices or system reports and verify that each payment fits within the proposed categories, but we acknowledge that the applicable standards, the scope of permissible fees, and the associated analysis may differ from current practice—including in foreign markets where settlement structures, mandatory charges, or local transfer fees can vary—so some monitoring steps may not align perfectly with the existing customary-fee review. These activities are generally similar to the review already performed under the current rule, while reflecting the proposal's clarified boundaries.
Funds or eligible affiliates that do not currently incur administrative fees when cross trading, because their existing cross trades occur in markets where such fees are not charged, would bear these costs to the extent they choose to begin making
de minimis
payments under the proposal. In practice, however, many registered funds already incur similar fees during settlement processes, especially in non-U.S. markets where stamp duties, settlement fees, and other mandatory charges are imposed as part of ordinary trade settlement, and the proposal would clarify that such existing fees may be paid in connection with a cross trade rather than introduce new fee types. Actual cost impact would vary based on a fund's existing settlement arrangements and whether different settlement-related vendors or processes might be needed to handle clearing, settlement, custody, recording, or reporting.
Uncertainty may persist about what constitutes a
de minimis
fee across registered funds of different sizes. Larger registered funds may view a particular amount as
de minimis
relative to their trade sizes, whereas smaller registered funds could experience proportionally greater costs. Accordingly, the overall economic effect could vary across complexes.
Because the proposal would not define a specific amount or percentage as
de minimis,
funds would need to determine how the standard applies to particular fees. Some funds may incur costs documenting or obtaining legal advice about routine settlement charges that would not require separate analysis under a specified threshold. Others may avoid cross trades involving any fee to reduce the risk that the payment is later found inconsistent with the rule. In such cases, the cost would take the form of forgone cross trading benefits rather than additional expenses.
Determining whether a payment in a non-U.S. market relates to clearing, settlement, custody, recording, or reporting may require analysis of local law and market practice. Funds that cross trade non-U.S. securities may therefore incur costs obtaining advice from local counsel or service providers and updating that analysis as requirements change. These costs would be concentrated among complexes with substantial non-U.S. holdings and would generally arise for each relevant market rather than for each transaction.
The proposal would not specify which participant must bear a permitted payment. When both participants are funds, the allocation of that payment would determine how the cost is divided between two groups of shareholders, while the adviser making that decision acts for both funds. Although each payment would be small, consistently assigning fees to one participant could create recurring transfers between affiliated funds. Funds may therefore incur costs developing and documenting an allocation methodology, and any unresolved discretion would add to the conflicts of interest discussed elsewhere in this section.
4. Best Interest Determination and Consistency With Fund Policies and Strategies
The current rule relies on board-approved procedures and quarterly board reviews to verify compliance with the rule's conditions, and these procedures do not require an evaluation of whether a particular cross trade is in the fund's best interest. Advisers already have existing fiduciary duties to act in the best interest of each client, including registered fund clients, but the current rule does not require a transaction-specific best-interest determination for each cross trade.
[
209
]
Many advisers already consider whether a trade aligns with a fund's broader investment strategy, perform informal pre-trade checks or consider execution quality as part of their broader trading processes, but such practices vary across complexes and are not mandated by the rule.
Under the proposed amendments, an adviser would be required to determine that the cross trade would be in the best interest of the fund. In addition, as a condition of the rule, the transaction must be consistent with the fund's policies and investment strategies. Because this determination must reflect the particular characteristics of the fund and the security involved and the circumstances of the trade, advisers may need to tailor aspects of their analysis to the circumstances of each transaction, which may influence the associated economic effects.
a. Benefits
The proposal could encourage more deliberate pre-trade analysis by requiring that advisers compare the cross trade with reasonable execution alternatives, such as available market quotes, which may reduce the likelihood that a registered fund enters into a cross trade when trading in the market would yield more favorable terms. This more structured review also may improve advisers' ability to identify instances where trade-specific factors—such as liquidity conditions, anticipated execution quality, or signs of potential price impact—suggest that a cross trade is unlikely to provide a better outcome than external execution. In addition, by requiring advisers to make a documented, transaction-specific best-interest determination, the proposal
(
printed page 65659)
may increase the
ex-ante
cost of improper practices such as cherry-picking, dumping, or parking, thereby discouraging such conduct.
Because of the express requirement that advisers evaluate best interest in connection with a cross trade, they may be more likely to identify instances where the proposed cross-trade price is not competitive with available external quotes.
For many advisers, the requirement would formalize review steps that are already part of existing trading practices, potentially resulting in more consistent documentation and more uniform application across trades. In complexes where pre-trade review practices are less developed or less consistently applied, the proposal could meaningfully strengthen the rigor and reliability of cross-trade decision-making. Tailoring the determination to the characteristics of the fund and the security may further enhance the accuracy of advisers' assessments, particularly in markets or asset classes where execution alternatives vary widely in quality. The extent of these benefits would vary depending on the robustness of an adviser's current pre-trade review processes. The costs section below discusses the transition and compliance burdens that may offset some of these gains.
b. Costs
Advisers would need additional time to make a best-interest determination for each cross trade and funds would need time to assess whether each cross trade is consistent with the fund's policies and investment strategies, although funds or advisers already performing similar analyses may experience smaller incremental costs. Costs may involve gathering information about external execution alternatives, such as indicative pricing, liquidity conditions, or available quotes, and comparing them to the proposed cross trade. Advisers also may incur incremental costs when tailoring their analysis to the specific characteristics of the fund or the security—for example, where market-based pricing inputs differ across asset classes or where the potential for market impact requires additional review. To the extent that portfolio management or trading personnel participate in these determinations, advisers may incur additional staff-time costs, including during periods when cross trades tend to occur in more concentrated windows. Advisers whose documentation is integrated into trading, order-management, or compliance systems also may incur one-time costs to modify those systems to capture the required elements of the determination. Supervisory review might also increase to ensure these determinations are completed and recorded consistently.
In situations where external pricing information is limited or changing rapidly, performing the best interest determination could lengthen the time required to reach a trading decision, creating variation in burdens across securities and complexes. Firms whose internal processes currently rely on more generalized or informal assessments may experience additional transition costs as they adapt workflows, including the allocation of review responsibilities among personnel. When both sides of a cross trade are registered funds, the proposal requires separate best-interest determinations. Although the same personnel may conduct both reviews, each determination would need to reflect the circumstances of the specific fund. If the conclusions differ, the trade would not occur and the costs of making the determinations would not produce a completed transaction.
The proposed best-interest requirement also may need to be applied differently depending on a fund's trading methods and strategies. For example, advisers using fully automated or algorithmically implemented strategies may determine that they cannot perform the discretionary, transaction-specific review required under the best interest standard.
The proposed amendment would require advisers to prepare a transaction-specific record explaining why a cross trade is in the participating fund's best interest. Preparing this documentation imposes an incremental, per trade cost, and advisers may choose to avoid cross trades in situations where the expected savings relative to external execution are small. As a result, some cross trades that would have produced modest benefits under the expanded eligibility criteria may not occur. The Commission cannot estimate how often advisers might decline trades for this reason but recognizes that higher documentation costs could reduce the use of cross trading at the margin.
For cross trades in certain thinly traded level 2 fixed-income securities, the best-interest determination may partially offset the operational savings described in section III.C.2. That section identifies the elimination of the multi-dealer quote requirement as a potential benefit of the pricing provisions. However, because the best-interest determination requires the adviser to evaluate whether the proposed cross-trade price is reasonable relative to external execution alternatives, there may be circumstances in which the best interest requirement causes an adviser to obtain additional market information—such as indicative dealer quotes or evaluated prices—beyond the information used to price the cross trade to support its best interest analysis. The extent to which this review would reintroduce quote-solicitation activity would depend on the adviser's existing valuation infrastructure and the liquidity of the security involved.
5. Oversight Requirements
Under the current rule, oversight is board-centric: the board adopts and updates procedures and determines each quarter whether cross trades complied with them. The current rule does not place any specific related compliance responsibility on the fund's CCO or anyone else. In practice, registered funds already have rule 38a-1 compliance programs that assign certain responsibilities to the CCO,
[
210
]
and the Commission staff has previously taken the position that a board may rely on a CCO representation that cross trades complied with the board-approved procedures,
[
211
]
rather than performing transaction-level reviews of cross trades itself under rule 17a-7. Some registered funds also conduct post-trade testing or surveillance, but these practices differ significantly across complexes.
Under the proposed amendments, oversight would shift to a more structured, CCO-centered framework. The CCO would be required to conduct a quarterly compliance review of all cross trades and report the results to the board. In addition, the CCO would be required to perform an annual review designed to identify whether a registered fund may have been disadvantaged, an analysis that would include reviewing the timing and price of subsequent sales of securities purchased in cross trades, along with other information necessary to evaluate the trade. To facilitate this review, registered funds would need systems that can identify cross-traded securities
(
printed page 65660)
and retrieve information about any subsequent sales of securities purchased in cross trades. The existing board-level quarterly determination would be replaced, and the board's role would pivot to reviewing the CCO's quarterly and annual reports.
a. Benefits
The proposed amendments may offer several oversight-related benefits. Shifting the oversight function to a structured, CCO-centered review within the fund's existing oversight framework under rule 38a-1, could reduce certain operational burdens. Regular quarterly checks and an annual look-back may help protect investors by enabling earlier detection of issues or unusual or anomalous patterns in cross-trading activity that could itself signal a potential concern, especially where such monitoring is not currently formalized. Board oversight could become more focused on broad themes, such as conflict risks or persistent pricing patterns, thereby enabling directors to identify systemic issues more effectively and avoid time-consuming, low-value transaction-level reviews.
[
212
]
Enhanced systems that can identify cross-traded securities and retrieve information about subsequent sales would support more effective annual reviews by the CCO and strengthen the fund's ability to detect whether it may have been disadvantaged. The scale of these benefits would depend on how frequently the registered fund engages in cross trading, the strength of existing surveillance tools, and how efficiently registered funds can automate tagging and reporting processes.
b. Costs
Registered funds would need systems capable of tagging and tracking each cross-traded security and producing analytics that compare cross-trade prices to subsequent market activity or other benchmarks. Depending on a fund's existing compliance and analytics infrastructure, the enhancements needed to support cross-trade reviews may overlap with systems already used for other regulatory or trading-quality assessments, such as execution-quality analytics or portfolio-level performance and pricing metrics. In such cases, advisers may be able to build on existing systems rather than develop entirely new ones, although some additional functionality may still be required to support the proposed cross trade-specific reviews. The CCO would need additional time to complete the required reviews, and registered funds would need to maintain documentation supporting those reviews, such as pricing determinations, and review outcomes, in addition to their existing recordkeeping obligations. At the same time, because the proposed amendments would eliminate the board's quarterly determination, registered funds may experience offsetting reductions in board-level oversight costs, reflecting lower demands on director time relative to the current rule. Further, assigning these reviews to a full-time CCO with direct or regular access to trade-level data may improve expertise matching and enhance the fund's ability to detect issues compared to periodic transaction-level checks by the board.
If additional CCO time or staffing is not available, these obligations could divert attention from other compliance responsibilities. Alternatively, adding compliance staff would increase costs to the fund and its investors or the fund's adviser. Concentrating these reviews in a single officer may also lead funds or advisers to adjust compensation, insurance coverage, or recruitment efforts for the CCO to reflect the increased scope of responsibilities.
The magnitude of these costs would vary based on the volume and complexity of a fund's cross-trading activity and how closely its existing compliance systems approximate what the proposed amendments would require. In addition, identifying which portion of a later disposition relates to securities acquired through cross trades may require tax-lot-level tracking or supplementary records, particularly where funds use average-cost accounting conventions that do not distinguish among different acquisition methods. For fixed-income securities held to maturity, the required systems may impose costs without generating a comparable disposition price, reducing the usefulness of the resulting data for the annual analysis. Differences between cross-trade prices and subsequent disposition prices may also reflect interim market movements rather than disadvantage, requiring the fund CCO to evaluate these distinctions as part of each review period. Further, because the disadvantage analysis occurs annually, any emerging pattern could persist for part of the year before detection, which may limit the effectiveness of this safeguard; this timing consideration is discussed more fully in section II.E. Additionally, shifting primary oversight responsibility from the board to the fund CCO may introduce governance-related costs. Under the proposal, only the fund CCO—not the adviser's CCO—would perform the quarterly and annual reviews and would prepare the required reports. Relative to other internal officers, fund CCOs have substantially fewer conflicts because they are subject to rule 38a-1's independence framework: they are approved, compensated, and removable only by the board, and must report directly and separately to the board at least annually. These features mitigate conflicts relative to relying on adviser personnel. At the same time, some information asymmetry may remain where the fund CCO relies on adviser systems or has corporate reporting lines within the adviser or an affiliated entity, which may require additional documentation or verification. While boards would continue to review quarterly and annual CCO reports, the move from direct determinations to report-based oversight may lessen transparency into transaction-level details. However, this shift is consistent with the compliance structure established under rule 38a-1 and may reduce low-value operational burdens for boards by allowing them to focus on higher-level oversight.
6. Reporting
Under current requirements, some registered funds report on Form N-CEN whether they relied on certain statutory or rule-based exemptions (including rule 17a-7) during the reporting year. This disclosure is limited to a yes/no indicator and does not provide any information about the volume, type, or characteristics of a fund's cross trades. Funds' financial statements also include related-party disclosures under Regulation S-X, which may capture cross trades in aggregated form, but these disclosures vary across complexes, are not presented in a standardized or structured format, and are not tagged or readily comparable across funds. As a result, while some information about affiliated transactions is currently available, there is no consistent, publicly available reporting that provides structured metrics specifically describing cross-trading activity or its composition by asset class. Advisers track cross trades internally for compliance and operational purposes, but these internal records are not
(
printed page 65661)
reported in a uniform or machine-readable manner to the public or the Commission.
Under the proposed amendments, Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP filers that engaged in cross trades of portfolio investments in reliance on rule 17a-7 during the preceding twelve-month period would be required to report four data points for each asset type (or category of investment, in the case of Form N-MFP) in U.S. dollars. These data points are: (1) the aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund purchased under rule 17a-7, (2) the aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund purchased, (3) the aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund sold under rule 17a-7, and (4) the aggregate value of portfolio investments the registered fund sold. These data would be provided for the reporting period and would appear on the same filing and public availability schedule that applies to each form.
Some funds, such as BDCs, would not be subject to these standardized cross-trade reporting requirements. As a result, cross-trading activity in BDC portfolios would remain outside the scope of structured public reporting, limiting comparability between registered funds and BDCs and reducing the completeness of aggregate cross-trading information available to regulators and the public.
This approach would provide consistent, comparable information about the level and composition of cross-trading activity while avoiding trade-level reporting. It would give the Commission and the public, for the first time, standardized, machine-readable cross-trade metrics, improving transparency relative to the current regime of binary annual reporting and non-standardized financial statement footnotes.
a. Benefits
Standardized reporting would provide investors, regulators, and other market participants with insights into cross-trading activity across registered funds. Because funds do not currently disclose structured numerical information about their cross-trading activity, neither regulators nor the public can compare levels or patterns across funds today. The proposed structured monthly reporting, which includes four data points per asset type, would provide a more consistent, quantitative basis for such comparisons.
[
213
]
In addition, because the reporting framework includes total purchases and total sales by asset class, the new structured data may also improve the Commission's ability to monitor reporting funds' overall trading activity across asset classes and over time, including during periods of market stress. The practical value of such comparability may depend on how frequently a given registered fund engages in cross trading, and on whether existing Form N-PORT asset-type categories provide sufficient granularity to distinguish among the types of securities involved in cross trades. Because the extent and nature of cross-trading opportunities vary across asset classes, the magnitude of cross-trading activity reported by filers will naturally differ across funds with different portfolio compositions. This contextual information may help market participants better interpret differences in reported cross-trading levels across funds.
Beyond cross-fund comparability, the reporting requirement would facilitate comparisons of the amount of aggregate cross-trading activity occurring in a given asset class to the amount of trading activity in external markets for that asset class. This may allow both market participants and regulators to assess how the informativeness of public markets for an asset class changes as the share of the asset class traded internally via cross trades changes.
Standardized reporting on Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP could also improve the Commission's ability to monitor the use of cross trading over time. Because the reporting would provide consistent, structured, and machine-readable data across filers, it may facilitate analyses designed to identify trends in the aggregate volume of cross trades, the asset classes in which cross trading is most prevalent, and how cross-trading activity evolves as funds adjust to the proposed amendments.
Reporting could also support retrospective evaluations of whether increased internalization of trades has implications for measures of liquidity or the informativeness of public transaction data.
[
214
]
While the aggregate, monthly nature of the Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP reporting would not provide real-time transparency or price-discovery benefits, it may nonetheless allow researchers and regulators to study whether, and to what extent, cross-trading activity relates to changes in publicly observed trading patterns in certain asset classes. Any such benefits would be indirect and depend on how the data are used, but the availability of consistent aggregate information may lower the cost of conducting such analyses.
Standardized public reporting may also modestly increase transparency around the extent to which funds use cross trading. Although any effect on investor behavior is likely limited given the lagged and aggregated nature of the disclosures, consistent public visibility into cross-trading volumes could provide some incremental disciplining effect at the margin. Market participants or examiners may take note of anomalous levels of reported cross-trading activity relative to peers, which may give advisers an additional incentive to avoid cross trading in situations where it is not in the best interest of investors. These effects are expected to be modest but may nonetheless contribute to greater public awareness of funds' cross-trading practices.
b. Costs
Registered funds would need to update reporting systems to capture and populate the new fields, assemble the data each month, and conduct internal verification prior to filing. Because funds are already required to maintain the underlying transaction-level information as part of their ordinary trading, accounting, and compliance processes—including data used for the CCO's required reviews—the incremental burden relates primarily to assembling and formatting existing data rather than generating new information, and may include modest increases in review effort to ensure the accuracy of the additional reported items.
[
215
]
The magnitude of these burdens will vary across funds depending on the extent of
(
printed page 65662)
their cross-trading activity and the degree to which their existing systems already capture and organize the relevant data.
In addition, the expansion of eligibility to level 2 securities may increase the number of cross trades executed by certain registered funds relative to the baseline. To the extent cross-trading volume increases, more funds would have cross-trade activity to report on Forms N-PORT and N-MFP, increasing the number of filers that must assemble and verify these values each month within their existing filings. The magnitude of any such increase would depend on each complex's trading activity, portfolio composition, and use of cross trading under the amended rule.
Because the two new data elements reporting a fund's total monthly gross purchases and total monthly gross sales by asset type would be publicly available under each form's existing filing and publication schedule, disclosure may impose costs beyond the direct costs associated with reporting holdings. These total gross purchase and sale aggregates—distinct from the rule 17a-7-specific purchase and sale amounts—could make the scale of trading activity within each asset type more visible, even in cases where end-of-month holdings show little net change, providing information that cannot be inferred solely from net month-end holdings.
For funds with highly concentrated strategies or exposure to very few asset types, monthly gross purchases and sales could provide incremental insight into repositioning or capacity constraints beyond what is already observable from quarterly holdings and public flow data. In such limited cases, market participants might be able to draw inferences that marginally affect the fund's future transaction costs. However, several features would help limit this risk: the data would be aggregated rather than transaction-specific, reported by asset type rather than security, and disclosed with a lag. We cannot estimate any remaining effect, which would depend on portfolio concentration and the extent to which reported activity could be linked to particular positions and be subsequently exploited by other market participants.
The scale of one-time system changes may also vary across fund complexes. Some registered funds may need only minor adjustments to existing Form N-PORT processes, whereas others might require broader data-integration work to aggregate cross-trade values by asset type. Routine effort would also differ depending on the number of portfolios within a complex and the complexity of their holdings.
Reporting purchases and sales by asset type would require funds to map transactions from their portfolio-management, accounting, and compliance systems to the categories used on the applicable form. Because internal existing system categories may not align with the asset-type categories used on the form, funds would need to develop mapping conventions and determine how to treat transactions that do not resemble ordinary purchases or sales of portfolio securities.
7. Recordkeeping
Under the current rule, registered funds must permanently retain their cross-trading procedures and maintain six-year records of each cross trade and the materials used for board oversight. At the same time, existing requirements under rule 31a-1, rule 38a-1, and rule 2a-5 already obligate funds to maintain a broad set of transaction, compliance, and valuation-related records, including records in detail of all purchases and sales of securities, written policies and procedures, valuation materials, and documentation supporting oversight and testing. Because rule 38a-1 already requires retention of a fund's written policies and procedures, the permanent-retention requirement for cross-trading procedures in current rule 17a-7 is duplicative. Conversely, the existing six-year recordkeeping requirement under rule 17a-7 does not capture all the types of materials that would be needed under the proposed oversight framework, such as documentation supporting annual pattern- or disposition-based testing.
Under the proposed amendments, the permanent-retention requirement would be removed, and procedural recordkeeping would be aligned with rule 38a-1. Registered funds would be required to maintain all information and materials used in the CCO's quarterly and annual reviews for a period of at least six years, such as any subsequent transaction data or other information needed to evaluate whether a registered fund may have been disadvantaged, although, for disposition-related analyses occurring many years after an original cross trade, the fund's permanent transaction records retained under rule 31a-1 and rule 31a-2 would supply the necessary data. Therefore, while the proposed amendments would require funds to retain cross-trade-specific oversight materials for six years, the long-term records needed for evaluating subsequent dispositions are already preserved under existing rules, and the proposal would not extend rule 17a-7 retention obligations beyond six years.
a. Benefits
In connection with the best-interest requirement described in III.C.4, the proposed recordkeeping amendments would help ensure that the adviser's determinations and the information used to support them are retained in a consistent and reviewable manner. This documentation would assist the adviser, the CCO, and the Commission in assessing whether cross trades complied with the rule's conditions. It would also support the proposal's oversight and testing requirements—specifically, the CCO's annual testing obligation to evaluate whether a registered fund may have been disadvantaged, which includes reviewing subsequent-transaction prices and conducting pattern- or disposition-based analyses. Aligning the procedural retention requirement with that in rule 38a-1 would eliminate a duplicative retention obligation and simplify compliance administration. The extent of these efficiencies would vary. Complexes that already maintain detailed cross trade and pricing documentation might experience limited incremental benefit, while those with less comprehensive recordkeeping practices could see more meaningful reductions in review time.
By requiring funds to maintain more comprehensive materials supporting pricing, best-interest determinations, and quarterly and annual reviews, the proposed recordkeeping amendments may reduce one-off information requests in examinations and also facilitate remedial actions, such as reversing a trade or making a fund whole, as discussed in section II.E.3, where the retained records allow the adviser and CCO to identify and substantiate any disadvantage.
b. Costs
Registered funds would need to collect and retain all materials used in the CCO's quarterly and annual reviews, including pricing data, subsequent-transaction records, analytics, and any other information needed to determine whether a registered fund may have been disadvantaged. Retaining these materials for six years would increase storage needs, although the magnitude would depend on the volume of cross-trading activity and each fund's recordkeeping systems.
Uncertainty remains regarding how much additional work the annual review would require across complexes. Registered funds that already maintain disposition-price or pattern-analysis files may face limited incremental
(
printed page 65663)
burden, while those without such processes might need more time to build the necessary documentation and workflow infrastructure.
D. Aggregate Monetized Benefits and Costs
In this section, we quantify and present aggregate monetized benefits and costs across affected entities and over time. The monetized benefits include the estimated transaction-cost savings from cross trading corporate bonds and other level 2 fixed-income assets, based on cross-trade volumes and bid-ask spreads. These estimates do not include benefits from cross trading equity securities, because equity securities generally have readily available market quotations (level 1); any equity securities that are classified as level 2 are not separately quantified due to insufficient data. We also exclude benefits from cross trading municipal securities, because municipal cross trades have continued under existing staff no-action letters. Additional potential cost savings from cross trading other level 2 assets—including certain additional fixed-income instruments or loans—cannot be quantified with available data. As a result, the monetized cross-trading benefits reported in this section should be interpreted as a lower bound. We do not quantify any potential benefits associated with the new reporting requirements on Forms N-PORT and N-MFP because we do not have data that would allow us to estimate the magnitude of these benefits—such as how standardized cross-trade reporting might affect investor decision-making, regulatory monitoring, or market liquidity.
We also quantify and include the monetized compliance costs associated with the proposed amendments to rule 17a-7, as well as the recurring internal and external costs associated with additional reporting requirements under Forms N-PORT and N-MFP, as described in the PRA. These estimates assume that each affected entity realizes the full amount of monetized benefits and costs shown; in practice, benefits and costs may vary depending on existing practices and how those practices change under the proposed amendments.

We estimate that the total aggregate annual monetized benefit is $173,018,571.
