E. Efficiency, Competition, and Capital Formation
The Commission considers the potential effects of its rules on efficiency, competition, and capital formation. This section describes the mechanisms through which the amendments could influence these areas. Potential channels include changes in how registered funds execute transactions, advisers' internal resource allocation, changes in how information is incorporated into public prices, and shifts in investor portfolio allocations in response to changes in net returns.
1. Efficiency
The proposed amendments may facilitate operational efficiency in two respects. First, by permitting cross trades of level 2 securities, the proposed amendments would allow registered funds with offsetting trading needs to internalize transactions that would otherwise be executed through external trading venues. When a registered fund internalizes a transaction, it avoids certain trading-related frictions, including bid-ask spreads, markups, and market-impact costs.
[
224
]
The extent of this efficiency would depend on how frequently registered funds have complementary trading needs in level 2 securities, where most of these frictions arise. Second, the proposed pricing conditions may reduce the operational steps required to price a cross trade. Under the current rule, cross trading in non-exchange-traded fixed-income securities—
i.e.,
securities that trade over-the-counter rather than on an exchange—historically required gathering multiple bids and offers from
(
printed page 65666)
broker-dealers through reasonable inquiry, which is a process that some assert had become more difficult as dealer willingness to provide such quotes declined. Under the proposed rule, a fund using NAV pricing would determine the cross-trade price within its existing valuation process, which is already subject to rule 2a-5 governance, rather than conducting a separate pricing exercise. A fund using current market pricing that relies on the same pricing source for both cross-trade pricing and NAV computation may be able to leverage due-diligence processes already maintained for that vendor, potentially combining that review with existing rule 2a-5 oversight. For complexes whose valuation and pricing systems already support level 2 observable inputs, these pricing provisions may lower administrative demands on compliance and trading staff.
The proposed amendments would also introduce new compliance steps that do not exist under the current rule. These include a pre-trade best-interest determination by the adviser for each cross trade, a periodic reasonableness review of current-market prices by the adviser, a quarterly CCO compliance review covering all cross trades during the preceding quarter, and an annual CCO review that includes disposition-price analysis of securities purchased in cross trades. Each of these steps would require real resources (
e.g.,
personnel time, recordkeeping infrastructure, and, in some cases, systems development) that funds do not currently expend in connection with cross trading. The magnitude of these costs would depend on the frequency and volume of cross-trading activity, the per-trade cost of making and documenting the best-interest determination, and the extent to which funds can integrate the new oversight steps into compliance processes already maintained under rule 38a-1 and rule 2a-5, as well as an adviser's obligations under the antifraud provisions of section206 of the Advisers Act.
The amendments may promote allocative efficiency by reducing the transaction costs that registered funds incur when adjusting their portfolios to reflect intended risk and return profiles. Most fixed-income securities have been ineligible for cross trading since the September 2022 compliance date of rule 2a-5. As a result, registered funds seeking to rebalance or otherwise adjust their fixed-income holdings must execute those transactions through external trading venues, incurring transaction costs even where an affiliated fund would be interested in taking the other side of the trade. By permitting cross trades of level 2 securities, the amendments may allow portfolio managers to reduce these frictions and maintain allocations that more closely reflect each fund's intended investment objectives and strategies. The timing of any such gains would depend on whether a fund's existing valuation and pricing systems already support level 2 observable inputs. Funds that already maintain these capabilities may realize gains more quickly than funds that choose to update their systems to support observable inputs.
A countervailing consideration is that level 2 securities, unlike level 1 securities, do not have readily available market quotations and are instead valued using observable inputs, either directly or indirectly. To the extent that the cross-trade price for a level 2 security does not accurately reflect the security's value, the cross trade may not move the security to the fund that most values it at a fair market price, which could reduce rather than improve allocative outcomes. The proposed pricing conditions, best-interest determination requirement, and CCO oversight provisions are designed to mitigate this risk, but their effectiveness in practice is uncertain and would depend on the quality and consistency of the pricing sources used.
Because the amended framework may make it easier for advisers to internalize certain offsetting transactions, some trades that would otherwise occur in public markets may instead be executed internally. To the extent this internalization occurs, and to the extent that market participants would otherwise have learned from the transaction, if conducted in the open market, due to information gleaned from the trading activity of the affiliated fund or the trade's counterparty (
e.g.,
a broker-dealer), the informational efficiency of prices could be reduced. In addition, reduced post-trade transparency in the market for level 2 securities such as corporate bonds due to such internalization may increase the transaction costs for trades that do continue to occur in public markets, which could result in less efficient investment allocations for investors.
[
225
]
The proposed reporting requirements on Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP, which would require registered funds to disclose aggregate cross-trading volumes by asset class, may partially offset the reduction in publicly observable transaction-level information by providing market participants with data on the scale of cross-trading activity relative to total trading activity in each asset class. The extent of this offset is uncertain and would depend on whether aggregate volume data are sufficient to inform participants' assessments of liquidity and pricing in the relevant markets. We discuss the cost implications of reduced observable pricing information in more detail in section III.C.1.b.
2. Competition
The amendments may affect competition among registered fund advisers and fund complexes through two mechanisms that operate in opposite directions. The first mechanism could lead to greater concentration of competitive advantage among larger fund complexes. Advisers with larger complexes and higher volumes of level 2 fixed-income trading are likely to have more frequent opportunities to internalize offsetting transactions and, therefore, more opportunities to realize the cost reductions the proposed amendments are designed to permit.
[
226
]
If those cost reductions are reflected in execution quality or net returns to fund shareholders, they may attract additional investor flows, increasing assets under management and further expanding the set of internalization opportunities available to larger complexes.
[
227
]
Larger fund complexes also may be able to leverage economies of scale in complying with the rule's
(
printed page 65667)
oversight and reporting requirements relative to smaller fund complexes, adding to this competitive advantage. This feedback between cost savings, net returns, and asset growth is a recognized feature of the asset-management industry and could allow scale-advantaged registered fund advisers to deepen their competitive position relative to smaller advisers that have fewer cross-trading opportunities. To the extent this mechanism operates, it could contribute to greater concentration within the registered-fund industry or shift the competitive balance among fund complexes of different sizes. The magnitude of any such effects is uncertain, but the direction of the mechanism suggests that larger complexes may benefit more than smaller advisers from the amended framework. The magnitude of any such competitive effect is uncertain and would depend on how frequently advisers of different sizes are able to generate offsetting cross-trade opportunities, and on the extent to which cost reductions ultimately benefit investors in the form of higher net returns or indirectly benefit advisers by supporting higher AUM-based fee revenue through improved performance or reduced pressure to lower advisory fees.
The second mechanism runs in the opposite direction. Several features of the proposed amendments may reduce some frictions currently associated with implementing cross-trading programs. The proposed pricing conditions would replace the current reasonable-inquiry standard (which some assert has become increasingly difficult to satisfy as dealer willingness to provide quotes has declined)
[
228
]
with two pricing methods that leverage existing valuation and vendor infrastructure. The proposed shift from board-level quarterly compliance determinations to CCO-conducted reviews would align cross-trading oversight with compliance infrastructure that funds already maintain under rule 38a-1. To the extent these changes enable advisers that previously found the compliance costs of cross trading prohibitive, including advisers with fewer resources or less developed internal systems, the resulting expansion in participation could increase competitive pressure on execution quality, pricing discipline, and governance practices across the industry. This pro-competitive effect would partially offset the scale-advantage mechanism described above.
The magnitude of any scale-advantage mechanism would depend on the distribution of cross-trading opportunities across fund complexes of different sizes, the extent to which cost reductions are reflected in net returns, and the degree to which those returns attract incremental investor flows. The magnitude of the pro-competitive mechanism would depend on whether the proposed pricing conditions and oversight framework meaningfully reduce the barriers to implementing a cross-trading program, and on the extent to which advisers that previously found those barriers prohibitive would in fact begin cross trading under the amended framework. Data on both of these questions are needed to assess each mechanism, and the Commission requests comment on both.
3. Capital Formation
The amendments may influence capital formation through several economic mechanisms, though these effects are uncertain and, to the extent they occur, are expected to arise only incrementally. Relative to the approximately $47 trillion in total assets held by registered funds, the estimated $173 million in annual transaction-cost savings represents a very small reduction in industrywide expenses. Using asset-weighted average expense ratios for registered funds, of 0.30% and 0.32%,
[
229
]
aggregate annual expenses are roughly between $140 billion to $150 billion. The estimated savings therefore amount to about 0.1 percent of total annual expenses, or approximately one basis point. If internalizing trades reduces transaction costs for registered funds and advisers, and if some portion of those savings is reflected in higher net returns for fund investors, investors could experience higher after-fee performance. This could lead some households to adjust the allocation of their existing savings toward registered funds. Because reallocations among savings vehicles do not change the total supply of household savings, this channel alone would not be expected to alter the aggregate amount of capital available to issuers. Higher net returns could also, in principle, lead some households to increase the level of their saving. Empirical research generally finds that household saving responds only weakly to changes in investment returns;
[
230
]
accordingly, even if the amendments modestly increase after-fee performance, the expected incremental effect on aggregate household saving—and thus on the supply of investable funds—is likely to be limited. To the extent any such response does occur, additional saving could place downward pressure on the cost of capital for firms by increasing the supply of investable funds, although the magnitude of this effect is expected to be small.
Reallocations of household savings could also shift investment toward assets that finance productive activity. If investors move funds from deposits or other lower-yield securities into registered funds that invest in corporate bonds or equities, increased demand for those securities could place downward pressure on required yields at the margin, thereby potentially lowering issuers' borrowing costs. This mechanism would operate only if transaction-cost reductions are passed through to investors in the form of higher net returns and if those higher returns induce the reallocations described above. At the same time, as discussed in the subsection on efficiency above, increased internalization may reduce the amount of transaction-level information reflected in public prices, which could, in turn, reduce price informativeness
(
printed page 65668)
and place upward pressure on required returns. The magnitude of each of these effects is uncertain and would depend on the factors described above. Because these channels operate through distinct mechanisms, we describe their effects qualitatively and separately.
F. Reasonable Alternatives
This section discusses reasonable alternatives to the proposed amendments, focusing on different approaches the Commission could have taken in designing the cross-trading conditions, pricing framework, and reporting requirements. For each alternative, we outline how the approach would operate and consider its potential economic effects.
1. Allowing Cross Trades in Any Security
As an alternative to the proposed rule permitting cross trades in securities with readily available market quotations or that are valued based on observable inputs, the Commission could have proposed allowing cross trades in any security without regard to the availability of market-based or observable pricing inputs. In this alternative, registered funds would have maximum flexibility to internalize trades, which would expand the set of transactions where registered funds could avoid external trading costs. To the extent that registered funds holding securities without observable inputs compute their NAVs on a daily basis, a valuation would already be computed as part of the fund's NAV process and could serve as the cross-trade price under this alternative.
Because this alternative would also permit cross trades in assets without observable inputs, its principal incremental effect would involve level 3 securities, where valuation uncertainty is greater, and transaction data are generally not observable regardless of execution venue. Permitting cross trades in these securities could therefore increase the risk of economically meaningful valuation dispersion across accounts. Valuation dispersion, for these purposes, refers to pricing differences large enough to shift value between participating accounts where valuations rely heavily on subjective, non-observable inputs, such differences may be more difficult to detect and resolve.
[
231
]
Compliance and monitoring processes could require greater investment and verifying the fairness of prices in illiquid or bespoke assets without observable inputs could become more challenging. The wider discretion afforded under this alternative could heighten the importance of managing advisers' incentives around trade direction, given that pricing for many newly eligible securities is highly subjective. This alternative could have the greatest incremental effect on BDCs, which generally hold a higher concentration of level 3 assets than registered funds and therefore would experience a larger expansion of securities eligible for cross trading under this approach. Finally, the broader scope of permissible trades under this alternative would introduce additional complexity for fund oversight personnel and fund boards.
Considering the greater valuation subjectivity associated with level 3 securities, this alternative may also necessitate additional safeguards beyond those in the proposal. For example, the Commission could require trade-by-trade board (or board committee) approval for cross trades in such securities, or enhanced documentation, escalation, and post-trade review processes to verify pricing fairness. These additional measures would aim to mitigate the heightened risk of valuation dispersion and adviser conflicts that would accompany permitting cross trades in securities without observable inputs.
This alternative could also affect competitive conditions if advisers differ in their ability to support more complex valuation or monitoring processes, and changes in the availability of transaction information may influence broader informational efficiency in the markets.
2. Alternative Approaches to Pricing Cross Trades
As an alternative to the two-method pricing framework proposed in the amendments, the Commission could have proposed a fully prescriptive single-method pricing requirement or, in contrast, a principles-based pricing regime that relies primarily on adviser discretion. At the most prescriptive end, the Commission could have proposed that all cross trades be valued using a single uniform method. For example, the Commission could have mandated use of the NAV price or for registered funds that do not compute NAV on a daily basis or for which a current NAV is not available at the time of execution, a price determined consistent with the procedures and methodologies used under rule 2a-5 for determining fair value (or, for securities with readily available market quotations, at current market value). A uniform pricing mandate would provide greater consistency in the required pricing approach across advisers and complexes and could reduce oversight and compliance burdens for registered funds already computing daily NAVs. It may also simplify monitoring for boards, examiners, and investors, given that all trades would rely on a single, standardized workflow. At the same time, however, a pricing regime limited to NAV or values determined consistently with a fund's NAV processes under rules 2a-4 and 2a-5 could constrain cross-trading activity for registered funds that rely on intraday information to make a best interest determination regarding whether an intraday cross trade is appropriate. For certain securities, advisers may conclude that the mandated method does not adequately reflect time-sensitive or security-specific information, and therefore may decide not to engage in cross trades even when such trades could otherwise be efficient.
[
232
]
A uniform pricing requirement may also have distributional effects if advisers with portfolios that align poorly with the mandated method, such as closed-end funds that do not calculate NAV daily, face operational adjustments or reduced pricing accuracy.
At the opposite end of the spectrum, the Commission could have proposed a principles-based pricing regime under which advisers set cross-trade prices according to board-approved valuation policies without any prescribed pricing method in the rule. For example, advisers could be permitted to select among intraday evaluated prices, executable dealer quotes, pricing-service feeds, or model-based estimates, or even adviser-originated prices, with the selection made based on the adviser's judgment of prevailing market conditions and the pricing information available at the time. The adviser would be required to document the basis for each pricing selection.
(
printed page 65669)
This could provide adaptability across market conditions and asset classes and allow advisers to incorporate the most relevant inputs available at the time of the trade. However, greater flexibility would likely require more robust controls and oversight to manage adviser discretion, particularly because, although advisers would still be subject to a best-interest obligation, the alternative would rely on adviser-performed pricing-reasonableness checks at the time of the trade rather than on periodic reasonableness reviews required under the proposed rule. Differences in advisers' valuation procedures and resources could also reduce comparability across registered funds and complicate investor assessments.
3. Trade-Level Reporting Alternatives for Cross Trades
As alternatives to the proposed reporting amendments, the Commission considered two distinct reporting frameworks for cross-trading activity: (1) public trade-level reporting of each cross trade, and (2) confidential trade-level reporting submitted only to the Commission.
Under the first alternative, the Commission could have required registered funds to provide anonymized trade-level reporting of each cross trade to a publicly available transaction-reporting mechanism, similar to the way corporate and municipal bond trades are currently reported to the TRACE and RTRS systems. Such a reporting system could capture and publish information such as the timing, price, and volume of each cross trade while shielding the identity of the fund complexes or accounts involved in the transaction. Public trade-level reporting would give investors and third-party analysts insight into the use of cross trades across registered funds. It would also provide additional pricing signals to the market that may enhance the informational efficiency of market prices for cross-traded securities and improve valuation models for those securities. Trade-level reporting would allow both market participants and regulators to monitor and evaluate the prices at which cross trades occur, providing a potential disciplining effect that might help ensure that registered funds and their advisers effect cross trades at prices that are most favorable under the circumstances for each fund to both sides of the transaction. In addition, if regulators were given private access to the identities of the counterparties involved in a cross trade along with the publicly available pricing information, it could improve monitoring of pricing quality and adherence to cross-trading conditions. However, generating trade-level submissions would require additional operational investment. Registered funds would need to implement systems capable of capturing, validating, and reconciling trade-level records on an ongoing basis. High-volume complexes could face higher recurring burdens, while smaller registered funds might experience relatively higher costs per trade, potentially discouraging the use of cross trades altogether.
[
233
]
These costs could be mitigated to the extent that the systems developed and maintained by funds to comply with the proposed rule's recordkeeping requirements could be leveraged for trade-level reporting purposes. Finally, adopting a trade level reporting mechanism would also raise separate operational, design, and cost considerations not contemplated by the proposed reporting amendments. For example, while registered funds have existing infrastructure for reporting on Forms N-PORT and N-MFP, funds and their advisers are not currently connected to systems like TRACE and RTRS. As a result, there would be costs associated with creating such connections, including operational, legal, and technology costs and potential costs associated with engaging a third-party vendor.
[
234
]
Under the second alternative, the Commission could have proposed requiring registered funds to provide detailed trade-level reports of each cross trade exclusively to the Commission on a confidential basis. This alternative could be structured either as a substitute for the proposed aggregate reporting or as a complement to it, in which case both requirements would apply simultaneously. Under this approach, regulators would retain access to rich trade-level data for oversight and analysis. Confidential trade-level reporting would provide regulators with granular supervisory data—including the timing, pricing, counterparty identity, and volume of individual cross trades—that aggregate monthly reporting does not supply. This additional detail could enhance the Commission's ability to detect pricing anomalies, identify patterns of potential self-dealing, and assess compliance with the rule's conditions at the transaction level. Confidential submission would also reduce reputational risk for registered funds engaging in unusually large or uncommon cross trades, because the transaction-level detail would not be publicly available.
The incremental costs of this alternative relative to the proposed aggregate reporting would stem primarily from the operational requirements of trade-level data capture and submission. Registered funds would need systems capable of generating, validating, and transmitting individual transaction records rather than monthly aggregates, and high-volume complexes would face recurring burdens proportional to their cross-trading activity. The submission mechanism itself would also require design and implementation investment beyond what the proposed reporting amendments contemplate, since the form is not currently structured for this type of transaction-level reporting. Finally, confidential trade-level reporting could expose funds to the risk that this data is inadvertently exposed to external parties. To the extent that confidential trade-level reporting were adopted in addition to the proposed aggregate public disclosure, these costs would be additional to the costs of the proposed amendments, rather than a substitute for them.
If adopted as a substitute for the proposed aggregate public reporting, confidential trade-level reporting would reduce public transparency.
[
235
]
Investors, researchers, and third-party analysts would have limited insight into registered funds' cross-trading practices, and the informational benefits of standardized reporting would be narrower. To the extent that public disclosure of cross-trading activity would also help improve price informativeness in public markets for securities that are cross traded, a less transparent option would forego such benefits.

B. Rule 17a-7
Rule 17a-7 provides an exemption from section 17(a) of the Investment Company Act for purchases and sales of securities between registered funds and eligible affiliates. The exemption is subject to conditions intended to reduce the likelihood of overreaching.
The current rule requires that the fund maintain and preserve permanently a written copy of the procedures adopted by the board. Under the rule, the board is required to determine, at least on a quarterly basis, that all affiliated transactions effected during the preceding quarter in reliance on the rule were made in compliance with these established procedures. The rule requires the fund to maintain written records of this board determination and each rule 17a-7 transaction for a period of not less than six years.

V. Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis
The Commission has prepared the following Initial Regulatory Flexibility Analysis (“IRFA”) in accordance with section 3(a) of the Regulatory Flexibility Act (“RFA”).
[

]
It relates to the proposed amendments to rule 17a-7, Form N-PORT, and Form N-MFP.
A. Reason for and Objectives of the Rule and Form Amendments
The Commission proposes to modernize and enhance rule 17a-7 primarily by expanding the types of securities that are eligible to be cross traded, updating the rule's pricing conditions, and replacing the rule's current board oversight requirements with a framework that is intended to allocate oversight responsibility in an effective manner and enhance investor protection. The amendments also include changes to the rule's recordkeeping requirements and provisions regarding certain payments in connection with cross trades. In addition, the Commission proposes to amend Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP to require registered funds that engaged in cross trades in reliance on rule 17a-7 during the preceding twelve-month period to report aggregate information, by asset class (or category of investment, in the case of Form N-MFP), about the value of securities a registered fund bought or sold, as well as the value of securities bought or sold in cross trades, during the reporting period.
[
248
]
The objectives of the amendments are to broaden registered funds' abilities to engage in cross trades that are beneficial to funds and their shareholders (
e.g.,
by
(
printed page 65674)
avoiding certain transaction costs) while enhancing investor protections around these activities through effective oversight and additional transparency. Each of these objectives is discussed in detail in section II above.
B. Legal Basis
The Commission proposes the rule and form amendments contained in this document under the authority set forth in the Investment Company Act, particularly sections 6(c), 8, 17, 24, 30, 31, and 38 [
15 U.S.C. 80a-1
et seq.
].
C. Small Entities Subject to Rule and Form Amendments
For purposes of Commission rulemaking in connection with the Regulatory Flexibility Act, an investment company is a small entity if, together with other investment companies in the same group of related investment companies, it has net assets of $50 million or less as of the end of its most recent fiscal year.
[
249
]
Commission staff estimates that, as of December 31, 2025, there are approximately 62 registered funds that are small entities. This includes 20 registered open-end mutual funds (including 1 money market fund), 7 registered ETFs, 34 registered closed-end funds, and 1 UIT that are small entities. Additionally, as of the same date, there are approximately 5 BDCs that are small entities.
D. Projected Reporting, Recordkeeping, and Other Compliance Requirements
The proposed amendments include reporting, recordkeeping, and other compliance requirements that would apply to small entities that rely on rule 17a-7 to conduct cross trades. We lack reliable data to estimate how many of the registered funds and BDCs that are small entities would choose to engage in cross trades under the proposed amendments. Because rule 17a-7 is an exemptive rule, registered funds are not required to engage in cross-trading activity. As a result, we expect that a registered fund—including a small entity—would choose to conduct cross trades under the proposed amendments to the extent that the benefits of cross trading (
e.g.,
the avoided transaction costs) would justify the regulatory costs (
e.g.,
the reporting, recordkeeping, and other compliance costs). We recognize that, due to economies of scale, smaller funds may be less likely to rely on rule 17a-7 to engage in cross trading as a general matter. This is because smaller funds may be less likely to benefit from cross trading (for example, due to fewer trading opportunities with eligible affiliates relative to larger funds). Due to the potential for smaller benefits, small entities likewise may be less willing to experience regulatory costs to be able to cross trade.
1. Reporting
Under the proposed amendments to Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP, registered funds that report on the forms and that engaged in cross trades of portfolio investments in reliance on rule 17a-7 during the preceding twelve-month period would be required to report the aggregate value of portfolio investments purchased or sold during the reporting period, calculated on a gross basis, and by asset type (or category of investment, in the case of Form N-MFP). Such registered funds also would be required to report the aggregate value of portfolio investments purchased or sold in cross trades in reliance on rule 17a-7 during the reporting period, by asset type (or category of investment). This information would assist investors, the Commission, and its staff in understanding the volume and nature of cross-trading activity across the registered fund industry. Further, the transparency provided by the reporting may help mitigate the potential conflicts of cross trading.
This reporting requirement would impose burdens on all Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP reporting funds that engage in cross trading, including those that are small entities. The specifics of these burdens are discussed in the Economic Analysis and Paperwork Reduction Act sections above. These sections also discuss the professional skills associated with complying with these requirements. The costs of compliance with the forms' reporting requirements would vary based on whether a registered fund engages in cross trading and, if so, the scope of those activities (
e.g.,
whether occurring in a single asset class or across multiple asset classes). As discussed above, we expect that registered funds that are small entities are less likely to engage in cross trades than larger funds. However, to the extent that small entities engage in cross trades, the compliance costs of Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP reporting likely would not be meaningfully different for smaller versus larger funds.
2. Recordkeeping
Registered funds that conduct cross trades under rule 17a-7 currently are required to maintain certain records related to their cross trades. In addition to requiring maintenance of those records, the proposed amendments would amend the recordkeeping requirements to require registered funds to maintain records of the information or materials the CCO uses to make the required determinations in connection with its quarterly and annual reviews and the CCO's reports to the board. The proposed amendments are designed to show compliance with the proposed amendments to rule 17a-7, help establish that a cross trade was in the best interests of the registered fund (rather than giving special treatment to affiliated party), and provide important information about cross-trading activity to Commission staff in connection with examinations.
The proposed recordkeeping amendments would impose burdens on all funds, including those that are small entities. We discuss the specifics of these burdens in the Economic Analysis and Paperwork Reduction Act sections above. These sections also discuss the professional skills associated with complying with these requirements. Small entities that currently rely on rule 17a-7 would already have recordkeeping systems related to their cross trades, but small entities that would newly engage in cross trades under the proposed rule may not have recordkeeping systems related to cross trades. As a result, the burdens of the recordkeeping requirements may differ between small entities based on whether they previously engaged in cross trading under the rule. Further, while small entities would already have recordkeeping systems related to their cross trades, those systems may need to be updated to the extent that the proposed amendments require different records from current practice. We would expect larger funds or funds that are part of a large fund complex to incur higher costs related to the new recordkeeping requirements in absolute terms relative to a smaller fund or a fund that is part of a smaller fund complex. However, we would expect a smaller fund to find it more costly, per dollar managed, to comply with the proposed recordkeeping requirements because it would not be able to benefit from a larger fund complex's economies of scale.
3. Oversight Requirements
The proposed amendments would require the fund's CCO, rather than the
(
printed page 65675)
fund's board, periodically to review the fund's cross trades, while still requiring oversight by the fund's board. Specifically, the proposed amendments would require a registered fund's CCO to conduct quarterly and annual reviews and to report the results of those reviews to the board. The quarterly review would involve a review of all cross trades during the period to determine their compliance with the rule. The annual review would involve a review of cross trades during the period, and other transactions by the fund or information necessary to evaluate the cross trades (including timing and price of any subsequent sales of securities purchased in cross trades), to determine if cross trades may have disadvantaged the registered fund relative to the eligible affiliate. The proposed amendments would eliminate provisions in the current rule that place additional requirements on fund boards, including to make at least quarterly determinations that cross trades were done in compliance with the fund's procedures and to adopt cross-trade procedures. The proposed amendments are designed to better align oversight requirements to business responsibilities, reduce burden on fund boards, and remove duplication with rule 38a-1.
The proposed CCO review and board reporting amendments would impose burdens on all funds, including those that are small entities. We discuss the specifics of these burdens in the Economic Analysis and Paperwork Reduction Act sections above. These sections also discuss the professional skills associated with complying with these requirements. We anticipate that the burdens associated with the proposed CCO review and board reporting requirements would vary depending on the volume and scope of a fund's cross-trading activities. To the extent that registered funds that are small entities engage in smaller volumes of cross trades relative to larger funds, as we anticipate would generally be the case, the burdens of the CCO review and board reporting requirements for small entities should likewise be smaller.
E. Duplicative, Overlapping, or Conflicting Federal Rules
The Commission has not identified any Federal rules that duplicate, overlap, or conflict with the proposed amendments.
F. Significant Alternatives
The RFA directs the Commission to consider significant alternatives that would accomplish our stated objectives, while minimizing any significant economic impact on small entities. We considered the following alternatives for small entities in relation to the proposed requirements to enhance the benefits of the proposal for small entities: (1) establishing different requirements that take into account the resources available to small entities; (2) exempting small entities from all or part of the requirements; (3) clarifying, consolidating, or simplifying requirements under the proposed rule for small entities; and (4) using performance rather than design standards.
Although we are not proposing different requirements for small entities, including consolidated or simplified requirements specifically for small entities, some aspects of the proposal, such as the ability to use NAV pricing to price cross trades, may help reduce compliance costs for small entities. Many registered funds, including many that are small entities, already compute their NAVs on a daily basis and have existing processes around these valuations. Rather than requiring a separate process for determining the price of cross trades, the proposed rule would allow registered funds to leverage their existing valuation processes to price cross trades. We are not proposing to allow only small entities to use NAV pricing because we view it as a fair and appropriate way to price cross trades generally, regardless of fund size.
With respect to consolidated or simplified requirements, we considered simplifying the oversight framework in the proposed rule for small entities. For example, rather than requiring separate quarterly and annual reviews, we considered requiring small entity CCOs to review and report to the board at least annually whether cross trades conducted during the review period complied with the rule and may have disadvantaged the fund relative to eligible affiliates. This annual review and report cadence would align with other review and reporting obligations for fund CCOs under rule 38a-1 and may reduce burdens on small entities by requiring less frequent reviews and reports to the fund's board. If small entities engage in cross trades infrequently and in small sizes, this annual review cadence may be effective at addressing conflict of interest and overreach concerns without undermining investor protection. However, the size of a registered fund does not necessarily dictate the frequency and volume of its cross trades. As a result, there is a risk that an annual review requirement would not be effective for all small entities, particularly those that engage in cross trading at some frequency. Thus, we propose the same oversight requirements for all registered funds, regardless of size, but request comment on whether the oversight requirements should be consolidated or simplified for small entities.
The conditions necessary to rely on proposed rule 17a-7, and the associated reporting and recordkeeping requirements, are designed to allow registered funds to engage in a broader range of cross trades where such trades are beneficial to fund shareholders, while preventing cross trades that involve overreaching or other investor protection concerns. We are not proposing to exempt small entities from some or all these requirements because the investor protection benefits should apply to investors in smaller funds as well as investors in larger funds. We considered exempting registered funds that are small entities from the proposed requirement to report aggregate cross trading on Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP. If small entities engage in cross trades infrequently and in small sizes, the value of the reported information would be less significant than for larger funds that cross trade more frequently and in larger amounts. At the same time, the size of a registered fund does not necessarily dictate the frequency and volume of its cross trades. In addition, even though a small entity's cross-trading activity is likely small relative to the overall market, that does not mean the activity is insignificant to the fund itself. Because we propose to mitigate the costs of Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP reporting by requiring aggregate cross-trading information, and because a small entity may engage in levels of cross trades that are significant in the context of that particular fund, we propose to require small entities to report cross-trading information on Form N-PORT and Form N-MFP. However, we are requesting comment on whether small entities should be excluded from the proposed amendments to these forms.
With respect to the use of performance rather than design standards, the proposed rule includes a mix of performance and design standards. For instance, the proposed rule includes performance standards in the current market pricing provision and in the provisions regarding CCO reviews. These provisions identify the objectives that funds must achieve (
e.g.,
using a price that reasonably represents the current market price, and reviewing cross trades for compliance with the rule) without mandating the particular approach to achieving the objectives. The proposed rule also includes some
(
printed page 65676)
design standards. For example, the proposed rule identifies the scope of securities that registered funds could cross trade under the rule. As discussed above, limiting the scope of securities under the rule is designed to prevent overreaching and ensure that there is independent pricing information about securities that registered funds are permitted to cross trade. We are not proposing to use solely performance standards in the proposed rule because cross trades involve conflicts of interest, and thus the conditions of the proposed rule must be specifically designed to protect investors from the overreaching that can result from such conflicts.
G. Request for Comment
The Commission requests comments regarding this IRFA. We request comments on the number of small entities that may be affected by our proposed amendments and whether the proposed amendments would have any effects not considered in this analysis. We request that commenters describe the nature of any effects on small entities subject to the rules and forms, and provide empirical data to support the nature and extent of such effects. We also request comment on the proposed compliance burdens and the effect these burdens would have on smaller entities.
VI. Congressional Review Act

§ 270.17a-7
Exemption of certain purchase or sale transactions between an investment company and certain affiliated persons thereof.
(a)
Exemption for certain cross trades.
If the conditions of paragraph (b) of this section are satisfied, a purchase or sale transaction between a fund and an eligible affiliate is exempt from section 17(a) of the Act.
(b)
Conditions.
(1) The transaction is a purchase or sale of a security for which market quotations are readily available or that would be valued by the fund based on inputs that are observable, either directly or indirectly.
(2) The transaction is effected at the independent current market price of the security. For purposes of this paragraph, the “independent current market price” is:
(i) The value the fund ascribes to the security in its next computation of the fund's current net asset value under section 2(a)(41) of the Act (
15 U.S.C. 80a-2(a)(41)
) and §§ 270.2a-4 and 270.2a-5 on the business day on which the transaction occurs; or
(ii) The price determined by the fund's investment adviser to reasonably represent the current market price for the security using one or more unaffiliated pricing sources, provided that the adviser periodically reviews the reasonableness of prices used under this paragraph (b)(2)(ii).
(3) The transaction involves no consideration, other than cash payment against prompt delivery of a security, and no remuneration is paid in connection with the transaction, other than
de minimis
payments to unaffiliated parties for services provided for clearing, settlement, custody, recording, or reporting of the transaction.
(4) The transaction is consistent with the fund's policies and investment strategies, as recited in its registration statement and reports filed under the Act.
(5) The fund's investment adviser determines prior to the transaction that it is in the best interest of the fund.
(6) The fund's board of directors satisfies the fund governance standards defined in § 270.0-1(a)(7).
(7) The fund's chief compliance officer:
(i) Reviews no less frequently than quarterly all transactions during the preceding quarter that were effected under this section to determine their compliance with this section;
(ii) Reviews no less frequently than annually transactions during the preceding period that were effected under this section, as well as other transactions by the fund or information necessary to evaluate transactions effected under this section (including the timing and price of a subsequent sale of a security purchased under this section), to determine whether any such transaction, or pattern of transactions, may have disadvantaged the fund relative to the eligible affiliate(s); and
(iii) Reports to the fund's board of directors no less frequently than
(
printed page 65677)
quarterly on the results of the review under paragraph (b)(7)(i) of this section and no less frequently than annually on the results of the review under paragraph (b)(7)(ii) of this section.
(c)
Recordkeeping.
The fund must maintain and preserve for a period not less than six years from the end of the fiscal year in which any transactions effected under this section occurred, the first two years in an easily accessible place, a written record of:
(1) Each transaction, setting forth a description of the security purchased or sold, the identity of the eligible affiliate on the other side of the transaction, and the terms of the purchase or sale transaction;
(2) The information or materials upon which the determination described in paragraph (b)(7)(i) of this section was made, including information or materials used to determine that each condition under paragraph (b)(1) through (6) of this section was satisfied with respect to each transaction;
(3) The information or materials upon which the determination described in paragraph (b)(7)(ii) of this section was made, including information or materials related to other transactions or information reviewed under paragraph (b)(7)(ii) of this section; and
(4) The reports to the fund's board of directors provided under paragraph (b)(7)(iii) of this section.
(d)
Definitions.
For purposes of this section:
Eligible affiliate
means, with respect to a fund:
(i) Another fund that is an affiliated person, or an affiliated person of an affiliated person, of such fund; and
(ii) A person that is an affiliated person, or an affiliated person of an affiliated person, of the fund solely by reason of having a common investment adviser, investment advisers that are affiliated persons of each other, common directors, and/or common officers.
Fund
means a registered investment company, including any separate series thereof.
Unaffiliated
means a person other than:
(i) An affiliated person or promoter of, or principal underwriter for, a fund; or
(ii) Any affiliated person of such person, promoter, or principal underwriter.
